CEM43 Cumulative equivalent minutes at 43 °C: a thermal dose that combines how hot tissue got and for how long. See Thermal. ITRUSST The International Transcranial Ultrasonic Stimulation Safety and Standards consortium. Its consensus documents define the non-significant-risk (NSR) levels the PRESTUS report compares against (e.g. MI ≤ 1.9, temperature rise ≤ 2 °C). See Reading your results.

items.title: Head Model
items.text: Segmentation Dividing the MRI into tissue types. PRESTUS uses SimNIBS charm. m2m folder The SimNIBS output folder of a subject (m2m_sub-XXX, under path.seg). PRESTUS reads it but never writes into it. Medium What the ultrasound travels through: water (free water), layered (a head from the segmentation, with layers such as skin, skull, and brain), or phantom (a designed test object). See Medium Setup. Medium properties Sound speed, density, attenuation, and thermal properties of each tissue (medium_properties). Pseudo-CT An image of skull density estimated from a special MRI (UTE/PETRA). It gives each skull voxel its own properties instead of one value per layer. See pseudo-CT. Placement mode (placement.mode) How the transducer position and target are obtained: typed in (manual), given in MNI coordinates (mni), searched automatically (heuristic, plantus, tus_entry), or read from neuronavigation (localite). See Placement. Voxel, RAS, MNI Three ways to give a position: as an index into the T1 image (voxel), in millimetres in the participant's scanner space (RAS), or in millimetres in a standard brain template (MNI). See Coordinate systems.

items.title: Simulation
items.text: k-Wave The open-source acoustic simulation toolbox that PRESTUS uses by default. BabelBrain and jwave are alternatives (Backends). Grid The 3D box of points on which the simulation is computed. grid.resolution_mm is the spacing between points: finer grids are more accurate but slower and need more memory. PPW Points per wavelength: how finely the grid samples the ultrasound wave. PRESTUS warns below 6. PML Perfectly matched layer: an absorbing border around the grid that stops waves from reflecting off its edges. Axisymmetric A 2D simulation that assumes the setup is rotationally symmetric around the beam axis. Much faster, for free water and simple tests. Acoustic FOV An optional smaller sub-grid around the beam for the acoustic simulation, to save time and memory (Partial FOV). Sonication protocol (timing.*) How the ultrasound is switched on and off: pulse duration (PD), pulse repetition interval (PRI), pulse train duration (PTD), and its repetitions (PTRI, PTRD). Needed for thermal simulations. code_type Which k-Wave implementation runs the simulation: MATLAB or C++, on CPU or GPU. A GPU makes head simulations much faster. Platform (platform) Where the run happens: in your MATLAB session (matlab) or as a job on a cluster (slurm, qsub). See Running on a cluster.

items.title: Files and Runs
items.text: Study config Your YAML file with the settings that differ from the defaults (Configuring a study). Output affix (io.output_affix) A label added to output file names, to keep several runs of the same subject apart (it appears as _desc-<label>). Cache Intermediate results (cache/ in the output folder) that PRESTUS reuses to skip work on re-runs. Study manifest A table with one row per run (subject, condition, and per-run settings) for running many subjects at once (Group analysis).

items.title: Group Analysis
items.text:
A study simulates many subjects or conditions, and comparing them needs the same settings applied to every run and the results collected in one place. PRESTUS runs every row of a study table with its own settings, measures per run how well the focus hits the target, and summarises the runs in group MNI maps and a group report. The report and the maps never run simulations; they read the per-run outputs that already exist on disk.

On this page:

  • Targeting Accuracy: how far each simulated focus lies from the planned focus, an MNI target, and an MNI ROI.
  • Group MNI Maps: focal-volume overlap, mean and SD intensity, and mean heating per condition.
  • Group HTML Report: one interactive report across runs, with a one-row-per-run CSV.

At a glance

  • When you need it: For studies with more than a handful of runs.
  • Before you start: A study config that works for one subject.

Running many subjects or conditions from a study manifest is described in Study Setup.

items.title: Targeting Accuracy
items.text:
With modules.run_targeting_analysis: 1 (default, layered or phantom media, run_nifti_creation on), each run writes sub-XXX_<medium><affix>_targeting.csv next to its per-subject CSV. The analysis reads the focal-mask NIfTIs and never fails the pipeline; unavailable measures are NaN. Targets and ROIs can differ per run: set analysis.target_mni_mm or analysis.target_roi_mni as manifest columns. With several transducers, the planned focus and beam axis of transducer(1) are used.

Targeting CSV columns Columns Meaning condition, placement_mode, target_label, transducer_name, n_transducers, focal_distance_ep_planned_mm, target_isppa_wcm2 The run's settings, shown in the report's study design table. focal_centroid_ras_*, peak_ras_* Centroid of the −3 dB focal volume (brain-masked) and the intensity peak inside it, in T1 RAS mm. planned_focus_ras_*, planned_trans_ras_* Focus and transducer positions resolved by placement, recorded before the grid stage, in RAS mm. focus_error_mm Distance between the focal centroid and the planned focus. focus_error_axial_mm, focus_error_lateral_mm That error along and across the planned beam axis (transducer → planned focus); axial > 0 means the simulated focus is deeper than planned. peak_error_mm Distance between the peak and the planned focus. focal_centroid_mni_*, peak_mni_* The same positions in MNI mm (needs io.save_MNI). target_mni_*, target_mni_source The intended MNI target: analysis.target_mni_mm, else the MNI target of the placement mode (placement.heuristic / placement.plantus .mni_target_mm, placement.mni.focus_pos_mm). target_error_mni_mm, peak_target_error_mni_mm Distance from the MNI focal centroid (or peak) to the MNI target. roi_volume_mm3, roi_overlap_mm3, roi_focal_fraction, roi_coverage, roi_mean_intensity, roi_max_intensity, roi_centroid_dist_mm With analysis.target_roi_mni (an MNI NIfTI mask, any grid): ROI volume, overlap with the focal volume, fraction of the focal volume inside the ROI, fraction of the ROI covered, intensity in the ROI (intensity_quantity = Ipa, else Itp), and the distance between the centroids.

The same analysis runs post hoc with targeting_analysis(parameters, 'PlannedFocus', f, 'PlannedTrans', t) (T1 voxel positions).

items.title: Group MNI Maps
items.text:
Experimental

The group maps and the group report are experimental: their layout, file names, and summary statistics may change between releases. Check group values against the per-run outputs before you report them.

prestus_group_report_start builds these by default ('Maps', false to skip), for layered media only (simulation.medium containing layered in the study or subject config); other media get the report without maps. They use each run's MNI NIfTIs and are computed per condition, or across all runs when there are no conditions. <out> is <path.sim>/group/<study.name>/ for a study and <path.sim>/group/<medium><affix>/ otherwise.

File in <out>/maps/ Content group_<cond>_focal_overlap_3dB.nii.gz Fraction of runs whose −3 dB focal volume covers each voxel (0–1). group_<cond>_<Ipa\|Itp>_mean.nii.gz, …_sd.nii.gz Voxelwise mean and SD intensity (Ipa when every run has it, else Itp when every run has that; no intensity maps otherwise). group_<cond>_heatrise_mean.nii.gz Mean temperature rise (when every run has heating maps).

<out>/plots/group_<cond>_focal_overlap.png shows three orthogonal MNI slices through the overlap peak, with the ROI outline, the per-run focal centroids, and the targets. The background is the mean MNI-space T1 of the subjects (<parent of path.seg>/mni/sub-XXX/T1_to_MNI_post-hoc.nii.gz, or the copy inside m2m_sub-XXX/toMNI/ of earlier outputs, when present). Runs whose MNI grid differs from the first run's are skipped with a warning.

items.title: Group HTML Report
items.text:
prestus_group_report_start('config/config_pilot.yaml');           % study: runs from the manifest
prestus_group_report_start('config/config_single.yaml');            % no manifest: auto-discover subjects
prestus_group_report_start('config/config_single.yaml', [1 2 3 5]); % explicit subject list
prestus_group_report_start(cfg, [], 'Maps', false);                 % report only
Mode Runs Written to Study (study.manifest set) Included manifest rows <path.sim>/group/<name>/group_<name>_report.html, group_<name>_runs.csv, plots/, maps/ Subjects All subjects in path.sim with sub-XXX_<medium><affix>.csv (or the given list) <path.sim>/group_<medium>_report<affix>.html, group_<medium>_runs<affix>.csv, group_plots/

With modules.generate_group_report: 1, prestus_pipeline rebuilds the subject-mode report after each subject (best-effort, without group maps). Runs started by prestus_study_start skip this and build one study report at the end.

The report reads each run's sub-XXX_<medium><affix>.csv (last row) and, when present, the targeting sidecar and the per-subject PNGs. Runs without a CSV are listed as missing. It opens with a safety banner for runs above any ITRUSST non-significant-risk reference level, a group safety dashboard, and a per-run filter; condition comparison and targeting sections appear when the study has conditions or targeting sidecars.

Report sections
  • Header: study, manifest, runs, subjects, conditions, missing runs, medium, and a link to the one-row-per-run CSV.
  • Safety banner: runs above any ITRUSST non-significant-risk reference level, with links to their rows.
  • Filter: checkboxes per run and per-condition buttons. The dashboard, roster, and cards update live; box plots and figures show the full set.
  • Group safety dashboard and other metrics: mean ± SD, range, and N per ITRUSST metric, coloured by the worst run against the NSR limit. The Mechanical sub-grid shows both MI (free water) and MItc tiles; the tile that does not apply to the medium is greyed out.
  • Study design (study, or more than one condition): runs per condition, the manifest keys and how many values each takes, and each run's placement mode, target, transducer, planned depth, target intensity, and manifest settings.
  • Condition comparison (more than one condition): mean ± SD (n) of the key metrics per condition, plus box plots. It is descriptive only: runs of one subject under several conditions are not independent.
  • Targeting accuracy (targeting sidecars present): focus and MNI-target errors, ROI measures per condition and per run, and a figure of the MNI centroids and the axial/lateral error.
  • Group MNI maps (when built): overlap figures and links to the NIfTIs.
  • Outliers: runs whose value lies far from their condition's median (modified z-score 0.6745·(x − median)/MAD, |z| > 3.5; Iglewicz & Hoaglin, 1993), for conditions with at least 5 runs. They are also flagged in the roster.
  • Data analysis: client-side distribution, correlation, and by-group views (group by subject, condition, placement mode, target, or transducer when they vary).
  • Roster: one sortable row per run with key metrics, NSR and outlier flags, and a link to the run's own report.
  • Group acoustic and thermal summaries: box plots (ISPPA per tissue, MI per tissue; maximum temperature, temperature rise, and CEM43 when thermal results exist).
  • Per-run cards: the run's settings and figures.
  • Configuration summary: of the loaded (study) config. Per-run settings are in the study design table.
Older entry point (prestus_group_start)

prestus_group_start(subject_list, config) runs prestus_group_report_start (group MNI maps + report). Plot options of earlier versions are ignored; for an ROI, set analysis.target_roi_mni. ROI statistics (intensity in the ROI, overlap, centroid distance) are part of the targeting analysis.

items.title: Study Setup
items.text:
A study runs many simulations, one per subject, target, or condition. A study manifest lists them with one row per run and the settings that vary, so one config and one command run them all, locally or on a cluster.

On this page:

  • Study Setup: the manifest, running a study, its columns, output names, and importing runs from Localite.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To run several subjects or conditions with one config.
  • Before you start: A working single-run study config (Configuring a Study).

items.title: Study Setup
items.text:
A study is a normal PRESTUS config (the study config) whose study.manifest names a table with one row per run. The study config holds everything the runs share. The manifest holds what differs between runs.

# config_pilot.yaml (study config)
path:
  sim: /project/sims
  seg: /project/simnibs
  anat: /project/simnibs
  t1_pattern: 'm2m_sub-%1$03d/T1.nii.gz'
simulation:
  medium: layered
transducer:
  serial: CTX_500_026
  target_isppa_wcm2: 30
placement:
  mode: localite
study:
  manifest: study.tsv      # relative to this config's folder
  name: pilot            # outputs in <path.sim>/group/pilot/

# study.tsv: one row per run; tab-separated (.tsv) or comma-separated (.csv)
subject_id  condition  placement.localite.session  placement.localite.target  transducer.target_isppa_wcm2  analysis.target_mni_mm
1           L_M1       ses-02                      L_M1                                                     [-38, -20, 58]
1           R_M1       ses-02                      R_M1                                                     [38, -20, 58]
2           L_M1       ses-02                      L_M1                       20                            [-38, -20, 58]

items.title: Running a Study
items.text:
prestus_study_start('config/config_pilot.yaml', 'DryRun', true)   % load + check every row, print the plan
prestus_study_start('config/config_pilot.yaml')                   % run / submit all included rows
prestus_study_start(cfg, 'Subjects', [1 3], 'Conditions', "L_M1")   % a subset
prestus_study_start(cfg, 'Rows', 1, 'Platform', 'matlab', ...
    'Overrides', {'grid.resolution_mm', 2})                         % quick debug run of one row
Dry run, platform, and the study report
  • Config errors surface first. All selected rows are loaded before anything runs. The dry run prints each row's placement mode, target, transducer, planned depth, target intensity, and platform, and writes <path.sim>/group/<name>/log/plan_<time>.tsv. A real launch writes launch_<time>.tsv with the job ID and status per row.
  • Platform. Each run is started with prestus_pipeline_start and its own platform. On matlab the rows run one after another; a failing row is logged and the others continue (unless 'StopOnError', true). On slurm/qsub there is one job per row, or a job graph for uncertainty, multi-ISPPA, and async rows.
  • One report at the end. Study runs switch off the per-subject group report (modules.generate_group_report = 0). prestus_study_start applies this after the manifest columns, so a manifest column cannot switch it back on; its 'Overrides' option can. The per-subject simulation report (modules.generate_report) is not affected. The study report is built once at the end: directly on matlab, and on HPC as a dependent CPU job (afterany, so it also runs when some subject jobs fail). Rows that submit a job graph return no single final job ID; for those, run prestus_group_report_start(cfg) once their jobs have finished.

items.title: Manifest Columns
items.text:
subject_id is the only required column; any dotted config key sets a per-run value.

Column reference and cell syntax Column Meaning subject_id Required. Integer, 003 or sub-003. condition Optional run label (target, protocol, session, …). Becomes the run's output affix and the grouping variable in the group report. include Optional 1/0, true/false, yes/no; default 1. config Optional per-row YAML merged over the study config. The path is relative to the manifest. notes Ignored free text (also note, comment). any dotted config key A per-run value, e.g. placement.localite.target, transducer.focal_distance_ep, grid.resolution_mm. Struct arrays take an index: transducer(2).trans_pos for the second transducer of a multi-transducer setup. A plain transducer.x is only allowed while the config defines one transducer.

Cells are parsed like YAML values: 30, [-38, 20, 52], L_M1, true. An empty cell keeps the study value, and [] sets an empty value. Lines starting with # are comments. In .csv files, quote cells that contain commas: "[-38, 20, 52]". Unknown keys are set anyway, with a warning (a typo guard).

items.title: Output Names
items.text:
Each run writes the usual per-subject outputs to <path.sim>/sub-XXX/, distinguished by its output affix.

Affix rules and clashes
  • An explicit io.output_affix column (or row-config value) is used as is.
  • Otherwise the condition is appended to the study affix with -. For example, study affix pilot with condition M1 gives _desc-pilot-M1; without a study affix, condition M1 gives _desc-M1.
  • The result is sanitised like any io.output_affix.

Two included rows that would write to the same files (same subject, affix, medium, and path.sim) are rejected before anything runs. Give them distinct conditions.

Merge order

For each row, later sources win:

config_default.yaml < study config < row config YAML < manifest columns < Overrides of prestus_study_start < the run's subject_id and output affix

All of this goes through one load_parameters call. Derived values (transducer geometry, thermal timing, …) are therefore computed from the row's own settings. load_parameters accepts the same kind of overrides directly: load_parameters('config.yaml', dir, {'subject_id', 3; 'placement.localite.target', 'L_M1'}).

items.title: Importing Runs from Localite
items.text:
Ingest the Localite recordings on the Nexus's Placement ▸ Localite page or with neuronav_gui (single sessions via Write outputs, many via Ingest all sessions… / the batch window), then use Import from Localite… on the Nexus's Study tab (or the shortcut on the Placement tab).

Importer files and row layouts

The importer reads what ingestion writes under path.localite_post: neuronav_ingest_summary.csv and the per-session InstrumentMarker_*.json files. It builds rows with placement.mode = localite, placement.localite.session, and placement.localite.target, in one of two ways:

  • One run per target (one transducer): the condition is the target, with the session appended when a subject has the same target in several sessions.
  • One run per session (several transducers): the session's targets are assigned to transducers 1, 2, … as placement.localite.target: [L_M1, R_M1]. Order them left first (L… before R…), alphabetically, or in a given order. Sessions whose target count does not match the configured transducers are skipped and listed. The condition is the session.

PRESTUS reads the ingested markers itself at run time, so no positions are copied into the manifest.

items.title: Head Model
items.text:
The skull reflects, attenuates, and refracts ultrasound, so how the head is represented in the simulation shapes the predicted focus and intensity. PRESTUS turns the tissue labels of the segmentation into that representation: it orients, resamples, smooths, and crops the labels into the simulation grid.

On this page:

  • From Segmentation to Grid: orientation, scaling, layer mapping, cropping, and smoothing of the property maps.
  • Air-Cavity Check: whether the beam crosses a sinus or other internal air.
  • Segmentation Report: checking each of these steps on your subject.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Rarely: the defaults suit most studies. Read it when the skull looks wrong in the report, or to understand why the grid has the size it has.
  • Before you start: A layered simulation with a SimNIBS segmentation.

items.title: From Segmentation to Grid
items.text: PRESTUS turns a layered segmentation into a simulation grid in three steps: a single resample that rotates and rescales each image (Orientation and Scaling), layer mapping with mask smoothing and skull hole filling, and cropping with padding. Optional smoothing of the property maps runs later, when the medium is set up. The settings of each step, with their defaults and options, are listed under Head model parameters.

items.title: Orientation
items.text: The head is rotated before cropping so that the beam runs along the grid's z axis. By default (focal_axis) the mean beam axis of all transducers is aligned with z; with one transducer this is its beam axis. transducer_axis follows transducer 1 instead, for set-ups where the other transducers are secondary, and ras_plus skips the rotation and keeps the world-space (RAS+) orientation. The options are listed under grid.mode.

items.title: Scaling
items.text: The planning image, the segmentation, and the bone mask (or (pseudo-)CT) are resliced to grid.resolution_mm by isotropic scaling and centred regridding, in the same resample as the rotation. Images with fewer than 20 distinct values, such as masks and segmentations, use nearest-neighbour interpolation; all others, such as the planning image or a (pseudo-)CT, use linear interpolation.

items.title: Layer Mapping and Smoothing
items.text:
The SimNIBS segmentation (10 tissues) is mapped onto the layers in layers. The default lists six: water, brain, skin, skull (label 4), skull_cortical, and skull_trabecular. Labels not assigned to another layer become water, which by default includes CSF (label 3), eyes, blood, and muscle. A requested layer without a segmentation label is dropped. A charm segmentation has no label 4, so the default skull layer is dropped and the head consists of brain, skin, cortical and trabecular bone in water; with a pseudo-CT the skull layers are merged into one skull layer. Each layer index corresponds to its position in medium_properties, so layers can be added or removed without changing the ids of the others.

Each layer mask is smoothed (Gaussian kernel of 1 mm FWHM by default) and binarised; voxels that no layer keeps become water. Holes in the skull are then filled where brain meets skin, by default with a rubber wrap that bridges holes up to about 10 mm wide; filled voxels become cortical skull. The filter, kernel width, thresholds, and fill method are set in headmodel.

With a two-layer skull, cortical and trabecular bone are first combined and smoothed as one skull, which becomes cortical bone; the trabecular layer is then smoothed and added inside it. Holes in the combined skull are filled afterwards and become cortical bone.

items.title: Cropping
items.text:
The grid is cropped tightly around the head and every transducer bowl, with a 1-voxel margin; k-Wave adds the PML outside the grid. This keeps the simulation as small as possible. The head region extends 20 mm beyond the CSF segmentation (headmodel.csf_expansion); voxels outside it become water and are eligible for cropping. The volume is padded automatically (with a warning) if a bowl centre falls outside it, so extra padding (headmodel.head_pad_mm) is rarely needed; padding beyond the head and bowls is cropped away and does not slow the simulation. See headmodel.

Crop bounds and FFT-friendly sizes

The crop box encloses the layered medium mask and the bowl geometry of every transducer, plus a 1-voxel margin; the PML lies outside the grid. With several transducers all bowls count, which matters for bilateral set-ups: without the contralateral bowl, that side of the grid would be bounded only by the CSF-expanded head and would carry unused space. Rotation follows the mean beam axis in the default focal_axis mode and transducer(1)'s axis in transducer_axis mode; all transducers are mapped into the same space before the bounds are computed. The box is then enlarged by up to grid.max_expand voxels per dimension to sizes with small prime factors (find_min_factor), which makes k-Wave's FFTs faster. The medium stays anchored at its origin, so transducer and target do not move relative to the head. All transformations are concatenated and applied to the transducer and target positions.

items.title: Property Map Smoothing
items.text:
Sharp transitions between tissues reflect sound. headmodel.smooth_properties: true smooths the acoustic and thermal property maps themselves during medium setup, with the same filter and kernel as the masks. It is off by default. Pseudo-CTs made with PRESTUS already smooth the skull edges (pseudo-CT), so property smoothing is usually not wanted with them. Recommended settings are an active area of investigation.

Which property each tissue gets is described in Medium properties.

items.title: Air-Cavity Check
items.text:
Air reflects almost all ultrasound that reaches it, but the head model fills the sinuses and mastoid air cells with their layer's properties, water by default. A beam that crosses the frontal sinus, as frontal approaches to medial prefrontal targets can, is therefore shown reaching the brain when in reality little of it would. The air-cavity check reports how much of the simulated beam enters these cavities, so you can recognise such placements and choose another.

The check runs by default for layered media. headmodel.air_cavities.source selects where the air comes from (none turns the check off):

  • simnibs (default) takes the internal air that SimNIBS charm segments (label 501, Air-Internal, in segmentation/labeling.nii.gz of the m2m folder): the sinuses, the nasal cavity and airway, and the mastoid air cells. It needs only the T1 segmentation. final_tissues.nii.gz does not contain this label: charm merges internal air into the background (0) there. If the labelling has been deleted from the m2m folder, the run warns and skips the check.
  • hu takes air from the CT or pseudo-CT. A pseudo-CT may show parts of the nasal cavity and airway as soft tissue, so it can find less air than simnibs.
  • segmentation takes the labels you list in labels, for a segmentation that labels air.

The check leaves the medium and the field unchanged. After the acoustic simulation it reports two measures: the peak pressure inside the cavities relative to the brain peak, and the largest share of the −6 dB beam cross-section that the cavities fill at any depth between the exit plane and the focus. When either exceeds its threshold (warn_db, warn_beam_fraction), the run log warns and the report flags the placement. The settings are listed under headmodel.air_cavities; the values are in the metrics table.

How the beam share is measured

Along each transducer's axis, from the exit plane to the focus, the field is cut into slabs one voxel thick, within a cylinder of the aperture radius. In each slab the −6 dB beam cross-section is the set of voxels with at least half the slab's peak pressure. The beam share is the fraction of these voxels inside the cavities; slabs with fewer than 5 beam voxels are skipped. The largest share over all slabs and transducers is reported, with its depth from the exit plane, and so is the share over the whole prefocal −6 dB volume. With source: simnibs, the charm labelling is mapped onto the simulation grid with the same rotation, scaling, and crop as the segmentation (nearest neighbour). With source: hu, voxels in hu_window are filtered by a 3-voxel majority vote, and the largest connected component (the air around the head) is removed, together with every component touching the grid edge unless keep_boundary is set, as in BabelBrain's air regions.

The check is a warning, not a model of the air: the field beyond a flagged cavity is not corrected.

items.title: Segmentation Report
items.text:
Each step above changes tissue labels, and a setting that suits one head can open or thicken the skull in another. The segmentation report shows what each step did on your subject, so you can check the head model before relying on the simulation.

A layered run writes sub-XXX_layered_segmentation_report<affix>.html next to the simulation report after the grid stage (report.segmentation: 1, default). It lists the steps in order: SimNIBS segmentation, tissue mapping and smoothing, skull hole filling, eyes to water, CSF-based crop, and grid crop. For each step it shows:

  • slices through the focus before and after the step, and the voxels it changed; choose the plane and size, and hover for the voxel index and tissue;
  • the voxels moved between tissues, with their volume and their share of the source tissue;
  • the settings that drove it.

A summary table lists the largest changes of every step, and a further table gives the volume of each tissue after each step. The header links to the SimNIBS charm_report.html, which checks the segmentation itself.

items.title: Running on a Cluster (HPC)
items.text:
A head simulation takes minutes to hours on a GPU, and a study runs many of them (subjects, targets, settings). The most efficient way to use PRESTUS is to run these simulations as parallel cluster jobs.

On this page:

  • Where a Run Executes: what each platform value does, and where job logs go.
  • Job Resources: wall time, memory, and the other hpc.* keys.
  • GPU Support: requesting GPUs and partitions.
  • Post-Job Resource Report: what a finished SLURM job used.

At a glance

  • When you need it: For head simulations without a local GPU, and whenever you run many simulations.
  • Before you start: Access to a cluster with SLURM or PBS/qsub, and PRESTUS and its dependencies installed there.

PRESTUS submits cluster jobs itself. You call the same prestus_pipeline_start(parameters) as for a local run, and platform decides where it runs:

platform: slurm          # auto | matlab | slurm | qsub
hpc:
  timelimit: '04:00:00'
  memorylimit: 20        # GB

Many subjects or conditions are submitted together from a study manifest with prestus_study_start. The PRESTUS Nexus can submit to a cluster, also over SSH from a laptop, and follows the jobs and their logs.

On the Donders cluster, see Donders HPC for interactive sessions and your own job scripts.

Recommended: the C++ k-Wave codes, on CPU and GPU. Set simulation.code_type: cpp_cpu for CPU jobs and cpp_gpu for GPU jobs. They run several times faster than matlab_cpu and matlab_gpu on the same hardware, so jobs hold their nodes and GPUs for less time, and they keep peak memory low. They need the k-Wave binaries (k-Wave) and node-local disk for their input and output files (Node-local scratch).

items.title: Where a Run Executes
items.text:
platform Effect auto (default) SLURM if sbatch is on the PATH, else qsub if qsub is; an error if neither is found. Set matlab on a workstation matlab Run in the current MATLAB session (recommended for debugging) slurm Submit a SLURM job (sbatch) qsub Submit a PBS/Torque job (qsub)

Job logs go to log_hpc/ in the subject's output folder (sub-XXX_slurm_output_<id>.log; sub-XXX_qsub_output_<id>.log for qsub). MATLAB returns as soon as the job is submitted, unless hpc.wait_for_job is set. A small dependent job then writes a resource report.

Some modes split one run into several chained jobs that pass results through caches: async multi-transducer runs, multi-intensity sweeps, and uncertainty runs (How PRESTUS works). Post-hoc free-water simulations (modules.run_posthoc_water_sims) are submitted as separate jobs.

To submit, PRESTUS saves the parameters to a temporary file, writes a small launcher that adds the PRESTUS paths and calls prestus_pipeline, and submits it.

items.title: Job Resources
items.text: Each job requests 4 hours of wall time (hpc.timelimit) and 20 GB of memory (hpc.memorylimit); post-hoc free-water jobs request 5 hours and 40 GB. Raise these for fine grids or heating runs. GPU type, partition, and reservation are described under GPU support, node-local disk under Node-local scratch, and hpc.name: 'snellius' selects the Snellius presets. All hpc keys, with their defaults, are listed under HPC parameters.

items.title: Node-local scratch
items.text:
The C++ k-Wave codes (cpp_cpu, cpp_gpu) write an input and an output .h5 file per simulation, often 5–15 GB together. Inside a job they go to $TMPDIR when the scheduler sets it, else to <output>/cache/. To reserve node-local disk for them and choose where they go, set hpc.tmp_gb:

hpc:
  tmp_gb: 50          # adds '#SBATCH --tmp=50G' to the job script; 0 = off (default)
  scratch_dir: auto   # or a path, e.g. '/scratch/${USER}/${SLURM_JOB_NAME}' (created if missing)

With scratch_dir: auto, PRESTUS takes the first existing folder of $PRESTUS_SCRATCH, $SLURM_TMPDIR, /scratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_NAME, and /scratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_ID. If none exists but /scratch/$USER does, it creates /scratch/$USER/$SLURM_JOB_NAME and removes it again at the end if it is empty. The last fallback is $TMPDIR. On a cluster whose scratch is not under /scratch, set PRESTUS_SCRATCH_BASE before MATLAB starts. The job log names the folder in a Node-local scratch: line, with the free space.

PRESTUS works in prestus_<jobid>/sub-NNN<affix>/ inside that folder and removes it when the run ends or fails, including .h5 files a failed k-Wave run left behind. A job killed by the scheduler leaves the folder to the cluster's own cleanup. cache/ always stays in the output folder, because later stages and runs read it.

If no node can provide --tmp=<tmp_gb>G, the job stays pending: lower hpc.tmp_gb or set it to 0.

All keys are listed in Parameters. Which simulations need a GPU and which settings are fastest is described in k-Wave. Predicted run time and memory, and the time and memory earlier runs needed, are on Run time and resources.

items.title: GPU Support
items.text:
TUS simulations are accelerated by GPUs, but requesting GPUs can lead to longer wait times (on the Donders cluster, the concurrent GPU limit per user is 4). To reduce wait times, run acoustic simulations first (to confirm targeting; they need less RAM) and then run thermal simulations with the final protocol. Avoid blanket simulations (e.g. circling through all participants with all permutations), especially for thermal simulations.

A job requests a GPU when a solver it runs computes on one: - k-Wave with simulation.code_type matlab_gpu or cpp_gpu, for the acoustic stage, k-Wave heating, or time reversal; - jwave, unless jwave.use_gpu is false; - BabelBrain, unless babelbrain.computing_backend is cpu.

hpc.partition and hpc.gpu override the partition and GPU type.

PRESTUS is a MATLAB toolbox and only supports Nvidia GPUs. When Nvidia GPUs are digitally partitioned, MATLAB R2024+ can fail to identify the assigned GPU. Submitted SLURM jobs therefore load matlab/R2023b, whichever MATLAB version submits them (MATLAB/2024b with hpc.name: 'snellius'). PBS jobs load matlab/R2022b, because the PBS nodes support CUDA 11.2 only.

hpc.gpu requests a specific GPU type and is usually not needed. On the Donders cluster, set hpc.partition: 'gpu40g' (GPUs with more than 40 GB vRAM) for most thermal simulations; hpc.reservation selects a reserved queue, if you have one. See HPC parameters.

How long a run takes on each GPU type, and how much GPU memory it needs, is on Run time and resources, with a calculator and the times of this project's earlier runs.

items.title: Post-Job Resource Report
items.text:
After a SLURM job finishes, hpc_job_report writes log_hpc/sub-XXX_job<ID>_report.txt with wall time, CPU/GPU allocation, peak memory, a CO₂e estimate and, where billing rates are known, the cost. The report runs from hpc_wait_for_completion when hpc.wait_for_job is set, and otherwise as a small dependent job. memory_efficiency and the --mem suggestion use peak_mem_gb.

Where the peak memory comes from

Peak memory comes from two sources:

  • max_rss_gb: SLURM's sacct MaxRSS, the maximum over job steps. SLURM samples it (every 30 s by default), so it can miss short spikes.
  • The job logs: on Linux, BabelBrain runs print memory lines to the console. MATLAB writes [memory] lines (from log_memory_usage) before and after the BabelBrain launch. The BabelBrain Python process writes [memory_bb] lines whenever its peak grows by 0.5 GB or more, plus one at exit. The report reads these lines from the pipeline log (io.log_file, fixed at submission) and from log_hpc/<subj>_slurm_output_<ID>.log:
    • log_cgroup_peak_gb: peak usage of the job's memory cgroup (MATLAB plus BabelBrain). This is the figure the out-of-memory killer acts on, and it includes page cache.
    • bb_peak_gb and matlab_peak_gb: the peak resident memory of each process.

peak_mem_gb is the larger of log_cgroup_peak_gb and max_rss_gb, and peak_mem_source names the source it came from. Both are lower bounds: the log lines stop at BabelBrain exit, so a later stage can go above them.

For local runs, each BabelBrain run also prints one summary line to the pipeline log, e.g. [memory_summary] BabelBrain: BabelBrain peak=7.2 GB | MATLAB peak=3.1 GB | cgroup peak=10.5 GB, limit=64.0 GB.

items.title: Donders HPC
items.text:
The Donders cluster runs SLURM, and PRESTUS submits its jobs there itself (Running on a Cluster). This page covers what is specific to the Donders cluster: starting an interactive session to submit from, writing your own MATLAB job scripts, and the PBS (qsub) queue.

On this page:

  • SLURM Workflow: an interactive session from which you submit PRESTUS jobs.
  • Your Own MATLAB Job Scripts: job scripts you submit yourself, and the launcher's argument pitfall.
  • PBS Workflow: the same on the PBS (qsub) queue.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you run PRESTUS on the Donders cluster.
  • Before you start: A Donders HPC account and access to the intranet.

Current resource usage is shown at https://grafana.dccn.nl/ (intranet required); the HPC wiki (intranet required) has the full documentation. The workflows below start an interactive session from which you submit PRESTUS jobs.

items.title: SLURM Workflow
items.text:
1. Log in to an access node (mentat005, mentat006, mentat007): ssh abcxyz@mentat005.dccn.nl
  2. Start the VNC manager (vncmanager - 2) and connect via VNC. TigerVNC: enter ip [e.g. mentat007.dccn.nl:12]
  3. Load SLURM: module load slurm
  4. Start an interactive job:
    • Without MATLAB GUI: srun --mem=8gb --time=01:00:00 --x11 -p interactive --pty bash -i
    • With MATLAB GUI: srun --partition=gpu --gres=gpu:1 --mem=8G --time=01:00:00 --x11 --pty /bin/bash -i
  5. Start MATLAB: module load matlab/R2023b then matlab. SLURM supports CUDA 12.2, see PRESTUS issue #50. The submitted jobs load matlab/R2023b whatever version this session runs, because R2024+ can fail to identify partitioned GPUs (GPU support).
  6. Run PRESTUS with platform: slurm (or auto). Check job status with squeue. For PBS→SLURM command migration see the Donders HPC wiki.

items.title: Your Own MATLAB Job Scripts
items.text:
PRESTUS writes its own job scripts. For a script you submit yourself (e.g. a library rebuild), put all MATLAB code in a .m file and pass only its name:

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --mem=16G
#SBATCH --output=/project/<project>/logs/my_job_%j.log
module load matlab/R2023b
cd /project/<project>/code   # folder that holds my_job.m
matlab -batch my_job

The Donders matlab launcher splits its arguments at spaces, so matlab -batch "a = 1; my_job(a)" fails before MATLAB starts (syntax error near unexpected token, job exit code 2). Pass parameters as environment variables (getenv) or write one .m file per job. Use /project/... paths, and load matlab/R2023b: PRESTUS needs MATLAB's Java (YAML loader), and some -batch starts under other versions ran without it.

items.title: PBS Workflow
items.text:
1. Log in to an access node (mentat001, mentat002, mentat003, mentat004): ssh abcxyz@mentat004.dccn.nl
  2. Start the VNC manager (vncmanager - 2) and connect via VNC. TigerVNC: enter ip [e.g. mentat004.dccn.nl:12]
  3. Load QSUB: module load qsub

  4. Start an interactive job:

    qsub -I -l 'nodes=1:gpus=1,feature=cuda,walltime=05:00:00,mem=24gb,reqattr=cudacap>=5.0'

  5. Start MATLAB: module load matlab/R2022b then matlab. PBS only supports CUDA 11.2, which is dropped from R2023 on; see PRESTUS issue #50.

  6. Run PRESTUS with platform: qsub (or auto). Check job status with qstat.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
PRESTUS runs in MATLAB and simulates with k-Wave by default; head simulations also need SimNIBS to segment the MRI. MATLAB, PRESTUS, and k-Wave are enough for a free-water simulation, and the Python environments further down serve optional features only. This page lists what each kind of simulation needs and how to install it, so you can install only what your study uses.

On this page:

  • Quick Install: three steps to a working free-water setup, and the Nexus.
  • Required Components: which component each kind of simulation requires.
  • Install PRESTUS: the clone with its submodules and the MATLAB path.
  • Install SimNIBS: the SimNIBS environment for head segmentation, and how PRESTUS finds it.
  • Install Optional Components: environments for other backends, placement tools, the Nexus, C++ binaries, and defacing.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Before your first simulation.
  • Before you start: MATLAB R2023b (other versions may work; R2023b is the tested default). Installing SimNIBS takes the most time, so start with the free-water simulation if you only want to try PRESTUS.

items.title: Quick Install
items.text:
1. Clone PRESTUS (or download it as a zip from GitHub):

    git clone https://github.com/Donders-Institute/PRESTUS.git

  2. In MATLAB, go to the PRESTUS folder and run:

    prestus_setup(Save=true)

    This puts PRESTUS on the MATLAB path for this and later sessions, fetches the required submodules (k-Wave, export_fig, FEX-minimize, xml2struct) with git, and prints what is installed and what is missing, with how to fix each item. Run prestus_check_install at any time to see the same report.

  3. Optional, for the PRESTUS Nexus: install its Python environment once.

    System Run macOS, Linux bash nexus/install.sh in the PRESTUS folder Windows double-click nexus\install.bat

    The installer uses conda if you have it and otherwise offers to install Miniforge. Then prestus_nexus in MATLAB finds the environment by itself.

That is enough for a free-water simulation: continue with First simulation. Head simulations also need SimNIBS.

items.title: Required Components
items.text: Component Needed for Where it comes from MATLAB R2023b Everything MathWorks. More recent versions can cause issues on HPCs with GPUs. PRESTUS with its submodules (k-Wave 1.4.1, export_fig, FEX-minimize, xml2struct) Everything The recursive clone below SimNIBS 4 Head simulations (segmentation with charm) Install SimNIBS k-Wave C++ binaries cpp_cpu, cpp_gpu, and cpp_mlx code types k-Wave C++ binaries Python environments BabelBrain or jwave backends, PlanTUS and TUS_entry placement, the Nexus Install Optional Components

items.title: Install PRESTUS
items.text:
Clone the repository and run prestus_setup in MATLAB, as in the Quick Install. prestus_setup fetches only the required submodules; --recurse-submodules also fetches the optional ones (BabelBrain, PlanTUS):

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Donders-Institute/PRESTUS.git
# or the development branch:
git clone --recurse-submodules -b development https://github.com/Donders-Institute/PRESTUS.git

prestus_setup adds functions/, config/, and external/ to the MATLAB path from any folder (run('/path/to/PRESTUS/prestus_setup')). Without Save=true the path holds for the current session only. If MATLAB cannot save the path (no write access to pathdef.m, common on clusters), add the run(...) line to your startup.m.

Submodules and manual downloads

k-Wave 1.4 is supported, but version 1.4.1 (currently GitHub only) adds GPU support for thermal simulations with kWaveDiffusion, so the submodule points there. If you updated an existing clone, prestus_setup fetches missing required submodules; to update all of them:

cd PRESTUS
git submodule init
git submodule update

Without git, download k-Wave, export_fig, FEX-minimize, and xml2struct yourself and place them in the matching external/ subfolders.

Donders Institute HPC cluster

On the Donders HPC, PRESTUS and its dependencies (SimNIBS, k-Wave) are installed centrally, but these versions lag behind main and development. Load a SimNIBS module (module avail simnibs lists them; put the module load line in your .bashrc) and add an installed PRESTUS to your MATLAB path, e.g. addpath('/opt/prestus/dev') (ls /opt/prestus lists the versions). For current features, clone PRESTUS yourself as above. The example dataset can be copied to your home directory:

cp /opt/prestus/example_data/PRESTUS_example_data.zip ${HOME}

The HPC scripts hardcode the MATLAB R2023b module. See Running on a cluster.

items.title: Install SimNIBS
items.text:
Head simulations need SimNIBS 4 for the charm segmentation.

On macOS and Windows, use the SimNIBS installer. prestus_check_install then reports the bin folder it installed charm into, as the value for startup.simnibs_bin_path.

On Linux and clusters, install SimNIBS in its own conda environment; this also works on clusters that restrict user permissions and lets several SimNIBS versions coexist. The quickest route is the setup script in examples/, which creates a PRESTUS_env_4.6.0 environment with SimNIBS and the optional PlanTUS and Connectome Workbench dependencies in one step:

bash examples/setup_PRESTUS_env.sh

Optional flags:

  • --no-plantus: skip the PlanTUS Python packages (nilearn, pyyaml, h5py, trimesh, vtk, PyQt5, potpourri3d, pynput)
  • --no-deface: skip pydeface, which only segmentation.deface: 1 needs
  • --no-workbench: skip Connectome Workbench (e.g. when wb_view is available as an HPC module)

When it finishes, the script prints the simnibs_bin_path value to put in your config; hpc.ld_library_path and the PlanTUS env_path follow it while they are empty. Alternatively, follow the official conda guide.

items.title: Point PRESTUS to SimNIBS
items.text:
Tell PRESTUS where the environment is, in the config or in MATLAB:

parameters.startup.simnibs_bin_path = fullfile('/home', 'neuromod', 'USER', '.conda', 'envs', 'simnibs_v4.6.0', 'bin');
parameters.hpc.ld_library_path = "/opt/gcc/7.2.0/lib64";   % only if charm reports 'undefined symbol' errors
Manual SimNIBS installation on a Linux cluster

Some steps and paths differ between clusters.

  1. Log in and start an interactive session (adjust walltime and memory):

    QSUB: qsub -I -X -N 'simnibs' -l walltime=01:00:00,mem=8g SLURM (Donders default): srun --pty --x11 -J simnibs -t 1:00:00 --mem=8G bash

  2. Download the environment file for the SimNIBS version you want to your home directory:

    wget https://github.com/simnibs/simnibs/releases/download/v4.6.0/environment_linux.yml -O ~/environment_linux_v4.6.0.yml

    Other versions: replace v4.6.0 with v4.0.0, v4.1.0, or v4.5.0, or use https://github.com/simnibs/simnibs/releases/latest/download/environment_linux.yml.

  3. Load anaconda and create the environment (it lands in ~/.conda/envs/):

    module load anaconda3/2020.07
conda env create -f ~/environment_linux_v4.6.0.yml -n simnibs_v4.6.0
source activate simnibs_v4.6.0

  4. Install SimNIBS into it:

    pip install https://github.com/simnibs/simnibs/releases/download/v4.6.0/simnibs-4.6.0-cp311-cp311-linux_x86_64.whl

    Other wheels: v4.0.0 and v4.1.0 are cp39, v4.5.0 and v4.6.0 are cp311; see the releases.

  5. Optional: menu icons, file associations, the MATLAB library, and the system path:

    mkdir $HOME/SimNIBS_v4.6.0
postinstall_simnibs --setup-links -d $HOME/SimNIBS_v4.6.0

To check the installation later: start an interactive session, module load anaconda3/2020.07, source activate simnibs_v4.6.0, simnibs_gui. The SimNIBS window should open. conda deactivate leaves the environment.

items.title: Install Optional Components
items.text:
PRESTUS itself is MATLAB, but several optional parts run in their own Python (or R) environment. Keep them separate: their dependencies conflict, and most are only needed on the machine that runs that part.

Environment Needed for Create with Where PRESTUS finds it SimNIBS (e.g. simnibs_v4.6.0, or PRESTUS_env_4.6.0 incl. PlanTUS and Workbench) Head segmentation (charm), PlanTUS placement examples/setup_PRESTUS_env.sh or the SimNIBS environment_linux.yml (see above) simnibs_bin_path BabelBrain acoustic_backend / thermal_backend: babelbrain external/BabelBrain/environment_<platform>.yml (BabelBrain) babelbrain.python_env jwave acoustic_backend: jwave conda create + pip install (jwave) jwave.python_env, jwave.python_env_gpu tus_entry TUS_entry placement (R) examples/environment_tus_entry.yml (Placement) placement.tus_entry.env_path prestus-nexus PRESTUS Nexus (config builder GUI) nexus/install.sh or nexus/install.bat (Nexus) found by prestus_nexus; override with Python='<env>/bin/python'

The Nexus runs where you edit configs and needs a display; the others run where the pipeline runs (typically the cluster). After setting up or updating a BabelBrain or jwave environment, run smoke_test_backends (in tests/).

items.title: k-Wave C++ Binaries
items.text: Only the cpp_cpu and cpp_gpu code types need these optional binaries: download the C++ binaries from the k-Wave website and place them in PRESTUS/external/k-wave/k-Wave/binaries/ (k-Wave instructions). Precompiled Linux binaries for the Donders HPC are in the PRESTUS_bin repository (which binary is which). The kspacefirstorder-unified repository is an alternative source for the same C++ code (OpenMP and CUDA variants, with macOS support). It also hosts the MLX port for Apple Silicon GPUs, which the cpp_mlx code type needs and which is not on the k-Wave website. Compiling and selecting binaries is described in k-Wave.

items.title: PlanTUS Dependencies
items.text:
The optional plantus placement mode needs PlanTUS 2.0 or later (git clone https://github.com/mlueckel/PlanTUS, then placement.plantus.script_path) and extra Python packages in the SimNIBS environment (the setup script installs them unless --no-plantus was given):

source activate simnibs_v4.6.0
pip install nilearn pyyaml h5py trimesh vtk PyQt5 potpourri3d pynput
python -c "import nilearn, yaml, h5py, trimesh, vtk, potpourri3d; print('PlanTUS dependencies OK')"

Connectome Workbench is needed only to choose the position in Workbench (wb_view). Either install it into the SimNIBS environment, where PRESTUS finds it in the environment's bin/ without further settings:

conda install -c conda-forge connectome-workbench

or, on a cluster where Workbench is a module that MATLAB's Python subprocess does not see, point PRESTUS at its binary folder:

placement:
  plantus:
    connectome_wb_path: "/path/to/workbench/bin_linux64"

items.title: MRI Defacing
items.text:
Optional MRI defacing (segmentation.deface: 1) needs pydeface in the SimNIBS environment:

source activate simnibs_v4.6.0
pip install pydeface
python -c "import pydeface; print('pydeface OK')"

items.title: jwave Acoustic Backend
items.text:
jwave implements the k-Wave acoustic equations independently, in JAX, so a jwave run of the same setup and tissue properties cross-checks a k-Wave field. Its default Helmholtz solver computes the continuous-wave steady state directly, in one linear solve instead of thousands of time steps. jwave covers the acoustic stage only; the thermal simulation runs in k-Wave.

On this page:

  • Quick Start: selecting the backend, the Python environment, and the solver.
  • Python Environment Setup: installing jwave and JAX for CPU or GPU.
  • Limitations: what jwave does not support.

Experimental

The jwave backend is not yet validated against measurements or the ITRUSST benchmarks in PRESTUS. The conservative Helmholtz operator became the default in October 2026 (Helmholtz operator). Use jwave to cross-check k-Wave, not to replace it.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To cross-check k-Wave with an independent implementation, or for a fast CW steady-state solve.
  • Before you start: A Python 3.11 environment with jax, jwave, h5py, and numpy (Python environment setup).

PRESTUS can run jwave in place of k-Wave for the acoustic stage. Pre-processing (segmentation, grid, medium masks, placement) and post-processing (focal metrics, NIfTI export, HTML report) run unchanged. jwave (University College London) implements the k-Wave pseudo-spectral equations in JAX, which gives JIT compilation, automatic differentiation, and NVIDIA GPU acceleration without compiled MATLAB/C++ binaries. It offers a time-domain solver equivalent to kspaceFirstOrder* and a frequency-domain Helmholtz solver that computes the CW steady state directly.

PRESTUS (k-Wave) jwave Solver Pseudo-spectral FDTD Pseudo-spectral (time-domain) or Helmholtz GMRES (frequency-domain) Physics Scalar linear acoustic Scalar linear acoustic Skull model Scalar ρ, c, α Scalar ρ, c, α Differentiable No Yes (JAX automatic differentiation) GPU backends CUDA (via MATLAB gpuArray or C++ binary) NVIDIA CUDA only Thermal simulation Yes (kWaveDiffusion) Not supported

jwave uses the same scalar acoustic model as k-Wave: no shear waves in bone and no Rayleigh pre-step. The medium_properties PRESTUS assigns apply to both equally, so results are directly comparable. See k-Wave for the k-Wave backend options.

items.title: Quick Start
items.text:
Set three things: the backend, the Python environment, and the solver.

acoustic_backend: jwave

jwave:
  python_env: '/home/user/.conda/envs/jwave_env/bin/python'   # CPU environment (see environment setup)
  solver: helmholtz          # 'helmholtz' (default) | 'pseudo_spectral' | 'finite_differences'
  python_env_gpu: ''         # GPU (CUDA) environment; leave empty for CPU-only
  use_gpu: ~                 # null = auto-detect via nvidia-smi | true = force GPU | false = force CPU
  dry_run: false             # write HDF5 inputs only, skip simulation (for debugging)

# PML thickness uses the same grid.pml_size field as k-Wave (default: 'auto'),
# but jwave resolves 'auto' to ~2.5 wavelengths of PML (clipped to [10, 40]
# grid points), not k-Wave's FFT-prime-factorization heuristic.
# grid:
#   pml_size: 20             # override if needed

Or in MATLAB:

parameters.acoustic_backend = 'jwave';

parameters.jwave.solver          = 'helmholtz';
parameters.jwave.python_env      = '/home/user/.conda/envs/jwave_env/bin/python';
parameters.jwave.python_env_gpu  = '/home/user/.conda/envs/jwave_env_gpu/bin/python';
parameters.jwave.dry_run         = false;
% parameters.jwave.use_gpu = true;   % override auto-detection
% parameters.grid.pml_size = 20;     % override the wavelength-based 'auto' PML

python_env is the path of the CPU environment (its root, its bin directory, or the Python executable). python_env_gpu points to the GPU (CUDA) environment. Leaving both empty falls back to the system python3, which is unlikely to have jwave installed. You get a sensor_data struct with the same fields as from k-Wave, so all downstream PRESTUS modules work unchanged.

Which environment runs use_gpu GPU detected (nvidia-smi) python_env_gpu set Environment used [] (auto) yes yes GPU [] (auto) yes no CPU (warning) [] (auto) no – CPU true – yes GPU true – no error false – – CPU

Progress and live view. The time-domain solvers report their steps to the Nexus progress bar. The Helmholtz solver reports nothing while it solves, unless simulation.live_view: 1 is set: it then solves in chunks of 10 GMRES restart cycles and reports the residual after each chunk. With live view, every solver saves the evolving pressure field (Helmholtz: the current iterate).

items.title: Python Environment Setup
items.text:
jwave needs a dedicated Python environment. A separate environment avoids version conflicts with other PRESTUS Python tools (BabelBrain, SimNIBS).

1. Create the environment

# conda
conda create -n jwave_env python=3.11
conda activate jwave_env

# venv (no conda)
python3.11 -m venv ~/.venvs/jwave_env
source ~/.venvs/jwave_env/bin/activate

2. Install jwave and its dependencies. jax[cpu] and jax[cuda12] install different builds of jaxlib and are mutually exclusive: installing one overwrites the other. Pick the variant that matches your hardware.

# CPU only (macOS, Windows, or CPU-only Linux)
pip install "jax[cpu]" jwave h5py numpy

# NVIDIA GPU (CUDA 12, Linux x86-64 only)
pip install "jax[cuda12]" jwave h5py numpy

JAX CUDA wheels are published for Linux x86-64 only; the jaxlib-cuda wheel is large (~2 GB). A CUDA install falls back to CPU when no GPU is present at runtime. On macOS or Windows, always use jax[cpu].

3. Verify the installation

python -c "import jwave, jax, h5py; print('jwave:', jwave.__version__); print('jax:', jax.__version__)"
python -c "import jax; print(jax.devices())"
# Expected on GPU host: [CudaDevice(id=0)]
# Expected on CPU host: [CpuDevice(id=0)]

4. Find the Python executable path and copy it into jwave.python_env:

which python   # inside the activated environment
# e.g. /home/user/.conda/envs/jwave_env/bin/python
#      /home/user/.venvs/jwave_env/bin/python
Parallel CPU and GPU environments

If you work on both CPU and GPU machines (a laptop and an HPC cluster with shared home directories), maintain two environments and point jwave.python_env and jwave.python_env_gpu to them:

# CPU environment (default, works everywhere)
conda create -n jwave_env python=3.11
conda activate jwave_env
pip install "jax[cpu]" jwave h5py numpy

# GPU environment (Linux + CUDA 12 hosts only)
conda create -n jwave_env_gpu python=3.11
conda activate jwave_env_gpu
pip install "jax[cuda12]" jwave h5py numpy

jwave:
  python_env: '/home/user/.conda/envs/jwave_env/bin/python'       # CPU
  # python_env: '/home/user/.conda/envs/jwave_env_gpu/bin/python'  # GPU

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• Acoustic only. jwave has no bio-heat solver. Thermal simulation (run_heating_sims) after a jwave acoustic run uses k-Wave (thermal_backend: kwave); BabelBrain thermal requires acoustic_backend: babelbrain.
  • No axisymmetric grids. jwave requires a full 3-D domain.
  • GPU: NVIDIA CUDA only. JAX does not officially support AMD ROCm or Apple Metal. CPU execution works on any platform.

The solvers and every jwave setting are described in jwave Configuration.

items.title: jwave Configuration
items.text:
jwave offers three solvers with different trade-offs between speed, memory, and accuracy. This page describes each solver and its convergence settings, and lists every jwave setting with its default.

On this page:

  • Solver Options: the Helmholtz, pseudo-spectral, and finite-difference solvers, convergence, and the density term.
  • Configuration Reference: every jwave setting with its default.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To choose a jwave solver or change its settings.
  • Before you start: jwave set up as in jwave Acoustic Backend.

items.title: Helmholtz Solver (Default)
items.text:
Frequency-domain GMRES solver. It computes the complex pressure field P(r) at the drive frequency in a single linear solve instead of thousands of time steps, so it is much faster than pseudo_spectral for CW simulations, with equivalent accuracy for monochromatic excitation in lossy tissue. It returns p_max_all = |P| [Pa], p_min_all = −|P| and p_final = Re(P) [Pa]. GMRES convergence is controlled by jwave.gmres_restart and jwave.gmres_maxiter.

Convergence is checked and enforced

After every Helmholtz solve, PRESTUS compares the relative GMRES residual (/diagnostics/residual_norm) against jwave.convergence_threshold (default 0.05). If the residual exceeds the threshold, the pipeline errors, because an unconverged GMRES iterate is dominated by solver noise rather than physics. The error message gives ranked fixes: revert gmres_restart/gmres_maxiter to jwave's own defaults rather than enlarging them (jwave runs in single precision, where a larger restart can destabilise GMRES); check the PML fraction of the domain via --debug; only then loosen gmres_tol. If you have reviewed the field and diagnostics and accept the residual anyway, set jwave.ignore_convergence_threshold: true to downgrade the error to a warning and keep the result.

How the Helmholtz residual, water attenuation, and source are handled

  • Residual. The residual is computed exactly, by re-evaluating the operator and source scaling of the solve on the solved field (conservative_residual, or compute_helmholtz_residual for helmholtz_operator: jwave, in run_jwave_sim.py), so it reflects the true solver error rather than an approximation.
  • Lossless water. alpha_coeff = 0 makes the Helmholtz operator near-singular (purely real wavenumber in the bulk), which stalls GMRES and underestimates peak pressure by ~18%. run_jwave_sim.py floors alpha_coeff to 0.002 dB/(cm·MHz²), the physical value for distilled water, before building the medium. The effect on the field is negligible (< 0.006 % attenuation over 100 mm at 500 kHz).
  • Source-amplitude window. The Helmholtz solver extracts the complex per-voxel drive amplitude via a single-frequency DFT of the CW source signal, restricted to sensor.record_start_index:end, the same steady-state window (last N periods, after the wavefront has crossed the domain) that k-Wave and jwave's time-domain solvers use for p_max_all/p_min_all. createCWSignals() applies a startup cosine up-ramp (default 4 periods) to the drive signal; a DFT over the full signal would average that lower-amplitude ramp in with the steady CW cycles and underestimate the drive amplitude. The steady-state window is built from an integer number of samples per period, which also removes most DFT scalloping loss.
  • Sources. Both source paths work: grid.use_kWaveArray: 1 (band-limited off-grid source, as for k-Wave; recommended, and needed for flat elements) and 0 (makeBowl/makeArc voxels). The stair-stepped makeBowl bowl is ~9 % low in focal pressure in free water at 0.5 mm (ITRUSST BM1). The kWaveArray source reaches jwave as a CWSourceMatrix and is written to the HDF5 input in factored form (per-voxel complex amplitude × [cos; −sin] basis), since its BLI weights make every voxel's signal distinct.

items.title: Density Term (helmholtz_operator)
items.text:
The default helmholtz_operator: conservative solves ρ∇·((1/ρ)∇p) + k²p, with 1/ρ averaged onto the staggered points where ∇p is evaluated (as k-Wave staggers its density), and scales the source by the sound speed at each source voxel (as k-Wave does). helmholtz_operator: jwave uses jwave's built-in operator, which writes the density term as ∇²p − ∇ρ·∇p/ρ with a spectral gradient of ρ and scales the source by the minimum sound speed of the medium (scale_source_helmholtz). In homogeneous media the two agree.

Why the conservative form is the default

Across a sharp density jump (water/skull) jwave's built-in form does not enforce continuity of (1/ρ)∂p/∂n and loses energy at every interface. In 1D plane-wave tests against the analytic transmission it gives −19 % through a density-only plate and −26 % through the ITRUSST BM3 cortical plate (6.5 mm) at 0.5 mm, still −17 % at 0.125 mm. Attenuation and sound-speed contrasts alone are reproduced (≤ 3 %). In 3D this showed as PRESTUS jwave fields 23–29 % below the k-Wave reference on ITRUSST BM3–7. The conservative form gives −0.2 % (BM3 plate) and −3 % (BM4 skin + three-layer skull) at 0.5 mm in the same tests.

items.title: Pseudo-Spectral Solver
items.text: Pseudo-spectral symplectic time-domain integrator with the same equations as kspaceFirstOrder*. It runs Nt time steps with a PML absorbing boundary and records pressure over the last Nt - record_start_index steps (the steady-state window). It returns p_max_all (peak positive pressure), p_min_all (peak negative pressure), and p_final (pressure at the final recorded time step), all in Pa. Use it for direct equivalence with k-Wave output or when you need the transient field.

items.title: Finite-Difference Solver
items.text: Finite-difference time-domain solver. jwave.fd_accuracy sets the spatial stencil order (default 8).

items.title: Configuration Reference
items.text: The jwave keys (solver, environments, GPU selection, GMRES settings, convergence threshold, and cache cleanup), with their defaults, are listed under jwave settings. The PML thickness is set by grid.pml_size, shared with k-Wave.

items.title: PML Size
items.text:
With grid.pml_size: auto, jwave's PML is sized to about 2.5 wavelengths (clipped to [10, 40] grid points), in line with jwave's own example notebooks. The wavelength is taken at the fastest sound speed in the medium (max(medium.sound_speed)), not the slowest. jwave's Helmholtz PML (complex_pml_on_grid) is a fixed function of voxel position: it does not scale with frequency or with the local sound speed, so a given thickness absorbs fewer wavelengths where it borders a fast medium such as skull. On a head-model partial-FOV crop, a 20-voxel (15 mm) PML sized from water (1500 m/s) covered 3.0 wavelengths in water but only 1.8 in skull, and skull bordered most of the transverse boundary. Smoothing the skull/water interface did not reduce the Helmholtz-vs-k-Wave gap, which points to PML coverage rather than interface discontinuities. Sizing from the fastest medium gives every bordering tissue the full target thickness.

Output fields

jwave_wrapper returns a sensor_data struct with the same fields as acoustic_simulation.m:

Field Size Description p_max_all [Nx Ny Nz] double [Pa] Peak positive pressure p_min_all [Nx Ny Nz] double [Pa] Peak negative (rarefaction) pressure p_final [Nx Ny Nz] double [Pa] Pressure at final time step (or Re(P) for Helmholtz) jwave_input_h5 string Path to the HDF5 file written to io.dir_cache; empty once deleted by cleanup_cache jwave_output_h5 string Path to the HDF5 file read from io.dir_cache

Checking the jwave environment

smoke_test_backends('jwave') (in tests/) checks in under 30 s that jwave and its dependencies import and that the PRESTUS bridge scripts are present, without running a simulation. Run it after changing the Python environment.

Automatic differentiation

Because jwave runs in JAX, the simulation is fully differentiable. This is not exposed through the PRESTUS wrapper but is available by calling run_jwave_sim.py directly or extending it. All of the examples below use jwave and jax directly in Python; no MATLAB changes are needed.

Sensitivity map: gradient of focal pressure with respect to every voxel's speed of sound. Cost: one reverse-mode pass, equivalent to a single forward simulation, regardless of grid size.

import jax
from jwave import simulate_wave_propagation

def focal_pressure(sound_speed):
    result = simulate_wave_propagation(domain, medium_with(sound_speed), source, ...)
    return result.pressure[focus_idx].real

grad_fn = jax.grad(focal_pressure)
sensitivity = grad_fn(medium.sound_speed)   # same shape as the grid

Phase optimisation: optimise per-element drive phases to maximise focal pressure.

phases = jax.grad(lambda phi: -focal_pressure_from_phases(phi))(initial_phases)

Full-waveform inversion (FWI): estimate skull acoustic properties from measured transmissions.

loss = lambda sos: jnp.mean((simulate_pressure(sos) - measured_pressure) ** 2)
sos_estimated = jax.scipy.optimize.minimize(loss, sos_init, method='BFGS')

items.title: k-Wave
items.text:
k-Wave is the default solver for the acoustic and the thermal simulation and is installed with PRESTUS. Its implementation (simulation.code_type) decides whether a run uses the CPU or the GPU, through MATLAB or a C++ binary. The elastic skull model changes the physics instead: it adds shear waves in the skull, which fluid skull models omit and which lowered the intracranial pressure in ex vivo measurements; in PRESTUS it is a draft and not yet validated.

On this page:

  • Solver Implementations (code_type): CPU or GPU, MATLAB or C++, and building the binaries.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To choose simulation.code_type for your hardware, or to model shear waves in the skull.
  • Before you start: Nothing; k-Wave is installed with PRESTUS. The C++ variants need the k-Wave binaries.

items.title: Solver Implementations (code_type)
items.text:
simulation.code_type selects the k-Wave implementation. This mainly affects the acoustic simulation; with either GPU variant, thermal simulations also use GPU acceleration (if k-Wave 1.4.1 is provided).

code_type Implementation Requirements matlab_cpu kspaceFirstOrder3D / kspaceFirstOrder2D / kspaceFirstOrderAS in MATLAB none matlab_gpu MATLAB with GPU acceleration via DataCast Parallel Computing Toolbox cpp_cpu kspaceFirstOrder3DC wraps the C++ binary kspaceFirstOrder-OMP The binary from k-Wave downloads cpp_gpu kspaceFirstOrder3DG wraps the C++/CUDA binary kspaceFirstOrder-CUDA, offloading computation to NVIDIA GPUs A CUDA-capable Nvidia GPU and the binary from k-Wave downloads cpp_mlx kspaceFirstOrder3DG wraps the C++/MLX binary kspaceFirstOrder-MLX, offloading computation to the Apple Silicon GPU An Apple Silicon Mac (macOS 14 or later) and the binary with mlx.metallib, built as described below 
simulation:
  code_type: cpp_gpu   # matlab_cpu | matlab_gpu (default) | cpp_cpu | cpp_gpu | cpp_mlx

Recommended: the C++ codes. Where the binaries are installed, use cpp_gpu on an NVIDIA GPU and cpp_cpu otherwise. They run several times faster than their MATLAB counterparts on the same hardware (Run Time), keep peak memory low by streaming the source from disk (Memory), and report their progress to the Nexus. In return they need a separate install and temporary disk space for their input and output files (HPC). The configuration default is matlab_gpu, because it runs without the binaries.

Precompiled binaries for the Donders HPC

The PRESTUS_bin repository holds three Linux x86-64 binaries. Place the ones you need into PRESTUS/external/k-wave/k-Wave/binaries/.

Binary What it is Used by kspaceFirstOrder-OMP k-Wave C++ 1.3 CPU solver (OpenMP, multi-threaded) from the k-Wave website cpp_cpu kspaceFirstOrder-CUDA k-Wave C++ 1.3 CUDA solver, compiled on the Donders HPC with CUDA 11.8 as described below. It loads cuFFT (CUDA 11) and HDF5 1.10 from the system, so it runs only where these libraries are installed. cpp_gpu acousticFieldPropagator-OMP C++ backend of k-Wave's acousticFieldPropagatorC, which computes the steady-state field of a continuous-wave source in a homogeneous medium not used by PRESTUS Compiling the CUDA binary for your GPU

To use C++ with GPU support you may need to recompile the binary for your GPU version (for example the A100 GPUs on the Donders HPC).

  • Download the Linux C++/CUDA source files (version 1.3; the C++ code is versioned separately from the k-Wave 1.4.1 MATLAB toolbox). This includes the Makefile to compile the binary.
  • Follow the compilation instructions by TU Delft. Include your GPU type in the Makefile.
  • On the Donders HPC, examples/hpc_compile_CUDA_a.sh downloads and unpacks the source into ~/kwave-1.3-Donders/source, and examples/hpc_compile_CUDA_b.sh loads cuda/11.8 (the version sets the newest GPU architecture it can target) and compiles kspaceFirstOrder-CUDA into ~/kwave-1.3-Donders/binaries.
  • For the Donders HPC, a precompiled binary is available in the PRESTUS_bin repository (see above).
  • Place the updated binary into PRESTUS/external/k-wave/k-Wave/binaries/
Building the MLX binary (macOS)

cpp_mlx is experimental and has not been validated on a PRESTUS head simulation. It runs the acoustic simulation on the Apple GPU; thermal simulations run on the CPU. Axisymmetric grids fall back to matlab_cpu, and kwave_elastic runs with matlab_cpu, because the port has no solver for either.

The binary is the MLX port of the k-Wave CUDA solver by S. Pichardo (kspacefirstorder-unified, pull request 31). Building it needs CMake and Xcode with the Metal Toolchain (xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain).

git clone --branch MLX-k-Wave-binary https://github.com/ProteusMRIgHIFU/kspacefirstorder-unified.git
cd kspacefirstorder-unified
cmake -S repos/kspaceFirstOrder-mlx-darwin -B build/mlx-darwin \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=14.0 -DKWAVE_BUNDLE_DEPS=ON
cmake --build build/mlx-darwin --parallel

Copy kspaceFirstOrder-MLX and mlx.metallib from build/mlx-darwin into PRESTUS/external/k-wave/k-Wave/binaries/. The two files must stay side by side, because the binary loads mlx.metallib from its own folder.

The elastic skull model (shear waves) is described in Elastic Skull (Shear Waves).

items.title: Elastic Skull (Shear Waves)
items.text:
Bone carries shear waves as well as pressure waves, and at oblique incidence part of the energy crosses the skull as shear. The elastic k-Wave model simulates both. This page covers its settings, the elastic skull properties, and its limits and cost.

On this page:

  • Elastic Skull Model (Shear Waves): settings, limitations, and cost.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When the beam meets the skull obliquely, or to test how much shear waves change a result.
  • Before you start: A working k-Wave setup (k-Wave).

items.title: Elastic Skull Model (Shear Waves)
items.text:
acoustic_backend: kwave_elastic runs k-Wave's pstdElastic3D / pstdElastic2D instead of kspaceFirstOrder*, so the skull supports shear as well as compressional waves. The motivation is Gao et al. (2026), who compared fluid and elastic k-Wave skull models against hydrophone scans through an ex vivo skull at normal and 40° incidence for shallow (cortical) foci. In those scans the fluid skull model overestimated the intracranial pressure by ~40 % on average and the −6 dB focal area by up to 170 %. The elastic model was also less sensitive to small transducer position errors.

Experimental

Not yet validated in PRESTUS against measurements or the ITRUSST benchmarks. Compare elastic results with a fluid kwave run before you use them.

items.title: Elastic Model Settings
items.text:
acoustic_backend: kwave_elastic
simulation:
  code_type: matlab_gpu      # cpp_* is overridden to matlab_* (no C++/CUDA elastic solver)
grid:
  axisymmetric: 0            # not supported
elastic:                     # defaults shown; see doc_parameters.md
  shear_mapping: pichardo    # pichardo | off
  shear_density_min: 1200
  poisson_min: 0.1
  alpha_coeff_shear: 43.63   # dB/(cm MHz^y)
  alpha_power_shear: 1.662
  alpha_coeff_long: 27.31    # dB/(cm MHz^y)
  alpha_power_long: 1.722
  long_attenuation: elastic

Compressional speed and density come from the usual medium setup (layer values or pseudo-CT mapping). The shear speed and the two attenuations follow Pichardo et al. (2017), the viscoelastic model behind BabelBrain, evaluated at the transducer's fundamental frequency. Expect the elastic model to be most reliable at low frequencies: Pichardo et al. found good agreement at 270 kHz (delay error 5 % of a wavelength) but only global agreement at 836 kHz (17 %), where trabecular scattering degraded the spatial prediction of an isotropic model.

Skull elastic properties

Pichardo et al. (2017) fitted shear speed and attenuation to transcranial scans at 40° incidence (10 locations, 3 formalin-fixed skulls, 270 and 836 kHz). Every value is evaluated at the transducer's fundamental frequency f0:

Property Pichardo et al. 2017 PRESTUS default at f0 Shear speed cS = 0.458·ρ + 545.52 (270 kHz); cS = 0.386·ρ + 815.51 (836 kHz) slope and intercept interpolated linearly in f. At 500 kHz: 0.429·ρ + 655.2, i.e. 1448 m/s at ρ = 1850 (cortical layer), 1384 m/s at ρ = 1700 (trabecular layer). Extrapolated, with a warning, outside 270–836 kHz Shear attenuation 57 Np/m (270 kHz), 373 Np/m (836 kHz), one value for the whole skull power law through both points: 43.63 dB/(cm·MHz^1.662); 0.68 Np/cm at 300 kHz, 1.59 Np/cm at 500 kHz Longitudinal attenuation 33 Np/m (270 kHz), 231 Np/m (836 kHz), from Pichardo et al. 2011; the shear values were fitted with these power law through both points: 27.31 dB/(cm·MHz^1.722); 0.40 Np/cm at 300 kHz, 0.95 Np/cm at 500 kHz

The shear-speed fits are BabelBrain's DensityToSSoSPichardo before averaging: BabelBrain uses their mean over the two frequencies (0.422·ρ + 680.5).

Why the skull longitudinal attenuation is replaced. The shear attenuation was fitted together with this longitudinal attenuation, so the pair is used as a set. The fluid/pCT skull values are fits for a fluid model, which have to absorb mode-conversion losses into the longitudinal attenuation. Set long_attenuation: medium to keep them anyway. The sources disagree by about 2×: Gao et al. (2026) used 0.5 Np/cm at 500 kHz with the same k-Wave solver (Pichardo pair: 0.95; PRESTUS fluid default 13.3 dB/(cm·MHz): 0.77).

Poisson-ratio floor. Combining a density-based shear speed with a density-based compressional speed can give unphysical bone. For example, the Gao et al. shear mapping with the k-Plan cL mapping gives ν ≈ 0 at ρ ≈ 1300 kg/m³; BabelBrain disables shear on its CT path for this reason. The Pichardo mapping is better behaved, but at ρ = 1200 kg/m³ it still gives ν from 0.17 (250 kHz) down to ≈0 (836 kHz), because cS rises with frequency while cL does not. poisson_min caps cS in those voxels and the run log reports how many.

Resolution. The slowest shear wave sets the grid requirement. A warning is issued below min_ppw_shear (6; Gao et al. used 6.6 with k-Wave, Pichardo et al. 8 with 4th-order FDTD). At 0.5 mm, 300 kHz gives ≈7.4 points per wavelength for cS = 1105 m/s (ρ = 1200); 500 kHz needs ≈0.39 mm.

How the elastic run differs from the fluid run Step Fluid kwave kwave_elastic Medium sound_speed, density, alpha_coeff/alpha_power the same maps, plus sound_speed_shear and alpha_coeff_shear in the skull and (by default) elastic.alpha_coeff_long as skull longitudinal attenuation (medium_elastic_properties, called from acoustic_wrapper with the final density map and skull masks) Absorption power law, alpha_power (remapped to y = 2 by fit_alpha_power) Kelvin-Voigt, fixed y = 2; every coefficient is rescaled so the attenuation at the source frequency is exact Source pressure source p_mask, p equivalent normal-stress source s_mask = p_mask, sxx = syy = szz = −p. k-Wave scales both by 2·dt·c0/dx and records p = −(sxx+syy+szz)/3, so the injected pressure is the same Solver kspaceFirstOrder3D/2D/AS, MATLAB or C++ pstdElastic3D/2D, MATLAB CPU or GPU (DataCast) Free-water baseline fluid solver same elastic solver (cS = 0), so ISPPA scaling uses one forward model

The fluid kwave_medium returned to the pipeline is unchanged; thermal simulation, NIfTI export and the report use it as for a fluid run. With simulation.debug: 1, the shear speed and shear absorption grids are written to debug/medium/matrix_*_shear*.nii.gz.

items.title: Elastic Model Limitations and Cost
items.text:
• Compute and memory: pstdElastic3D holds ≈65–75 single-precision arrays of the padded grid (split stress and velocity fields, staggered material maps, derivatives), i.e. ≈0.27–0.30 GB per million voxels, or ≈26–30 GB for a 512×512×384 padded grid. Runtime is several times that of the C++/CUDA fluid solver (MATLAB time loop, ~3× the FFT work); Gao et al. report ~15 min for 320×256×384 on an RTX 3090 at CFL 0.3. Keep grid.source_cfl ≤ 0.3; the PRESTUS default 0.15 is conservative.
  • Not supported: axisymmetric grids and C++/CUDA binaries. Nonlinearity (BonA) is not passed to the elastic solver.
