items.title: Transducer Placement
items.text:
The transducer position decides where the beam enters the head, which part of the skull it crosses, and where the focus lies relative to the target, so it shapes every acoustic and thermal result of a head simulation. This page covers how PRESTUS obtains the transducer and focus positions: entered by hand, or derived by one of several placement modes that share one exit-plane geometry.

On this page:

  • Choosing a Placement Mode: the modes, what each optimises, and what each needs.
  • Importing a Trajectory: positions from Brainsight, 3D Slicer, or k-Plan.
  • Exporting a Pose: the placed pose for Brainsight, 3D Slicer, or k-Plan.
  • Placement Report: the HTML report written after placement.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Every head simulation. Free-water simulations need no target.
  • Before you start: The T1w planning image; most modes also need a SimNIBS segmentation.

PRESTUS works with the transducer (transducer.trans_pos) and the target (transducer.focus_pos) as voxels of the T1w planning image. The transducer coordinate is the bowl apex, not the exit plane of a curved transducer. All modes put the exit plane curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm in front of the apex (BabelBrain's FocalLength − NaturalOutPlaneDistance) and, where they place the transducer on the scalp, leave placement.skin_gap_mm (default 5 mm) between scalp and exit plane. You can enter both points directly (in voxels, subject RAS mm, or MNI mm), or let a placement mode derive them.

items.title: Choosing a Placement Mode
items.text:
Mode Primary objective Requires manual User-specified Coordinates in config (T1 voxels, RAS+ mm or MNI mm) localite Recorded neuronavigation pose Localite XML mni Transducer and focus given in MNI mm; transducer snapped to the scalp SimNIBS m2m_sub-XXX folder heuristic Skull-surface proximity to MNI target SimNIBS segmentation plantus Beam–target overlap + skull acoustics SimNIBS mesh + PlanTUS install tus_entry Transducer-scalp coupling geometry Scalp mask + TUS_entry R install

Each mode has its own page: manual, MNI, heuristic, PlanTUS, TUS_entry and Localite. Whatever the mode, the resolved positions are written to sub-XXX_placement<affix>.json in the output folder. Coordinate conventions are described in Coordinate systems.

Heuristic or PlanTUS? heuristic plantus Input final_tissues.nii.gz (label volume) Full SimNIBS mesh (sub-XXX.msh) + SimNIBS Python env Strategy Single-objective sphere-expansion on skull surface Multi-objective optimisation (beam overlap, skin/skull angles, skull thickness, target distance) Focal distance sweep No Yes External dependency None PlanTUS + SimNIBS installation

Use heuristic when only a tissue-label segmentation is available or for batch jobs on an HPC cluster. Use plantus when the full SimNIBS mesh is available and you want multi-objective optimisation or transducer selection across focal distances.

items.title: Importing a Trajectory
items.text:
To reuse a plan from another tool, use Import trajectory on the Nexus Placement tab. It writes focus_pos and trans_pos for manual placement, except for a Localite export: that sets the localite placement mode with placement.localite.file, so each run averages the chosen series' triggers and converts the pose again. Reading a Localite export needs MATLAB.

Source File Sets Brainsight target export (.txt, NIfTI coordinates) focus and beam direction; transducer on the axis at the focal depth setting 3D Slicer ITK transform (.tfm, .txt) as Brainsight k-Plan .kdp (device parameters), PLAN-*-RESULTS.h5 transducer at the plan's bowl apex, focus at its target, focal depth setting matched to the target k-Plan .kps (transducer positions) transducer at the bowl apex; focus on the axis at the focal depth setting Localite TriggerMarkers, InstrumentMarker, or GUMMarkers export (.xml) the series you choose: placement.localite.target if its description is unique in the file, else .position k-Plan trajectories
  • Image: k-Plan counts its coordinates from the first voxel of its planning image. The import is right when that image had the T1's voxels: the T1 itself, or, for an oblique T1, a copy with the rotation removed from the header. With a rotated or flipped T1, the import says so.
  • Focal depth: set from the selected transducer's own exit plane, so it can differ from k-Plan's value for the same apex and target. k-Plan's CTX-500, for example, puts its exit plane 10.82 mm in front of the apex, PRESTUS's 10.56 mm.
  • Not imported: k-Plan's transducer model, drive, and fields.

items.title: Exporting a Pose
items.text:
To plan or navigate with the PRESTUS pose elsewhere, list the formats in placement.export_formats. After placement, PRESTUS writes them to io.dir_output, one set per transducer (_txN with several):

Format Output Contents 'brainsight' sub-XXX_placement_brainsight.txt target and beam direction (NIfTI scanner coordinates) 'slicer' sub-XXX_placement_slicer.tfm the same pose as an ITK transform, in BabelBrain's convention 'kplan' sub-XXX_placement_kplan/ T1 and CT or pseudo-CT with the rotation removed from the header, the transducer position (.kps), and an entry sheet with the target and focal distance

Each export imports back into the Nexus with Import trajectory. For k-Plan, upload the exported images, not the originals: k-Plan counts its coordinates from their first voxel. The T1 must have (obliquely) R, A, S voxel axes. The entry sheet gives k-Plan's focal distance for the CTX-500 (exit plane 10.82 mm in front of the apex), and for other devices how to work it out.

items.title: Placement Report
items.text:
After placement, PRESTUS writes a stand-alone HTML report, sub-XXX_placement_<mode><affix>.html, to io.dir_reports (placement.report, default true).

Report contents

It holds the target, the transducer and focus positions (T1 voxels and subject RAS mm, with transducer–focus and focus–target distances), the T1 overlay figure, and the placement configuration. For placement.mode: 'plantus' it adds the criteria evaluation: diagnostics, each criterion at the placed spot, the criterion maps, and the weight sweep. A failed report is a warning, not an error. The report is skipped when no output directory is known.

items.title: Heuristic Transducer Placement
items.text:
When only a target is known, the transducer position still has to be chosen, and it decides how much skull lies in front of the transducer. placement.mode: 'heuristic' searches the skull surface for a transducer position whose geometric focus reaches an MNI target, keeps candidates whose exit plane intersects little skull and selects the one closest to the target. Besides the target and the focal depth (transducer.focal_distance_ep or focal_distance_bowl), which sets the search radius, no manual input is needed, which suits automatic end-to-end workflows.

On this page:

  • Candidate Table: the metrics computed for every candidate position.
  • Ear Exclusion Zones: optionally excluding candidates over the ears.
  • Position Selection: the selection criteria and the coordinate output.
  • Placement Figures: the overview and T1 overlay figures.
  • Localite Planning Image: a header-adjusted T1 for Localite.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you have a target but no planned transducer position, e.g. for many subjects at once.
  • Before you start: A SimNIBS segmentation, an MNI target, and the focal depth (transducer.focal_distance_ep).
placement:
  mode: 'heuristic'
  heuristic:
    mni_target_mm: [-29, -6, 7]   # target in MNI mm
    target_name: 'target'         # used in output file names

The search converts the target to subject space with SimNIBS tools, finds candidate positions on the skull by expanding a sphere, scores each candidate (target distance, intersection with skin, mean and variance of the distances to skin and skull), optionally removes positions over the ears, and selects one position by the criteria below. Candidates and the selected position are written to the placement run folder, <path.placement>/sub-XXX/heuristic/<target_name>/; a copy of the selected position also goes to path.localite_export when set. All parameters: overview.

transducer_positioning runs the search; transducer_positioning_start calls it. Candidate positions come from an expanding sphere on the skull. For each candidate it computes the intersection proportion between the transducer and skin, mean and variance of the distances to skin and skull, and the geometric focus and exit plane positions. Each candidate's exit plane lies placement.skin_gap_mm (default 5 mm) off the scalp.

items.title: Candidate Table
items.text:
tpars_sub-XXX_target.csv lists every candidate with the columns below. Use it to pick a candidate yourself, e.g. one with prop_intersect < 0.05 and minimal distance to the target, supported by visual inspection.

Metric Description Interpretation idx index trans_x Transducer x-coordinate (voxels) trans_y Transducer y-coordinate (voxels) trans_z Transducer z-coordinate (voxels) targ_x Target x-coordinate (voxels) targ_y Target y-coordinate (voxels) targ_z Target z-coordinate (voxels) dist_to_target Euclidean distance transducer-to-target (voxels) prop_intersect Fraction of voxels in the transducer’s orthogonal plane that intersect with the skull mask. Low values (≈ 0) indicate minimal skull obstruction; high values (> 0.3) indicate significant bone interference. mean_dist_skin Mean distance from non‑intersecting voxels to the skin boundary. Average proximity of the plane to the skin surface. var_dist_skin Variance of distances from non‑intersecting voxels to the skin boundary. Higher variance: surface curvature or oblique intersection. mean_dist_skull Mean distance from all voxels in the plane to the nearest skull boundary. Average clearance between the plane and skull. var_dist_skull Variance of distances to the skull boundary. Irregularity of skull spacing within the beam footprint.

items.title: Ear Exclusion Zones
items.text: Optional. Transducer locations over the ears are not wanted. Candidates within placement.heuristic.ear_radius (radius of the no-go zone in voxels, default 35) around left_ear_center and right_ear_center (approximate ear coordinates, voxels) are removed when the centres are set.

items.title: Position Selection
items.text:
The accepted intersection with the skull is set by placement.heuristic.criterion_intersection. If no candidate meets it, the criterion is expanded by expand_step (default: 1%) until one does, up to 0.3; if none qualifies then, placement stops with an error. The keys below sit under placement.heuristic; an empty value ([], the default) switches a criterion off.

Four further criteria, off by default, keep the candidates whose mean distance from the exit plane to skin or skull is short (criterion_skin_mean, criterion_skull_mean) or whose distance varies little across the exit plane (criterion_skin_var, criterion_skull_var), each as a quantile. See Heuristic placement parameters.

Among the candidates that meet the criteria, the one closest to the target is selected. To place another candidate instead, set placement.heuristic.candidate to its idx in the candidate table; the criteria are then not applied (an idx the table does not hold stops the run). The Nexus Heuristic sub-tab sets it: it plots and lists the candidates of the last run, and Place here places the one you click, reusing the candidate table rather than recomputing it. The output table gives its coordinates in voxel (grid space), mm (Localite space), and mm (RAS+ space), based on the image header of the segmentation image.

Warning

Localite mm coordinates assume that the Localite planning image has canonical_affine_transform applied (see Localite planning image). They are the 0-based voxel indices (MATLAB index − 1) rescaled by the voxel sizes in the header, with no affine transformation. Always verify coordinates visually.

Example coordinate output table 
trans_x 161
trans_y 138
trans_z 246
targ_x  117
targ_y  139
targ_z  161

<...>

LOCALITE_Transducer_mm  Inf
loc_trans_x_mm  144.9

loc_trans_z_mm  221.02

LOCALITE_Target_mm  Inf
loc_targ_x_mm   105.3
loc_targ_y_mm   124.88

RAS_Transducer_mm   Inf

ras_trans_y_mm  -16.17

items.title: Placement Figures
items.text:
PRESTUS generates an overview of the selected transducer placement:

If path.localite_export is set, a copy of the plot and the position table is also written to <path.localite_export>/sub-XXX/ (io.dir_localite_export).

A T1 overlay plot (plot_placement_t1_overlay) is generated after the position is selected. It shows the transducer position and target on orthogonal T1 slices and is written to the subject output folder next to the standard placement figure.

items.title: Localite Planning Image
items.text: Optional. Localite can struggle with images that contain affine matrices in the image header. With placement.heuristic.save_localite_t1: true, PRESTUS writes a header-adjusted T1 planning image for Localite, based on the T1.nii.gz in the SimNIBS m2m directory. path.localite_export must be set; the image is written as <path.localite_export>/sub-XXX/sub-XXX_T1_forneuronav.nii.

items.title: Manual Transducer Placement
items.text:
When the transducer and target positions are already known, for example from an fMRI hotspot, an anatomical marker, or a previous session, no search is needed. placement.mode: 'manual' takes both points from the config and uses them exactly as given.

On this page:

  • Entering Coordinates: positions in voxels, RAS mm, or MNI mm, and how they are converted.

At a glance

  • When you need it: You already know where the transducer sits and where it aims.
  • Before you start: The T1w planning image; for MNI coordinates also the SimNIBS m2m_sub-XXX folder.

items.title: Entering Coordinates
items.text:
By default the coordinates are 1-based T1 voxel indices. Set placement.manual.coordinate_space to enter millimetres instead:

placement:
  mode: 'manual'
  manual:
    coordinate_space: 'ras'   # 'voxel' (default) | 'ras' | 'mni'
transducer:
  trans_pos: [-62.1, 12.4, 48.0]   # bowl apex, subject RAS+ mm
  focus_pos: [-21.5, 10.2, 2.3]
  • ras: subject RAS+ mm of the T1 (read from a viewer or neuronavigation), converted with ras_to_grid() via the T1 affine.
  • mni: MNI mm. Both points are converted with charm's nonlinear warp, as in MNI placement, but the transducer is not snapped to the scalp, and the warp is less exact near the scalp: check the placement figure. The points are used exactly as given. Requires the SimNIBS m2m_sub-XXX folder.

Conversion happens once per transducer in the placement stage, so modules.run_transducer_placement must be 1.

After conversion, the positions become voxel indices and coordinate_space is set to 'voxel'. The original inputs are kept in placement.manual.input_trans_pos / input_focus_pos. If neither focal_distance_ep nor focal_distance_bowl is set, the distance fallback from the positions is computed after conversion.

items.title: MNI Transducer Placement
items.text:
A transducer site and target given in MNI coordinates let one plan apply to every subject, but each subject's simulation needs both points in its own anatomy. placement.mode: 'mni' converts both points to the subject's T1 grid, snaps the transducer to the scalp, and sets its exit plane placement.skin_gap_mm (default 5 mm) off the scalp; no search is performed, so the result is deterministic. The heuristic mode, by contrast, takes only an MNI target and searches the scalp for a transducer position.

On this page:

  • How a Position Is Resolved: coordinate conversion, scalp snap, and standoff.
  • Limitations: the transducer types the mode assumes and what to check.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you know both points in template space, e.g. a group target and a standard scalp position.
  • Before you start: A SimNIBS segmentation of the subject (for the MNI-to-subject transforms).
placement:
  mode: 'mni'
  mni:
    trans_pos_mm: [-52,  -8,  58]   # desired transducer (scalp entry) in MNI mm
    focus_pos_mm: [-29,  -6,   7]   # focus / target in MNI mm
  skin_gap_mm: 5                    # gap between scalp and exit plane [mm]

A SimNIBS m2m_sub-XXX folder (under path.seg) is required: the conversion relies on final_tissues.nii.gz and the SimNIBS coordinate transforms.

items.title: How a Position Is Resolved
items.text:
1. Coordinate conversion. Both points are mapped MNI → subject RAS+ → grid voxel with charm's nonlinear warp (nonl), the only MNI transform SimNIBS 4 writes; the focus as the heuristic target.

  2. Snap to scalp. The warp is less exact near the scalp, so the converted transducer voxel is snapped to the nearest scalp voxel; a slightly off MNI entry coordinate still lands on the head surface.

  3. Standoff. The transducer is offset outward from the scalp along the focal axis (target → scalp) so that its exit plane lies placement.skin_gap_mm (default 5 mm) off the scalp, as in the heuristic. The bowl apex sits a further curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm behind the exit plane.

The resolved trans_pos / focus_pos (T1 grid voxels) are written into every configured transducer, and a QC overlay is saved. The log prints the resulting bowl-to-focus distance, and warns if it differs from a set transducer.focal_distance_bowl by more than 5 mm: the requested focus may then lie outside what the transducer can reach. Downstream simulation is unchanged.

Functions involved
  • Conversion: transform_coordinates and mni2subject_coords_LDfix, shared with the heuristic.
  • Scalp snap: tp_scalp_boundary (nearest scalp / outer-boundary voxel).
  • Standoff: transducer_scalp_geometry, shared with tp_candidate_mesh; the geometry the heuristic applies to every candidate.
  • QC overlay: plot_placement_t1_overlay.

items.title: Limitations
items.text:
• The standoff geometry assumes annular-style transducer fields (curv_radius_mm, elem_od_mm), as the heuristic does. The mode is intended for annular (CTX-style) transducers.
  • trans_pos_mm is a desired scalp entry. It is snapped to the scalp, so the converted point need not lie exactly on the surface.
  • Check the QC overlay. Converting a scalp coordinate through any registration is approximate.

See also: Transducer Placement overview, Heuristic placement, Coordinate systems.

items.title: Neuronavigation Read-In
items.text:
PRESTUS reads transducer poses recorded with the Localite neuronavigation system and simulates them post hoc, to verify the focus of the realised stimulation. The recorded pose decides where the simulated transducer sits and where its beam points, so the file you read it from and the offset from the tracker to the transducer shape every focus position and intensity the simulation reports. An example demo (without data) is in examples/demo_localite.m.

On this page:

  • Placement from a Recorded Pose: placement.mode: 'localite' and the focal distance it needs.
  • Realised Angle vs Planned Trajectory: which Localite export answers which question, and how the recorded pose becomes the simulated transducer and focus.

At a glance

  • When you need it: After a session, to simulate where the transducer actually was.
  • Before you start: Localite exports of the session and the planning T1 that was loaded into Localite.

Localite data pass through two stages. Ingestion (neuronav_gui, or neuronav_ingest_markers in a script; see GUI and script workflows) reads the raw exports of one subject and session, averages each recorded series and writes one normalised file pair. Placement (placement.mode: 'localite') reads that pair, or in file mode a single XML you point to.

Subpages:

  • Placing from a Recorded Pose: automatic and file mode, several transducers, many sessions; for anyone setting up a Localite run.
  • Localite Files, Offset, and Coordinates: folder layout and path keys, the tracker-to-bowl offset, and coordinate transforms; for anyone setting up paths, checking the transducer offset, or converting positions to voxels or MNI.
  • Localite Ingestion: GUI and Script Workflows: turning raw exports into named, averaged targets in neuronav_gui or with neuronav_ingest_batch; for anyone ingesting sessions.
  • Named Target Coordinates: resolving several named targets per session from several sources in your own script; for studies with more than one target per subject.

items.title: Placement from a Recorded Pose
items.text:
Set placement.mode: 'localite'. The pose's column 4 (position) and column 1 (beam direction) become the transducer and focus positions.

Focal distance required

transducer.focal_distance_ep (or focal_distance_bowl) must be set for Localite placement; config_default.yaml ships it as []. Other placement modes derive it from trans_pos/focus_pos, but here those positions are what the step produces. If neither is set, localite_matrix_to_positions raises PRESTUS:localite:missingConfig naming the missing field. The same check covers placement.mode = 'plantus', which resolves its final position through the same function.

How to select the recorded pose (automatic or file mode, several transducers, many sessions) is described in Placing from a Recorded Pose.

items.title: Realised Angle vs Planned Trajectory
items.text:
The Localite file types answer different questions. The wrong one silently mismatches the reported angle and the reported target.

  • The realised angle at the moment of stimulation is only available from TriggerMarkers (the tracked pose during the pulses, averaged per series) or InstrumentMarker (a static saved pose). Both store a measured rotation.
  • GUMMarkers (EntryTargetPair) carries no measured angle. Its 4×4 matrix is synthesised from the static Target point and a RotationReference vector, which is often unset in the source file (<Rotation angle="0.0" used="false">). With used="false", the angle neuronav_compute_series_statistics produces is a placeholder. Treat it as a real angle only if the source XML has Rotation used="true".
  • Static planned Entry/Target coordinates are never read by placement. This includes the Target field of a GUMMarkers EntryTargetPair and a standalone EntryTarget.xml. For single-target placement they are optional: TriggerMarkers or InstrumentMarker alone is sufficient. They matter only for target resolution, which uses them to identify which planned target a coil's series corresponds to (neuronav_match_entry_targets) and as a cross-check against pre-hoc planned coordinates (neuronav_resolve_target).
  • The reported focus position is axis-projected, not a stored coordinate. localite_matrix_to_positions computes focus_pos = trans_pos + focal_distance_bowl * ref_vec, where trans_pos = ref_pos + d * ref_vec is the bowl rear centre and d is the resolved transducer offset (with the default exit-plane origin this equals ref_pos + focal_distance_ep * ref_vec): it projects forward from the tracked position along the tracked beam axis by the calibrated focal distance. This keeps the reported target self-consistent with the reported angle. A separately clicked static Target point need not lie on the tracked beam axis.
Localite XML file formats

All formats are parsed by neuronav_compute_series_statistics, which handles single markers, repeated trigger trains, and multi-position recordings alike.

TriggerMarkers. Multiple triggers can be sent during stimulation to record the transducer location over time. Files are named TMSTrigger/TriggerMarkers_Coil0_<timestamp>. Recorded locations are averaged within each position series (identified by time-gap segmentation). Multiple positions per recording session are supported.

GUMMarkers. One or more static marker positions. Each Element is expected to be of type EntryTargetPair (with a Target/Marker/ColVec3D position and a Rotation/RotationReference/ColVec3D beam direction), from which a synthetic 4×4 matrix is constructed. Some Localite versions write a GUMMarkerList file that mixes EntryTargetPair and InstrumentMarker elements (type="InstrumentMarker" on the Element tag). Each element becomes its own series: InstrumentMarker elements keep their recorded 4×4 pose, EntryTargetPair elements the synthesised matrix. Only the former are instrument poses; placement refuses an EntryTargetPair series (PRESTUS:localite:notAPose).

InstrumentMarker. Static instrument positions stored as full 4×4 matrices in an InstrumentMarkerList file. Each InstrumentMarker entry contains a Marker/Matrix4D block with the same data{row}{col} field layout as TriggerMarkers. The ingested output of neuronav_ingest_markers uses this format.

EntryTarget (not for position or angle). Some Localite versions export an EntryTargetList XML with flat Target/Marker/ColVec3D and Rotation/RotationReference/ColVec3D entries at the top level (not wrapped in GUMMarkerList/Element). neuronav_compute_series_statistics does not read it, and placement never uses it. neuronav_read_entry_target reads it for one purpose: matching an operator-confirmed brain-target label against a target_map in multi-target studies (see Target coordinates from several sources).

items.title: Localite Files, Offset, and Coordinates
items.text:
A Localite pose is a 4×4 matrix in the coordinates of the planning image, and its origin is a point on the tracked instrument that need not be the transducer. A wrong origin offset shifts the whole simulation along the beam axis, and converting with the wrong image header displaces positions by tens of millimetres. This page gives the folders PRESTUS reads and writes, how the offset from the tracked origin to the transducer is set, and how positions are converted to voxels and MNI space.

On this page:

  • Localite File Layout: the folder layout PRESTUS reads from and writes to, and the path keys.
  • Transducer Offset (tracker_to_bowl_mm): from the tracked matrix origin to the bowl apex.
  • Coordinate Transforms: planning-image space, native voxels, and MNI.

At a glance

  • When you need it: You set up the Localite paths, check where the tracked origin sits on the transducer, or convert Localite positions to voxels or MNI.
  • Before you start: The planning T1 that was loaded into Localite and the transducer geometry (curv_radius_mm, dist_geom_ep_mm).

items.title: Input Layout
items.text:
<path.localite_raw>/
└── sub-XXX/                          subject folder (pipeline: sub-%03d of subject_id)
    └── ses-XX/                       session (a number n in the config means ses-0n)
        └── <placement.localite.loc_folder>/     default 'loc'; '' = no such level
            └── …any depth…           e.g. Session_<ts>/ or <patient>/Sessions/Session_<ts>/
                │                     (optionally restricted by placement.localite.session_folder_pattern)
                ├── TMSTrigger/TriggerMarkers_Coil<N>_<yyyyMMddHHmmssSSS>.xml
                ├── GUMMarkers<yyyyMMddHHmmssSSS>.xml       any depth
                └── EntryTarget<yyyyMMddHHmmssSSS>.xml      any depth; planned targets, used for naming only

This is Localite's own export structure placed below a sub-XXX/ses-XX/ pair; nothing inside the export needs renaming. Selection rules:

Rule Detail Marker type TriggerMarkers first; GUMMarkers only if no usable TriggerMarkers file exists Newest wins Files are ordered by the 17-digit timestamp in the file name (file dates change on copying) Size TriggerMarkers files ≤ 10 kB (no or few pulses) are skipped De-duplication A file byte-identical to one in the previous session (ses-(XX-1)) is skipped; Localite re-exports older sessions Series TriggerMarkers pulses are split into series at time gaps > 3× the median interval; series whose pulse count differs from expected_segment_length (default 80) by more than 20 are dropped ([] keeps all) Coils Without neuronav.coil_map: Coil0 only. With it: one TriggerMarkers_Coil<N> file per entry; each coil contributes one series per configured sequence; untracked blocks (all positions at 0) are skipped

The planning T1 that Localite coordinates refer to (see Coordinate transforms) is looked up as <path.localite_t1>/[sub-XXX/]<path.localite_t1_pattern> (default pattern sub-XXX_*T1*.nii*; path.localite_t1 defaults to path.localite_raw).

items.title: Output Layout
items.text:
<path.localite_post>/sub-XXX/ses-XX/
├── InstrumentMarker_sub-XXX_ses-XX.xml    InstrumentMarkerList, one entry per target:
│                                          Marker description = target name, Matrix4D = mean pose of the series
└── InstrumentMarker_sub-XXX_ses-XX.json   QC sidecar, one object per target (key = target name)
JSON field Meaning series_index Index of the detected series (after the pulse-count filter; as used by placement.localite.position) transducer_id Coil index markertype TriggerMarkers or GUMMarkers source_file Raw file the series came from N_pulses Pulses averaged position_dev_mm.mean/std Distance of the pulses from the series mean position [mm] rotation_dev_rad.mean/std Angle of the pulses from the mean orientation [rad]

With io.overwrite_files: 'never', an existing pair is kept.

items.title: Path Keys
items.text: Key Meaning path.localite_raw Raw Localite exports (read-only) path.localite_post Ingested outputs (written by ingestion, read by placement) path.localite_t1 Planning T1s; empty = path.localite_raw path.localite_t1_pattern File-name template of the planning T1 (%s = sub-XXX) path.localite_export Outputs meant for import into Localite (heuristic placement: position table, plot, Localite-ready T1), per subject in sub-XXX/ path.localite Deprecated. Read as path.localite_raw and as path.localite_export when those are empty (with a warning for the former)

items.title: Transducer Offset (tracker_to_bowl_mm)
items.text:
PRESTUS models the transducer position as the bowl rear centre, the bowl apex (trans_pos; bowl_pos in k-Wave's makeBowl); the acoustic focus lies focal_distance_bowl beyond it along the beam direction. What the Localite matrix origin (column 4) refers to depends on how the instrument was registered in Localite. The offset from that origin to the bowl rear centre is taken, in this order, from placement.localite.tracker_to_bowl_mm (explicit), the transducer geometry -(curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm) (assumes the origin is at the exit plane), or placement.localite.reference_distance_mm (fallback). All three share one sign convention along the beam direction (column 1, towards the head): negative puts the bowl rear centre behind the matrix origin, positive in front of it. A wrong assumption shifts the whole simulation along the beam axis by the difference between the assumed and actual origin.

placement:
  localite:
    tracker_to_bowl_mm: -15   # example: mm from the Localite matrix origin to the bowl rear centre
                              # negative = bowl rear is on the housing side (away from head)

The shipped fallback reference_distance_mm: 15 is positive: it places the bowl rear centre 15 mm in front of the matrix origin, which fits only an origin behind the bowl rear. PRESTUS does not document which physical origin this value assumes. The geometry-derived offset is used whenever curv_radius_mm and dist_geom_ep_mm are set (a flat element gives 0); with empty geometry PRESTUS falls back to reference_distance_mm. Set tracker_to_bowl_mm when the origin is not at the exit plane.

Determining the offset

Column 4 of the Localite 4×4 matrix is the position in RAS mm; column 1 is the beam direction (from the transducer face toward the target). These are the only two columns PRESTUS uses.

Possible matrix origin Value of tracker_to_bowl_mm Exit plane centre -(curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm) (negative; bowl rear is behind exit plane) Bowl rear centre 0 IR tracker cluster centroid Measured distance from cluster to bowl rear centre (positive when the cluster sits behind the bowl rear) Housing reference point Measured distance from reference to bowl rear centre

Option 1: Localite instrument definition file (recommended). The instrument definition is an XML file, stored in the Localite installation under Instruments/ or provided by the manufacturer. Its <ReferencePoint> or <Origin> tag describes which physical point the matrix origin corresponds to and its distance from transducer landmarks in mm.

Option 2: Empirical measurement (ruler / phantom). Place the transducer on a flat phantom surface and record a Localite position. Measure the distance from the phantom surface (= exit plane) to the IR tracker attachment on the housing. The bowl rear centre is about curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm mm behind the exit plane. Set tracker_to_bowl_mm = (bowl rear centre position) − (matrix origin position), in mm along the beam axis. Alternatively, acquire an MR image of a gel phantom with the transducer in place and compare the PRESTUS-predicted bowl voxel position against the visible gel/transducer interface.

Option 3: Contact Localite support (https://www.localite.de) with the instrument type and firmware version used during the recording.

tracker_to_bowl_mm takes priority over the geometry-derived distance and over reference_distance_mm. The geometry-derived value is correct only when the matrix origin is at the exit plane.

items.title: Coordinate Transforms
items.text:
See the coordinate system documentation.

Recorded Localite coordinates are relative to the planning image (e.g. T1_forneuronav) loaded in the neuronavigation software. That image has a zero-origin, diagonal affine (world = voxel × voxel_size_mm), not a scanner-isocentre world-space affine. Localite trigger matrices are therefore in planning-image space, not scanner world-space RAS.

The InstrumentMarker XML written by neuronav_ingest_markers keeps these coordinates as they are and labels the space "RAS": the axes are RAS-oriented, but the origin remains at the image corner. To convert to voxels, use ras_to_grid() with the planning T1 header, not the SimNIBS m2m T1 header. The m2m T1 has a full world-space affine; applying its inverse to planning-image coordinates displaces positions by tens of millimetres.

When SimNIBS is run on the planning T1, the resulting m2m_{sub}/T1.nii.gz shares the same voxel grid (SimNIBS keeps voxel dimensions and layout and updates only the affine). Voxel indices from ras_to_grid(localite_mm, planning_t1_header) are therefore valid for PRESTUS simulations that load the m2m T1; no reprojection is needed. See Coordinate Reference Systems.

SimNIBS' nonlinear transform matrices to MNI are relative to the final_tissues.nii.gz segmentation image, so PRESTUS applies a transform from the planning to the segmentation image before porting coordinates to MNI space. The chain is:

  1. Trigger to voxel (neuronav_convert_trigger_to_voxels): subject voxel indices
  2. Voxel to mm (neuronav_grid_to_mm_batch): subject mm
  3. Native mm to MNI mm (neuronav_apply_deformation): MNI mm

Optional, to average positions across subjects:

  1. Aggregate means in MNI mm across subjects (neuronav_get_group_mean_mni)
  2. Group mean MNI mm to subject mm and voxel indices (neuronav_convert_MNI_to_native)
Coordinate spaces of the neuronav functions Function Input Operation Output neuronav_convert_trigger_to_voxels Localite/trigger data (planning-image space mm, zero-origin RAS) Planning T1 header Subject (native) voxel indices grid_to_ras Subject voxel indices (i, j, k) Subject T1 NIfTI affine Subject native mm (scanner/world space) neuronav_apply_deformation (forward warp) Native mm locations Queries the subject's Conform2MNI_nonl.nii.gz MNI mm (for reporting, plotting, averaging) neuronav_get_group_mean_mni <path.sim>/sub-*/*_info.csv (trans_MNI_mm_*, target_MNI_mm_*) Mean across subjects/sessions (non-interpolated rows) MNI group-mean locations in mm and MNI voxel indices neuronav_convert_MNI_to_native (inverse warp) MNI mm group-mean locations SimNIBS nonlinear warp of the subject Native mm and segmentation voxel indices neuronav_export_session_csv Native voxel indices for target and transducer, native mm, MNI mm (from the deformation step), and MNI voxel indices (may be inaccurate with limited FOVs)

items.title: Placing from a Recorded Pose
items.text:
Localite placement reads one recorded pose per transducer, either from the ingested markers of a session or from a single XML file you name. The series or marker it reads sets the position and beam axis of the simulated transducer, so a wrong target or position simulates another pose than the one used for stimulation.

On this page:

  • Automatic Mode: Ingested Markers: reading the ingested pair of a subject and session.
  • File Mode: A Single XML File: reading one TriggerMarkers, GUMMarkers, or InstrumentMarker file.
  • Several Transducers (Bilateral Setups): one pose per transducer.
  • Many Subjects and Sessions: manifest rows from the Nexus, and the functions for standalone use.

At a glance

  • When you need it: You set placement.mode: 'localite' for a run.
  • Before you start: transducer.focal_distance_ep set (see Placement from a Recorded Pose), and either sessions ingested as in Localite Ingestion or a single Localite XML file. Folder layout and path keys: Localite File Layout.

items.title: Automatic Mode: Ingested Markers
items.text:
Leave placement.localite.file empty. The ingested pair under path.localite_post is read. If it does not exist yet and path.localite_raw is set, ingestion runs first (with neuronav.coil_map if configured, otherwise for the requested series only, named series_<position> or target).

path:
  localite_raw:  '/data/localite_raw'
  localite_post: '/data/derivatives/localite'
placement:
  mode: 'localite'
  localite:
    session: 2          # -> ses-02
    target: 'L_M1'      # ingested target name, or leave '' and use:
    position: 2         # detected-series index, matched against series_index in the JSON sidecar

To choose series and names interactively, ingest with neuronav_gui first; placement then only reads the result. A raw series that was not ingested is an error (PRESTUS:localite:noSeries), and an untracked series (position at the origin) is refused.

items.title: File Mode: A Single XML File
items.text:
Set placement.localite.file. TriggerMarkers, GUMMarkers, and InstrumentMarker files are accepted; the type is detected from the content.

placement:
  mode: 'localite'
  localite:
    file: '/path/to/TriggerMarkers_Coil0_20240820122011842.xml'
    position: 2        # detected series in the file (1-based, after the pulse-count filter), or:
    target: ''         # description of an InstrumentMarker / GUMMarkers entry

items.title: Several Transducers (Bilateral Setups)
items.text:
target and position take one entry per transducer; transducer i uses entry i, and each gets its own pose. A single value applies to every transducer. A list of the wrong length is an error (PRESTUS:localite:listLength).

placement:
  mode: 'localite'
  localite:
    session: 2
    target: [L_M1, R_M1]   # transducer(1) -> L_M1, transducer(2) -> R_M1

items.title: Many Subjects and Sessions
items.text:
For a study, the Nexus's Study tab turns the neuronav_gui outputs into manifest rows (Import from Localite…). It reads neuronav_ingest_summary.csv and the per-session InstrumentMarker_*.json files under path.localite_post, and makes either one run per target, or one run per session with the targets assigned to transducers 1, 2, … (left first, alphabetical, or a given order). The runs use placement.mode: localite, so PRESTUS reads the ingested markers itself. See Group analysis.

Entry points and standalone use

Placement runs in preproc_transducer_placement; the older placement.localite.enabled = 1 switch in preproc_head uses the same code. Both go through neuronav_localite_pose, and the pose's column 4 (position) and column 1 (beam direction) go to localite_matrix_to_positions. All paths share the same XML parser and position math.

For multi-position or multi-session workflows outside the pipeline, call neuronav_ingest_markers → neuronav_select_localite → neuronav_compute_series_statistics → neuronav_convert_trigger_to_voxels directly (see examples/demo_localite.m and Target coordinates from several sources). Average transducer and target locations can be provided in several coordinate spaces; native image space is the one PRESTUS uses. Standard-space definitions (experimental) allow e.g. plotting average transducer positions in standard space.

items.title: Named Target Coordinates
items.text:
When a session has several named targets, each simulated focus needs a coordinate and a record of how far that coordinate can be trusted. neuronav_resolve_target takes each target's coordinate from the best source available, from a pre-hoc lookup table down to a projection along the tracked transducer axis, and reports which source it used.

On this page:

  • Target Coordinates from Several Sources: what the functions resolve and when to use them.
  • Inputs You Provide: the recordings, the target_map, and the optional sources.
  • Resolution Order: the four tiers and their confidence.
  • Worked Example: a loop over subjects and sessions.
  • Exported Session CSV: the per-session output and the function reference.

At a glance

  • When you need it: A study has more than one named target per subject and session, or needs a documented answer to where each target coordinate came from.
  • Before you start: The raw Localite exports and the planning T1 per subject; ingestion as in Localite Ingestion.

items.title: Target Coordinates from Several Sources
items.text: When a session has several named targets, your own extraction script resolves named, per-session brain-target coordinates (e.g. this subject's L_V1 on ses-03) from whichever raw Localite export the operator recorded, with a logged account of how confident each resolved coordinate is. The resolved coordinate is what a simulation uses as focus_pos. This is not a pipeline mode: the functions read the ingested files and add to the single-target placement pipeline rather than replacing it. Use them when a study needs more than one named target per subject, or a documented answer to where each reported coordinate came from. Localite file formats are in Neuronavigation read-in and coordinate spaces in Localite Files, Offset, and Coordinates.

items.title: Inputs You Provide
items.text:
1. Raw entry-point recordings per subject and session, in any supported format (TriggerMarkers, GUMMarkers, or InstrumentMarker). This supplies the transducer/coil position, always read from the current session's own recording.

  2. A target_map naming your targets, built by neuronav_build_target_map from the neuronav.coil_map you construct per subject and session:

    coil_map(1).coil   = 0;              % hardware coil index (0-based)
coil_map(1).target = 'L_V1';        % target_name -- your convention
coil_map(2).coil   = 1;
coil_map(2).target = 'R_V1';
target_map = neuronav_build_target_map(coil_map);
parameters.neuronav.coil_map = coil_map;   % ingest reads one file per coil

    A coil that records several position blocks in one session lists them as coil_map(i).sequences(j).target; ingest then takes that many series from the coil's file, in order (untracked blocks with every pulse at the origin are skipped), matching the series_index that neuronav_build_target_map assigns.

The following inputs are optional. Each one you provide moves more targets up the confidence ranking (see Resolution order).

  • EntryTarget exports, for at least some sessions, if your operator uses Localite's target-confirmation feature. target_map(i).localite_key is matched (case-insensitive substring) against each EntryTarget description. Set it whenever your description convention differs from target_name, and pass a cell array of candidates if more than one convention is in use across sessions:

    coil_map(1).localite_key = {'LEFT V1', 'L_V1', 'LEFT V', 'L_V'};

  • A pre-hoc target lookup table, if your study establishes targets before the session (e.g. a placement or optimisation step run ahead of time). This is the highest-confidence source when present and is cross-checked against EntryTarget wherever both exist. neuronav_read_target_lookup.m documents the CSV schema (subject_id, target_name, space, x, y, z). Build this file with your own per-study script from whatever your planning step produces.

Why several sources

Across one study, the same target was confirmed in different ways for different subjects and sessions: an operator-confirmed EntryTarget export for the exact session; an EntryTarget export only from an earlier session; no EntryTarget export at all (workflows that only used GUMMarkers, which has no separate target confirmation); two label conventions in the EntryTarget description across sessions ("LEFT V" and "L_V"); and a pre-hoc planned coordinate from individual anatomical segmentation, independent of Localite. neuronav_resolve_target resolves each target from the best source available for that target and reports which one it used.

items.title: Resolution Order
items.text:
neuronav_resolve_target tries these in order per target and returns which one supplied each row (target_source). Check this before treating a coordinate as ground truth.

Tier target_source value What it is Confidence 1 target_lookup Your pre-hoc lookup table (see above) Highest: established before the session 2 entrytarget_current This session's own EntryTarget export, label-matched High: operator-confirmed, same day 3 entrytarget:<session> Another session's EntryTarget export (nearest prior session tried first) Medium: operator-confirmed, different day 4 projected Transducer-axis geometric projection from the tracked entry pose Estimate only: no operator confirmation exists for this target

Because of tier 4, the resolved coordinate is never NaN: every target gets a value, but tier-4 rows are not confirmed. In one cross-check, tier-4 estimates differed from the tier-1 target by 3-5 voxels for a subject without any EntryTarget export, while tier-1 and tier-2 values matched to within 0-1 voxel. If a study needs sub-voxel target accuracy and some subjects stay on tier 4, provide a lookup table (tier 1) for those subjects.

items.title: Worked Example
items.text:
for i_sub = 1:numel(all_subjects)
    sub_id = all_subjects{i_sub};
    for i_ses = 1:numel(sessions)
        session = sessions{i_ses};

        coil_map = build_my_coil_map(sub_id, session);   % your own logic
        target_map = neuronav_build_target_map(coil_map);
        parameters.neuronav.coil_map = coil_map;

        [xml_path, ~, results] = neuronav_ingest_markers(parameters, sub_id, session, target_map);
        active_sides = find(~cellfun(@isempty, results));

        [trans_ras, trans_pos, target_ras, target_pos_projected] = ...
            neuronav_convert_trigger_to_voxels(sub_id, active_sides, results, parameters);

        t1_header = niftiinfo(my_planning_t1_path(sub_id));   % see doc_placement_neuronav_coordinates.md

        [target_vox, target_mm, target_source] = neuronav_resolve_target( ...
            parameters, sub_id, session, sessions, target_map, t1_header, ...
            target_pos_projected, my_target_lookup_csv_path);

        % target_vox is what you feed into PRESTUS as focus_pos.
        % target_source tells you, per row, whether that's confirmed or estimated.

        neuronav_export_session_csv(sub_id, session, {target_map.target_name}, ...
            outputs_folder, trans_pos, target_vox, trans_ras, target_ras, ...
            [], [], [], [], 0, target_mm, target_source);
    end
end

items.title: Exported Session CSV
items.text:
neuronav_export_session_csv writes one row per target with, among other columns:

  • trans_native_vox_x/y/z: transducer/coil position, always from the current session's own recording.
  • target_native_vox_x/y/z: the resolved target (target_vox above). A simulation script reads this as focus_pos.
  • target_localite_mm_x/y/z: the EntryTarget-matched mm coordinate, tiers 2-3 only. NaN for tier 1 and tier 4 rows, so it stays a reliable operator-confirmed signal independent of target_source.
  • target_projected_mm_x/y/z: the tier-4 geometric estimate, always computed whichever tier was used, kept for comparison.
  • target_source: see the resolution-order table above.
Function reference

The ingestion functions (neuronav_ingest_markers, neuronav_ingest_batch, neuronav_scan_sessions) are listed under GUI workflow; the naming functions under Series naming.

Function Role neuronav_build_target_map Expands your coil_map into the flat target_map every other function here consumes neuronav_convert_trigger_to_voxels Converts ingested marker positions to native voxel/mm space; also computes the tier-4 axis-projected target neuronav_read_entry_target Reads the latest EntryTarget*.xml snapshot for one subject/session neuronav_match_entry_targets Label-matches target_map entries against EntryTarget descriptions (tiers 2-3's matching step) neuronav_read_target_lookup Reads your pre-hoc lookup CSV (tier 1) neuronav_resolve_target The orchestrator: runs all four tiers in order for one subject/session and returns the resolved coordinate + provenance per target. Call this one function rather than the matching/lookup functions individually. neuronav_export_session_csv Writes the per-session summary CSV, including a target_source column neuronav_plot_placement QC plot of every target_map entry's entry/target pair on the segmented head neuronav_get_group_mean_mni / neuronav_apply_inverse_deformation Group-mean-MNI fallback for subjects missing trigger data entirely (a more severe gap than a missing target confirmation; see Coordinate transforms)

items.title: Localite Ingestion: GUI and Script Workflows
items.text:
Localite placement simulates the transducer pose the operator recorded, and ingestion decides which recorded series become simulated targets and what each is called. A series kept by mistake, or a name given to the wrong series, puts the simulated focus on another target than the one stimulated. This page turns raw Localite exports into the named, averaged targets that placement.mode: localite reads.

On this page:

  • Shared Settings File: the config keys that the GUI and scripts share.
  • Series Naming: the naming rule and the label map for inconsistent operator labels.
  • GUI Workflow: single sessions, batches, and the MNI view in neuronav_gui.
  • Script Workflow: batch ingestion with neuronav_ingest_batch and the summary CSV.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Once per session (or in batch for a whole study) before simulating recorded poses.
  • Before you start: The raw Localite exports (path.localite_raw).

Ingestion turns recorded Localite positions into named, averaged targets per subject and session (folder layout and output files: Localite file layout). Run it in neuronav_gui, on the PRESTUS Nexus's Placement ▸ Localite page (settings from the study config; see Localite page), or scripted with neuronav_ingest_batch. All three run the same functions on the same settings:

GUI (neuronav_gui) Script (neuronav_ingest_batch) Best for Checking a session, choosing series by eye, setting up the label map Many subjects and sessions, reproducible re-runs, HPC Session selection Single session, or tickboxes in the Batch window (All / None / Not yet ingested) A table or {sub, ses} list, e.g. rows of neuronav_scan_sessions Settings Form fields, ⬆ Load settings… / ⬇ Save settings… (YAML) The same YAML via load_parameters Output InstrumentMarker_<sub>_<ses>.xml/.json + neuronav_ingest_summary.csv identical

Resolving the coordinates of several named targets per session in your own script is described in Named Target Coordinates.

items.title: Shared Settings File
items.text:
Every setting that affects ingestion and naming is a config key. Keep them in the study YAML (or a separate neuronav_settings.yaml saved from the GUI) and use that file in both workflows:

path:
  localite_raw:  '/data/localite_raw'          # <raw>/sub-XXX/ses-XX/[loc/]…
  localite_post: '/data/derivatives/localite'  # ingested outputs + summary CSV
  localite_t1:   '/data/localite_raw'          # planning T1s (for voxel coordinates); default = localite_raw

placement:
  localite:
    loc_folder: 'loc'              # '' if the export sits directly under ses-XX/
    expected_segment_length: 80    # pulses per TriggerMarkers series ([] = keep all)

io:
  overwrite_files: 'always'        # 'never' keeps existing ingested files

neuronav:
  coil_map: []                     # multi-coil setups, see doc_placement_neuronav_targets.md
  suggest_names: true              # name series after the planned target on their beam axis
  axis_tolerance_mm: 10
  target_depth_mm: [0, 150]
  target_labels:                   # planned-target labels as recorded -> study target names
    - target: 'L_V1'
      labels: ['LEFT V1', 'L_V1*']
    - target: 'R_V1'
      labels: ['RIGHT V1', 'R_V1*']
  batch_write: 'all'               # or 'named'

A file saved with ⬇ Save settings… contains exactly these keys and is a valid PRESTUS config: load_parameters('neuronav_settings.yaml') merges it with the defaults. Settings the GUI has no field for (for example transducer geometry, needed for focus coordinates) come from a config loaded with ⬆ Load settings…; load the study config first, then adjust.

items.title: Series Naming
items.text:
Each detected series gets a name by one rule (neuronav_name_series), the same in the GUI and the batch:

  1. Coil table / neuronav.coil_map: a target name given there for that coil/block.
  2. Planned target on the beam axis (if suggest_names is true). The session's named planned targets (the latest EntryTarget export and the EntryTargetPairs of its GUMMarkers exports, each label at its most recent position) are collected by neuronav_read_label_candidates. A recorded series takes the target closest to its beam axis if it lies within axis_tolerance_mm and at a depth inside target_depth_mm. A GUMMarkers EntryTargetPair series uses its own label. The label is then passed through target_labels.
  3. Default: series_<k>.

Repeated names get _rep2, _rep3, …; a planned pair that shares its label with a recorded pose in the same file becomes <label>_target.

items.title: The Label Map (neuronav.target_labels)
items.text:
Operators label planned targets inconsistently across sessions (LEFT V1 in one session, L_V1_1 in the next). target_labels maps recorded labels to the names your study uses. Each entry lists label patterns (* and ? wildcards, case-insensitive); the first matching entry wins; a label that matches no entry is kept as recorded. neuronav_map_label('L_V1_1', map) shows the result for a single label. When target_labels is empty, labels are used as found.

To see which labels the data contain, scan all sessions:

parameters = load_parameters('study.yaml');
[sessions, labels] = neuronav_scan_sessions(parameters);
labels(:, {'label', 'stem', 'target', 'n_subjects', 'n_sessions'})

labels.target is the name each label gets with the current map; labels.stem groups numbered variants (the label without a trailing _<number>, e.g. L_caudateV2_1, L_caudateV2_2 → L_caudateV2). Turn either into a map and store it:

map = neuronav_label_map_from_scan(labels, 'stem');   % or edit labels.target, then 'target'
parameters.neuronav.target_labels = map;
yaml.dumpFile('target_labels.yaml', struct('neuronav', struct('target_labels', map)));

In the GUI, the Batch window shows the same label table: Group labels by stem fills the target column of unmapped labels from their stems (existing mappings are kept), Use labels as found resets all of them, and any cell can be edited. Only labels whose target differs from the label end up in the saved map. The map applies to single-session naming too.

Check the name sources afterwards: the GUI's Name from column and the summary's rule, label, axis_dist_mm, and depth_mm columns show where each name came from. A match far from the usual focal depth usually means the intended target is missing from the export; narrow target_depth_mm to reject such matches.

items.title: GUI Workflow
items.text:
neuronav_gui                   % empty form
neuronav_gui('study.yaml')     % pre-fill from a study config
neuronav_gui(parameters)       % pre-fill from a parameter struct

items.title: Single Session
items.text:
1. Set the raw root (containing <sub>/<ses>/<loc folder>/…; leave Localite folder empty if the export sits directly under <ses>/) and the output root. The full layout is in Localite file layout. The subject and session dropdowns list the sub-* / ses-* folders found; they can also be typed (a bare number 2 means ses-02).
  2. ▶ Detect series detects the series into a temporary folder; nothing is written yet. Check the series table and the plots.
  3. Tick the series to keep, check each target name (and optionally set a #rrggbb colour), then ✓ Write outputs. Changing any input after detection disables writing until series are detected again.
Settings read from a config, the series table, and the pulse filter

Settings read from a config (all optional): path.localite_raw (falls back to path.localite), path.localite_post, placement.localite.loc_folder / voxel_size / expected_segment_length / session, io.overwrite_files, neuronav.coil_map.

The series table lists every detected series with pulse count, position deviation (mm from the series mean position), rotation deviation (rad from the mean orientation) and a flag for untracked series (all positions at the origin). The tabs show a 3-D plot of every pulse position (small dot = one pulse, ring = series mean, arrow = beam direction; no arrow for GUMMarkers), per-pulse deviation traces (one dot per pulse), all raw marker files found with the one used marked, and the captured log/warnings.

The Pulses per series filter (expected_segment_length, default 80) drops TriggerMarkers series whose pulse count differs from it by more than 20; leave it blank to keep all series.

items.title: Suggested Target Names
items.text:
With Suggest from planned targets ticked (default), detection also names each series after the planned target it was aimed at. The Name from column shows the source and the off-axis distance and depth of each match (or the nearest miss), and the 3-D plot marks the candidates (×) and the axis to each matched target. Names typed into the coil table are kept. ↻ Re-apply to series re-runs the naming after changing the tolerance or depth window.

A pose aimed at a target missing from the export takes the nearest remaining one, so check depth and distance: a match far outside the usual focal depth is suspect. Narrow Target depth around the focal distance to reject it. On the example data, all recorded poses whose planned target was in the export matched it, 0.7–4 mm off-axis.

How series are matched to planned targets

The naming runs neuronav_read_label_candidates and neuronav_suggest_target_names:

  • Candidates are the named, set targets of the session's latest EntryTarget export and of the EntryTargetPairs in its GUMMarkers exports. Each label is kept once, at its most recent position.
  • A recorded pose (TriggerMarkers series, or a GUMMarkers InstrumentMarker) takes the candidate closest to its beam axis (the line from the mean position along matrix column 1), provided it lies within Axis tolerance (default 10 mm) and at a depth inside Target depth (default 0–150 mm).
  • A GUMMarkers EntryTargetPair series uses its own label; when a pose in the same file matched that label, the pair becomes <label>_target and the pose keeps the bare name. Repeated blocks on one target get _rep2, _rep3, ….
Single-coil and multi-coil

With the coil table empty, ingest uses the newest non-duplicate TriggerMarkers_Coil0 file (falling back to GUMMarkers) and every detected series becomes a row. With one row per coil, ingest uses neuronav.coil_map: it reads one file per coil and keeps one series per target listed for that coil, skipping untracked blocks. For a coil that recorded several blocks, enter comma-separated target names (e.g. L_M1, L_M1 → L_M1_1, L_M1_2).

items.title: Many Sessions
items.text:
▦ Batch… opens a window that scans the raw root and lists every session with its marker files, planned labels, and whether it is already ingested.

  1. Tick sessions (All, None, Not yet ingested, or individually).
  2. Check the label table on the right; group or rename targets.
  3. Choose Write all or named, then ▶ Run batch. Each session's status updates as it is processed; written targets are listed below and in the summary CSV.

⬇ Save settings… writes the settings (including the label map) as YAML for scripts or later GUI sessions.

The Batch window calls neuronav_ingest_batch with the main window's settings, so a saved settings file reproduces a GUI batch run in a script:

p = load_parameters('neuronav_settings.yaml');
neuronav_ingest_batch(p, {'sub-001', 'ses-01'; 'sub-002', 'ses-01'});

items.title: MNI View
items.text:
◎ MNI view… (in the Batch window) maps the summary CSV to MNI space and plots transducer, focus and beam axis of every subject and session over an MNI head outline.

Loading, filtering, and saving the MNI view

MNI view reads the summary CSV (default <output root>/neuronav_ingest_summary.csv, i.e. every session ingested so far) and, on ▶ Load & map to MNI, maps each target's transducer, focus, and Localite pose to MNI mm. Set SimNIBS root (path.seg); the planning T1 is found as in the main window (path.localite_t1). Subjects without a warp or planning T1 are listed in the status line and left out. The 3-D plot shows transducers (●), foci (◆), the beam axis between them, and optionally the tracker pose (▲) over a head outline. Tick or untick subjects, sessions, and targets in the three tables, colour by target, subject, or session, and hover a point for its subject, session, and target. ⬇ Save CSV… writes the summary with the MNI columns.

Warp and head outline

The mapping uses neuronav_summary_to_mni: planning T1 → m2m_<sub>/final_tissues.nii.gz → m2m_<sub>/toMNI/Conform2MNI_nonl.nii.gz. The outline is taken from Head template: SimNIBS's MNI152_T1_1mm.nii.gz when a SimNIBS installation is found (startup.simnibs_bin_path, or the default install folder); left empty, it is taken from the first mapped subject's final_tissues_MNI.nii.gz.

Functions Function Role neuronav_scan_sessions Inventory: sessions, marker files, planned labels, label table with stems neuronav_label_map_from_scan Label table → neuronav.target_labels neuronav_map_label Apply the label map to one label neuronav_detect_series Detect the series of one session without writing neuronav_name_series Naming rule (coil table > planned target > default) neuronav_ingest_batch Loop: detect, name, write, summary CSV neuronav_ingest_markers Write one session's ingested XML/JSON for a given target map neuronav_summary_to_mni Add MNI coordinates (pose, transducer, focus) to the summary via the SimNIBS nonlinear warp

items.title: Script Workflow
items.text:
parameters = load_parameters('study.yaml');   % paths, ingestion, naming, transducer

% 1. Inventory: which sessions exist, which labels they contain
[sessions, labels] = neuronav_scan_sessions(parameters);

% 2. Optional: set or refine the label map (see above)
% parameters.neuronav.target_labels = neuronav_label_map_from_scan(labels, 'stem');

% 3. Ingest all sessions with marker files, or a subset
todo = sessions(sessions.n_trigger + sessions.n_gum > 0, :);
% todo = todo(ismember(todo.sub, {'sub-001', 'sub-004'}), :);
% todo = todo(~todo.ingested, :);          % only sessions not ingested yet
summary = neuronav_ingest_batch(parameters, todo);

neuronav_ingest_batch(parameters) without a selection processes every session found. For a single session, neuronav_ingest_batch(parameters, {'sub-001', 'ses-02'}). Per session, the batch detects the series (nothing is written yet), names them, writes every tracked series (batch_write: 'all') or only the named ones ('named'), and adds one summary row per written target. Untracked series and coil dropouts are never written. Sessions that fail or have nothing to write get one row whose status says why; the batch continues with the next session.

items.title: Summary CSV
items.text:
<path.localite_post>/neuronav_ingest_summary.csv collects all sessions. Re-running a subset replaces that subset's rows and keeps the others. Columns:

Column Meaning sub, ses, target Session and target name (empty when nothing was written) series_index, coil Detected series (as in placement.localite.position) and coil index rule coil_map, heuristic, or default (see naming) label, label_source Planned-target label as recorded, and the file it came from axis_dist_mm, depth_mm Distance of that target from the beam axis, and its depth along it n_pulses, pos_dev_mm, rot_dev_rad Series QC (as in the JSON sidecar) markertype, source_file Raw file the series came from pose_x/y/z, beam_x/y/z Mean instrument position and beam direction (Localite planning-image mm) trans_ras_*, focus_ras_* Transducer (bowl rear centre) and focus [mm], via localite_matrix_to_positions trans_vox_*, focus_vox_* The same in planning-T1 voxels xml, status Ingested file and outcome

Transducer, focus, and voxel coordinates need the transducer focal distance (transducer.focal_distance_ep or _bowl) and the planning T1 (path.localite_t1, pattern path.localite_t1_pattern); when either is missing they are NaN and status says why. The pose columns are always filled.

placement.mode: 'localite' reads the ingested files for simulation.

items.title: PlanTUS Placement
items.text:
The entry point decides which part of the skull the beam crosses and whether the focus can reach the target. Given a T1-weighted image, a SimNIBS head mesh, a target-ROI mask, and a transducer configuration, PlanTUS (placement.mode: 'plantus') scores every skin vertex as a candidate transducer position on skin–target distance, skin and skull angles, skull thickness, and beam–target overlap. PRESTUS places the transducer at the vertex with the best weighted score, or at a vertex you choose on the maps on the Nexus PlanTUS page (or in Connectome Workbench).

On this page:

  • Running PlanTUS: the steps of a placement run.
  • Choosing the Position: automatic, on the Nexus PlanTUS page, or in Workbench.
  • External Dependencies: the tools each mode needs.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you want an optimised, documented choice of entry point, or to compare focal depths.
  • Before you start: The full SimNIBS mesh and a PlanTUS installation, 2.0 or later (Installation).

Experimental

PlanTUS placement is under active development. Verify results manually before use in a study.

Limitations

  • The Nexus PlanTUS page needs the maps of an earlier run (save_metrics: true) and draws them where the Nexus runs; the run itself can be headless.
  • Choosing in Workbench needs a display (desktop or VNC), Connectome Workbench wb_view, and pynput. On macOS, the terminal or MATLAB needs Accessibility permission for pynput. Without a display (Linux), PlanTUS runs headless.
  • The Workbench review dialog needs PyQt5 in the SimNIBS Python. It ships with SimNIBS; without it, the last clicked vertex is placed without review.
  • To see errors from the launcher directly, run prestus_plantus_gui_launcher.py from a terminal (step 5b).

items.title: Running PlanTUS
items.text:
1. Set placement.mode: plantus, the placement.plantus paths and target, and the calibrated focal_distance_list / flhm_list.

    placement:
  mode: plantus
  plantus:
    script_path: /path/to/PlanTUS     # contains code/PlanTUS.py
    target_name: target               # names the output folder
    mni_target_mm: [-29, -6, 7]       # example; empty = transducer.focus_pos

  2. In the Nexus, click Compute maps on the Placement card (or on Placement ▸ PlanTUS). PlanTUS computes the criterion maps (a few minutes) and places the transducer at the composite-score optimum; no simulation runs. In MATLAB, run the pipeline with placement.plantus.vertex: [].

  3. Open Placement ▸ PlanTUS. The skin is coloured by the composite score; choose a criterion under Map to see one map. Click a skin position: the panel lists its criteria, composite score, and rank, and the view shows the beam axis and the transducer there, in the housing Placement ▸ 3D draws.
  4. Click Place here. The Nexus sets placement.plantus.vertex and places the transducer at that vertex on the same maps, without recomputing them. The config keeps the choice, so a later simulation run uses it.
  5. Check the placement report and the Viewer. Section 5a explains the evaluation it contains.

items.title: Choosing the Position
items.text:
placement.plantus.vertex and placement.plantus.interactive ([], the default, follows simulation.interactive) select how the vertex is chosen:

Setting Script Vertex selection Automatic (vertex: [], interactive: 0) prestus_plantus_launcher.py Weighted composite score; no display required Chosen vertex (vertex: N) prestus_plantus_launcher.py --do_only_trajectory N Vertex N (0-based) of the maps of an earlier run in the same placement run folder, chosen on the Nexus PlanTUS page; the maps are not recomputed Workbench (vertex: [], interactive: 1) prestus_plantus_gui_launcher.py The five criterion maps in Connectome Workbench; you click a vertex, close wb_view, see the transducer there, and confirm it in a review dialog

Automatic and Workbench runs compute the same maps and composite score (steps 2 to 5a) and write the same files. A chosen vertex is placed only while the target is where the maps were computed for: if the target moved more than 1 mm, the run stops and asks you to clear placement.plantus.vertex and compute the maps again. A chosen vertex belongs to one subject's maps; for a study, give it per run in a manifest column. Only Workbench runs need pynput, wb_view, and PyQt5.

Both modes share all code except vertex selection (plantus_common.py). The scripts replicate PlanTUS_wrapper.py (Mainz group, at placement.plantus.script_path) but take CLI arguments instead of hard-coded paths.

How a run computes its criteria, composite score, and placement is described in PlanTUS: How It Works.

items.title: External Dependencies
items.text:
Tool Automatic / chosen vertex Workbench Used in step SimNIBS Python (nibabel, scipy, nilearn, vtk, h5py), see installation guide ✓ ✓ All steps PlanTUS Python library (PlanTUS.py) ✓ ✓ All steps trimesh, pandas ✓ ✓ Surfaces, avoidance mask, target model PyYAML (or built-in fallback) ✓ ✓ YAML config loading Connectome Workbench wb_view – ✓ Interactive scene display pynput Python package – ✓ Mouse click listener for wb_view PyQt5 (part of SimNIBS) – ✓ Review dialog

The launchers check for these tools before they start.

Install trimesh, potpourri3d, and pynput (Workbench picker) in the SimNIBS conda environment. PlanTUS uses potpourri3d for exact geodesic distances when it shrinks the avoidance mask; without it, PlanTUS falls back to an approximation, so the mask can differ slightly between installs:

conda activate simnibs_v4.6.0
pip install trimesh potpourri3d pynput

items.title: PlanTUS: How It Works
items.text:
PlanTUS scores every position on the scalp and places the transducer at the best one. This page follows a run step by step: what it reads, how each criterion and the composite score are computed, and how the chosen position becomes the PRESTUS placement.

On this page:

  • Step-by-Step Pipeline: inputs, avoidance mask, criteria, composite score, evaluation, and placement geometry.
  • Coordinate Conventions: the frames PlanTUS and PRESTUS exchange.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To understand or tune a PlanTUS placement, or to check why a position was chosen.
  • Before you start: A PlanTUS run set up as in PlanTUS Placement.

items.title: 1  Parse Inputs
items.text:
PRESTUS writes a flat transducer YAML for PlanTUS.

The skin–target distance window

position_transducer_plantus.m derives the skin–target distance window from the transducer calibration, unless placement.plantus.min_distance_mm, max_distance_mm, and optimal_distance_mm are set:

Field Value written by PRESTUS (when not set) min_distance max(0, min(focal_distance_list) − max(flhm_list)) max_distance max(focal_distance_list) + max(flhm_list) optimal_distance mean(focal_distance_list), the desired skin–target distance

If max(flhm_list) is NaN or ≤ 0, a 10 mm margin is used instead. For a steerable array, list the steering depths in focal_distance_list and set the window to the steering range. The default margin (the largest FLHM, often > 50 mm) otherwise admits skin spots the focus cannot reach.

Launcher inputs and the FLHM fit

Input Description t1_filepath Subject T1.nii.gz (SimNIBS output) simnibs_mesh_filepath Head mesh sub-XXX.msh (charm output) target_mask_filepath Binary NIfTI sphere centred on the target tx_config_yaml Transducer + placement parameters (written by PRESTUS)

The YAML is flat. Key fields: max_distance, min_distance, optimal_distance, transducer_diameter, plane_offset, additional_offset, focal_distance_list, flhm_list, five weight_* scalars. Without optimal_distance in the YAML, the launcher uses (min_distance + max_distance) / 2.

PlanTUS fits FLHM against focal distance with a cubic, which needs at least 4 points. With fewer (e.g. the single O'Neil estimate when no axial profile CSV is given), the launchers (plantus_compat.py) interpolate linearly and hold FLHM constant outside the calibrated range. Non-finite pairs are dropped.

items.title: 2  Convert SimNIBS Mesh to Surfaces
items.text:
PlanTUS.convert_simnibs_mesh_to_surfaces extracts .surf.gii surfaces from the .msh mesh. The skin surface is then smoothed with placement.plantus.skin_smoothing_iterations Taubin passes (default 2, as in PlanTUS) before any criterion is computed; this reduces mesh noise in the normals and so in the angle maps.

Surfaces extracted

Surface SimNIBS tags File Skin 1005 skin.surf.gii Skull 1007, 1008 skull.surf.gii

SimNIBS also produces skull.stl, used for the skull-entry angle (4d).

items.title: 3  Build the Avoidance Mask
items.text:
Skin vertices over air cavities and near the eyes and ears are excluded from the composite score.

Excluded vertices and required tools

Skin vertices over air cavities and sinuses, within 30 mm of each eye centre and within 15 mm of the tragus are excluded from the composite score (avoidance == 0), and the mask is eroded by transducer_radius mm as a safety margin. The step needs final_tissues.nii.gz and eeg_positions/Fiducials.csv from the m2m folder, and PlanTUS builds the mask in Python. If any of these is missing, the step is skipped with a warning and all vertices remain eligible.

How the mask is built (create_avoidance_mask)

  1. Air cavities / sinuses: vertices whose outward normal ray hits air in final_tissues.nii.gz (holes filled and the air surface extracted in Python).
  2. Eyes: vertices within 30 mm of each eye centre (tag 1006, centres by k-means on x).
  3. Ears (tragus): vertices within 15 mm of LPA/RPA from eeg_positions/Fiducials.csv, shifted 1.5 cm posterior.
  4. Erosion: the mask is eroded by transducer_radius mm.

items.title: 4  Score Each Vertex
items.text:
PlanTUS scores every skin vertex on five metrics: 4a to 4d here, 4e below.

Metrics 4a to 4d

Metric Definition Better 4a Skin–target distance d_i Euclidean distance from vertex i to the target mask's centre of mass (PlanTUS.roi_center_of_gravity). The score uses the absolute deviation from optimal_distance; vertices outside [min_distance, max_distance] are excluded (see 5a). Lower deviation 4b Skin–target angle α_i Angle (degrees) between the skin normal and the vector to the target centre. Lower 4c Skin–target intersection x_i Path length of the 200 mm outward-normal ray inside the target mask STL (PlanTUS.stl_from_nii); chords are summed for several entry–exit pairs. Higher 4d Skin–skull angle β_i Angle between the skin normal and the skull normal where the 40 mm ray meets the skull. NaN (worst) where it meets no skull. Lower

items.title: 4e  Skull Thickness
items.text:
Bone path length (mm) along the 4d ray.

Sampling and missing values

final_tissues.nii.gz (next to the SimNIBS mesh) is sampled every 0.25 mm (nearest voxel) up to 50 mm from the skin. Bone samples (labels 4, 7, 8: bone, compact, spongy) are counted until the first intracranial sample (labels 1–3: WM, GM, CSF). Lower is better.

t_i is NaN (worst) where the ray meets no bone or reaches no intracranial tissue within 50 mm (face, neck, skull base). Without final_tissues.nii.gz, t_i is NaN everywhere, a warning is logged, and weight_skull_thickness is ignored.

A few vertices get implausibly thin values (≤ 1 mm): neck rays reaching the spinal canal, and skin next to the ear where charm places bone or CSF directly under the skin. These vertices also have large skin–target angles and are rarely chosen unless thickness dominates the weights.

items.title: 5a  Combine and Evaluate Scores
items.text:
PlanTUS combines the normalised metrics into a weighted composite score; headless mode places the vertex with the minimum score.

The composite score

Each metric is min–max normalised to [0, 1] over its finite values. NaN or infinite values are set to 1 (worst), also for the inverted intersection metric.

score_i = ( w_dist  × norm(|d_i − optimal_distance|)
          + w_ang   × norm(α_i)
          + w_inter × (1 − norm(x_i))
          + w_skull × norm(β_i)
          + w_thick × norm(t_i) )
        ÷ (w_dist + w_ang + w_inter + w_skull + w_thick)

If t_i is unavailable (all NaN, or an older plantus_metrics.mat without it), w_thick is dropped from numerator and denominator. Vertices with avoidance == 0, d_i < min_distance or d_i > max_distance get score = inf. Headless mode places the vertex with the minimum score. Interactive mode reports that optimum before wb_view opens, and the score and rank of each placed vertex. A few outlying vertices (e.g. 40 mm skull-base rays for t_i) compress the spread and weaken that criterion below its nominal weight.

Criteria evaluation (placement.plantus.evaluate) re-scores the placement under 12 weight sets and flags settings under which a criterion cannot discriminate.

Criteria evaluation

Criteria evaluation (placement.plantus.evaluate, default true; needs save_metrics) re-scores the placement under 12 weight sets (configured, equal, one criterion at 0.55 with the rest sharing 0.45, and each criterion alone) and writes, next to the metrics file:

File Contents plantus_evaluation.json Placed vertex (rank, each criterion's value, and % of eligible vertices that are better), per-criterion ranges over eligible vertices, the weight sweep, and diagnostics; read by the placement report plantus_weight_sensitivity.csv One row per weight set: chosen vertex, its criteria, distance to the placed vertex plantus_criteria_maps.png Each criterion and the composite score on the skin (4 views) plantus_weight_sensitivity.png Criteria at the placed spot and at each weight set's choice; all chosen spots on the skin

Diagnostics flag settings under which a criterion cannot discriminate between positions:
