Code Condition distance_range_unconstrained [min_distance, max_distance] excludes < 5% of the skin outside the avoidance mask (e.g. a large flhm_list value) intersection_sparse Beam–target intersection non-zero at < 2% of eligible vertices (small target mask) <criterion>_unavailable / _nan Criterion undefined at all / > 25% of eligible vertices placed_ineligible Placed vertex excluded under the configured scoring (interactive selection) placed_not_optimum Placed vertex is not the composite optimum (interactive selection) tradeoff_<criterion> At the placed vertex a weighted criterion is worse than at > 50% of eligible vertices weight_sensitive A single-criterion-heavy weight set moves the chosen spot > 20 mm

Warnings also go to the placement log. Evaluation failures never abort a placement.

plantus_metrics.mat and offline re-scoring

plantus_metrics.mat (placement.plantus.save_metrics, default true) is written to <output_dir>/plantus_metrics.mat. It holds skin coordinates, normals and faces, the target centre, d_i, α_i, x_i, β_i, t_i (skull_thickness), the avoidance mask, the composite score, best_vertex (composite optimum), selected_vertex (vertex placed), selection_mode (auto headless, gui interactive, manual after --do_only_trajectory), min_distance, max_distance, optimal_distance, and the weights. Vertex indices and faces are 0-based. Each run deletes an existing plantus_metrics.mat first, even with save_metrics: false.

Use compute_composite_score in plantus_common.py to re-score under other weights without new ray casts. The evaluation runs plantus_evaluation.py on the metrics; to evaluate an existing metrics file, run python functions/neuronav/plantus_evaluation.py <plantus_metrics.mat>.

items.title: 5b  Select a Vertex Interactively
items.text:
With placement.plantus.interactive = 1, wb_view opens a scene with the maps 4a–4d, one per tab. The skull-thickness map (skull_thickness_skin.func.gii) is loaded too and can be chosen as an overlay in any tab. Each click replaces the selection and prints the vertex's criteria, composite score, and rank (and the composite optimum) to the log.

Review dialog and requirements

Closing wb_view places the last selected vertex (step 6) and opens its placement scene (transducer and focus on skin and T1) in a second wb_view. A review dialog then offers Use this position, Choose another vertex (the planning scene reopens; metrics are not recomputed) or Cancel (the launcher exits non-zero and PRESTUS stops). Closing the planning scene without a click reviews the previous vertex, or aborts if there is none.

Interactive mode requires:

  • A graphical display (desktop or VNC session; not a batch/HPC job). The MATLAB desktop is not needed: placement.plantus.interactive = 1 also works under matlab -batch and from the Nexus
  • pynput (mouse listener); on Linux it needs an X display, on macOS Accessibility permission for the terminal/MATLAB
  • Connectome Workbench wb_view, on PATH or via placement.plantus.connectome_wb_path
  • PyQt5 for the review dialog (part of SimNIBS)

The --selection launcher option

--selection sets how a vertex is confirmed: review (the dialog above; PRESTUS uses it), prompt (Generate transducer placement for vertex N? (yes/no) after each click, for a terminal), last_click (no review), and auto (default: prompt when stdin is a terminal, else review if PyQt5 is available, else last_click). If no vertex is confirmed, the launcher exits non-zero. If wb_view exits at once without a click, the planning scene is reopened without the skull-thickness map.

items.title: 6  Compute the Placement Geometry
items.text:
For the selected vertex, PlanTUS computes the beam direction and the transducer centre (prepare_acoustic_simulation) and writes a 4 × 4 Localite position matrix (RAS mm).

Output files

Outputs go to <output_dir>/vtx<N>/, where <output_dir> is the per-target placement run folder <path.placement>/sub-XXX/plantus/<target_name>/:

File Contents *_Localite.mat position_matrix (4×4, RAS mm), used by PRESTUS *_Localite.txt Plain-text copy *_kPlan.mat Same matrix in k-Plan convention (m, axes permuted) *_Localite_XML.txt, *_Localite_dummyXML.txt (2.x) Fake Localite XML snippet (rewritten on each run) *_Trajectory_Brainsight.txt, *_Trajectory_BabelBrain.txt Trajectory for Brainsight and BabelBrain *Focus*, *TransducerModel*.surf.gii Focus and transducer surface models at the position scene.scene Workbench placement scene (all modes; opened only by the Workbench picker)

PlanTUS names the files <mask>_vtx<N>_….

<output_dir> itself holds the skin/skull surfaces, the metric maps (distances_skin, distances_skin_thresholded, angles_skin, target_intersection_skin, skin_skull_angles_skin, skull_thickness_skin, avoidance_skin; .func.gii), the planning scene.scene, and plantus_metrics.mat.

Beam direction and transducer centre

For the selected vertex v:

  1. Beam direction: PlanTUS aims from the skin vertex at the target centre (its default target_centered orientation), as a unit vector pointing into the head; the PlanTUS page draws this axis.
  2. Transducer centre: transducer_centre = skin_coordinate_v − (plane_offset + additional_offset) × beam_direction. plane_offset is the distance from the bowl apex to the exit plane (curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm); additional_offset is placement.skin_gap_mm, the gap between skin and exit plane.
  3. Localite position matrix (PlanTUS.create_Localite_position_matrix): column 3 = transducer_centre, column 0 = beam_direction, columns 1–2 by Gram–Schmidt.

items.title: 7  Read the Output into PRESTUS
items.text: position_transducer_plantus.m loads the most recent *Localite.mat under <path.placement>/sub-XXX/plantus/<target_name>/ written during the current run. If there is none, it errors (PRESTUS:plantus:noOutput). localite_matrix_to_positions converts position_matrix into trans_pos and focus_pos in voxel coordinates. A T1 overlay plot (plot_placement_t1_overlay) of the transducer and target is written to the subject output folder.

items.title: Coordinate Conventions
items.text: Frame Units Description Voxel / grid integer indices PRESTUS simulation grid RAS+ (subject) mm T1 image world space; used by Localite matrix MNI mm Template space; target specified here, mapped to RAS via SimNIBS k-Plan m, permuted axes Not used by PRESTUS

items.title: TUS_entry Transducer Placement
items.text:
A simulated transducer position is useful only if the real transducer can be placed there with good contact on the scalp. placement.mode: 'tus_entry' runs the TUS_entry R toolbox, which selects the scalp entry point with the smallest coupling geometry error (the standard deviation of the transducer-disk-edge to scalp distances), subject to an optional depth constraint. TUS_entry optimises mechanical fit (how perpendicular the transducer disk sits on the scalp); PlanTUS optimises acoustic objectives (beam–target overlap, skull thickness).

On this page:

  • Installation: R, its packages, and TUS_entry in a conda environment.
  • Required Configuration: the two paths PRESTUS needs and the head mask it builds.
  • Optional Configuration: masks, depth window, and other settings.
  • Candidate List: the full ranked candidate list.
  • Coordinate Conventions: voxel and world frames, and how the exit plane and focus are set.
  • Output Files: the files written per run.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When good mechanical contact of the transducer is the main concern.
  • Before you start: R with TUS_entry in a conda environment, and a SimNIBS segmentation (or another head mask).

Experimental feature

TUS_entry placement is under active development and is not yet covered by the PRESTUS test suite. Check the placement report before simulating.

placement:
  mode: tus_entry
  tus_entry:
    script_path: /path/to/TUS_entry/TUS_entry.R
    env_path:    /home/user/.conda/envs/tus_entry
    mni_target_mm: [-40, 20, 50]     # DLPFC example
    minimal_distance_cm: 4.24
    maximal_distance_cm: 7.46
    transducer_size_cm:  6.4
    target_name: DLPFC
How TUS_entry selects the entry point
  1. Distance filter: candidate entry points on a sphere of radius maximal_distance around the target centroid. Only trajectories that cross the scalp surface and avoid the exclusion zone are kept.
  2. Spatial decimation: candidates are thinned by resolution.
  3. Angle scoring: for each candidate, a circular transducer footprint (diameter transducer_size) perpendicular to the trajectory is scored by the SD of disk-edge-to-scalp distances. A lower SD is a better-coupled placement.
  4. Final selection: the angle-ranked candidates are fine-tuned in turn; the first that satisfies minimal_distance ≤ depth ≤ maximal_distance is returned.

items.title: Installation
items.text:
TUS_entry requires R and four CRAN packages. Use a dedicated conda environment:

conda env create -f examples/environment_tus_entry.yml
conda activate tus_entry

environment_tus_entry.yml is in examples/ (run the command there or give its path). Then clone TUS_entry:

git clone https://github.com/CyrilAtkinson/TUS_entry /path/to/TUS_entry

Point placement.tus_entry.script_path to TUS_entry.R and placement.tus_entry.env_path to the conda env prefix (e.g. ~/.conda/envs/tus_entry).

items.title: Required Configuration
items.text:
Both placement.tus_entry.script_path (path to TUS_entry.R) and placement.tus_entry.env_path (conda environment with Rscript) are required.

TUS_entry needs a solid head mask. It walks each candidate ray from outside the head towards the target and takes the last voxel outside the mask as the scalp entry. With a hollow skin shell the head interior counts as outside, every candidate collapses onto the target, and TUS_entry fails (replacement has 1 row, data has 0). PRESTUS therefore builds the head mask itself: it reads placement.tus_entry.scalp_mask (default: the SimNIBS m2m_sub-<ID>/final_tissues.nii.gz), treats every nonzero voxel as head, fills it (3D and slice-wise, which also closes a skin shell open at the neck) and writes the result to the work directory. The source file is only read.

items.title: Optional Configuration
items.text:
The optional keys set the target and exclusion masks, the depth range, the transducer size, the sampling resolution, and the output folder. They are listed, with their defaults, under TUS_entry placement.

Units

TUS_entry uses centimetres internally. PRESTUS converts distance outputs to millimetres, as for all other PRESTUS coordinates.

All keys are also listed in Parameters.

items.title: Candidate List
items.text:
By default, TUS_entry returns a single selected entry point. With return_candidates = true, the runner script saves the full angle-ranked candidate list to tus_entry_candidates.rds in the working directory. Inspect it in R:

cands <- readRDS("tus_entry_candidates.rds")
head(cands)

MATLAB cannot read RDS files directly. To filter ranked candidates in PRESTUS (e.g. the entry with the lowest skull thickness among the top-10 coupling candidates), load the RDS in R, export to CSV, and load that in MATLAB. The candidates output argument of position_transducer_tus_entry is reserved for a future native implementation and returns an empty struct array.

items.title: Coordinate Conventions
items.text:
Space What TUS_entry provides PRESTUS convention Voxel 1-based array indices (same as MATLAB) trans_pos, focus_pos: 1-based World NIfTI affine applied to voxel indices trans_pos_ras, focus_pos_ras: RAS mm

TUS_entry operates in the native voxel space of the input masks. Use the same T1 as the reference for both SimNIBS segmentation and PRESTUS placement.

The exit plane lies placement.skin_gap_mm (default 5 mm) outward from the Scalp_coordinates returned by TUS_entry, along the trajectory. trans_pos lies a further curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm outward, the offset used by all placement modes. focus_pos is derived by stepping inward from the exit plane by transducer.focal_distance_ep (or focal_distance_bowl minus the apex-to-exit-plane offset, as focal_distance_calculation converts it; if neither is set, the geometric focus dist_geom_ep_mm).

items.title: Output Files
items.text:
All outputs are written to the placement run folder, <path.placement>/sub-<ID>/tus_entry/<target_name>/ (override with placement.tus_entry.work_dir):

File Content run_tus_entry.R Auto-generated runner script (for reproducibility / debugging) tus_entry_report.csv Selected entry: voxel coords, distance [mm], angle score tus_entry_candidates.rds Full ranked candidate list (only if return_candidates = true) sub-<ID>_tus_entry_head_mask.nii.gz Solid head mask passed to TUS_entry as scalp placement_run.json Run record: resolved positions and the settings they depend on (reused per placement.reuse) sub-<ID>_<target_name>_trajectory.txt Brainsight trajectory export sub-<ID>_<target_name>_target_mask.nii.gz Auto-generated spherical target mask (if no target mask was provided) References

When using TUS_entry placement, cite: Atkinson C, et al. TUS_entry: A tool for optimising transducer entry point selection in transcranial ultrasound stimulation. GitHub: https://github.com/CyrilAtkinson/TUS_entry

items.title: CT-Based Skull Mapping
items.text:
By default each skull layer of a layered simulation takes one value per property, although skull bone properties can vary within and between individuals. A CT gives the skull subject-specific properties instead. With pct.enabled: 1, PRESTUS maps the Hounsfield units (HU) of a CT to density, sound speed, and attenuation within the skull layer. The CT is one of two images:

  • a measured CT of the subject (path.ct_pattern), or
  • a pseudo-CT that PRESTUS generates from a UTE/PETRA MR image, used when path.ct_pattern is empty.

Both feed the same HU-to-property mapping; only the pseudo-CT needs the UTE-to-HU step first.

On this page:

  • Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run: the scan, the tools, the minimum config, and the outputs.
  • Using a Measured CT: the CT's requirements and the minimum config.
  • Skull from the CT: taking the skull from an HU threshold instead of the segmentation, as BabelBrain does.
  • Soft Tissue from the CT: letting an HU threshold separate soft tissue from water, as planning tools that segment the CT by density do.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you want skull properties that follow the individual skull, and have a CT or a UTE/PETRA scan.
  • Before you start: A CT co-registered to the T1w, or a UTE/PETRA image per subject plus FSL and ANTs.

Subpages:

  • From UTE to Pseudo-HU: for choosing pct.skull_mapping and the matching pct.density_calibration; read it whenever you change either from the default.
  • Skull Property Mappings: for choosing how pHU become skull density, sound speed, and attenuation, with the equations and references.

Experimental

(pseudo-)HU mapping is an experimental feature in active development. The most suitable mapping remains an active area of research; treat all mappings as experimental. See PRESTUS issue #43.

items.title: Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run
items.text:
1. Acquire an MR sequence with detailed bone contrast (PETRA UTE; example parameters below).
  2. Run SimNIBS with the T1w and the PETRA UTE scan (instead of the T2w) as inputs, either in PRESTUS (default) or in the SimNIBS GUI. The UTE image is the one in path.t2_pattern, which SimNIBS registers to the T1 as m2m_sub-XXX/T2_reg.nii.gz (UTE_reg.nii.gz is also read).
  3. Set pct.enabled: 1. PRESTUS runs pct_create_pseudoCT.sh after segmentation if pseudoCT.nii.gz does not exist yet. This needs FSL (fslmaths), ANTs (N4BiasFieldCorrection, SmoothImage), and MATLAB on PATH; set startup.fsl_bin_path and startup.ants_bin_path so PRESTUS can prepend them. On HPC, also set startup.matlab_bin_path.

Minimum config:

path:
  t2_pattern: 'sub-%1$03d_UTE.nii.gz'  # UTE image (used for both SimNIBS and pseudoCT)

startup:
  fsl_bin_path: '/opt/fsl/bin'           # prepended to PATH for fslmaths
  ants_bin_path: '/opt/ants/bin'          # prepended to PATH for N4BiasFieldCorrection, SmoothImage
  matlab_bin_path: '/opt/matlab/R2024a/bin/matlab'  # required on HPC; local falls back to matlabroot

pct:
  enabled: 1
  skull_mapping: 'kosciessa' # UTE→HU linear mapping algorithm
  debug: 1                   # keep intermediate images in the debug_pct/ subfolder
  mapping_density: 'k-plan'
  density_calibration: ''    # HU->density table for k-plan; '' = k-Plan default (see Matching the CT Calibration)
  mapping_soundspeed: 'k-plan'
  mapping_attenuation: 'k-plan'

Outputs go to <path.pct>/sub-XXX/, or to <parent of path.seg>/pct/sub-XXX/ when path.pct is empty:

File / folder Content pseudoCT.nii.gz, tissues_mask.nii.gz pseudo-CT and tissue mask pseudoCT.json sidecar: skull mapping, segmentation folder, PRESTUS version debug_pct/ intermediate images and the log log_hpc/ cluster job logs

Reuse. An existing pseudoCT.nii.gz is used and not regenerated. Its pseudoCT.json must record the current pct.skull_mapping; otherwise the run stops with prestus:cache:signatureMismatch (see io.cache_signature_check). To regenerate, move the folder aside or set path.pct to another folder. A pseudo-CT without a sidecar is used with the warning prestus:cache:unverified. A pseudo-CT inside m2m_sub-XXX/ is used with the warning PRESTUS:pct:legacyLocation; move it to the pseudo-CT folder. See Starting from earlier stage outputs.

Manual. You can also run pct_create_pseudoCT.sh in bash before starting PRESTUS. An example wrapper is at examples/createPseudoCT.sh. Required modules: SimNIBS, FSL, ANTs.

Example PETRA UTE parameters

From Carpino et al. (2024):

  • TR: 3.32 ms
  • TE: 0.07 ms
  • voxel size: 0.8 mm3
  • 352 sagittal slices
  • flip angle: 2°
  • FoV: 294 mm

items.title: Using a Measured CT
items.text:
Set path.ct_pattern to the subject's CT and pct.enabled: 1. The run then needs no UTE image and generates no pseudo-CT.

path:
  ct_pattern: 'sub-%1$03d_CT.nii.gz'  # relative to path.anat, like t1_pattern

pct:
  enabled: 1
  density_calibration: ''  # this CT's HU->density table; '' = k-Plan default
  mapping_density: 'k-plan'
  mapping_soundspeed: 'k-plan'
  mapping_attenuation: 'k-plan'
  • Units. The CT must hold Hounsfield units (NIfTI scaling is applied).
  • Registration. The CT must be co-registered to the T1w: PRESTUS resamples it onto the segmentation grid through both images' world coordinates and does not register it. Voxels outside the CT are set to air (-1000 HU). The run logs the median HU of the skull voxels and warns (PRESTUS:pct:ctMisregistered) when it is below 300 HU.
  • Skull voxels. The skull layer comes from the SimNIBS segmentation, built as for the pseudo-CT, unless pct.bone_source is hu or mask (Skull from the CT). No files are written to the pseudo-CT folder.
  • Calibration. HU depend on scanner, kVp, and kernel. Set pct.density_calibration to this CT's HU-to-density table when you have one; with the k-Plan default, PRESTUS warns (prestus:pct:ctDefaultCalibration).
  • Reuse. Grid and medium caches record the CT's name, size, and date, so replacing the CT rebuilds them.

items.title: Skull from the CT
items.text:
By default the skull layer is the segmentation's skull, and the (pseudo-)CT only sets its properties. With pct.bone_source: hu, the skull is instead where the HU exceed pct.bone_hu_threshold on the simulation grid. This reproduces how BabelBrain defines bone on its CT path, so a PRESTUS run can use the same skull as a BabelBrain plan.

pct:
  enabled: 1
  bone_source: 'hu'
  bone_hu_threshold: 300   # BabelBrain's values
  bone_median_mm: 2.6
  bone_close_mm: 5
  limits:
    hu_max: 2100

The steps run after the pseudo-CT is resampled onto the simulation grid and limited to limits.hu_* (Limits and Interpolation): threshold, median-filter the bone mask, open it with a cube of bone_open_mm edge (removing specks and spurs), close holes with a cube of bone_close_mm edge, and keep the largest connected component. Bone voxels below the threshold, which the closing added, are raised to it. Bone outside the segmentation's skull becomes skull. Segmentation skull voxels outside this bone take the medium of the nearest voxel outside both skull definitions, so the outer side joins the skin and the inner side the brain or CSF (bone_soft_layer: nearest); a layer name assigns one layer to all of them. headmodel.skull_fill_method is not used.

With pct.bone_source: mask, the bone comes from a file instead, for example the bone of another planning tool (path.bone_mask_pattern; nonzero voxels are bone, co-registered to the T1w). It is carried onto the simulation grid with the segmentation and then treated as the HU bone above: the same filter, closing and largest component, the same HU floor at bone_hu_threshold, and the same handling of segmentation skull outside it. Without a CT, the skull keeps the homogeneous properties of its layer.

Differences from BabelBrain

BabelBrain resamples the CT with a cubic spline onto its own grid (6 points per wavelength); PRESTUS resamples onto grid.resolution_mm with pct.interpolation (spline as BabelBrain). BabelBrain also quantises bone HU into steps for its material table; PRESTUS keeps the continuous HU. BabelBrain first sets segmentation skull outside its bone to brain and then median-filters the label map, which leaves skin on the outer side; bone_soft_layer: nearest reaches that result directly. BabelBrain's split into cortical and trabecular bone has no effect on its CT path, so PRESTUS does not reproduce it.

items.title: Soft Tissue from the CT
items.text:
By default the segmentation decides where tissue ends and water begins. With pct.soft_hu_threshold, the CT decides instead, on the simulation grid and outside the skull: tissue below the threshold becomes water (for example air spaces), and water at or above it takes the medium of the nearest soft tissue. This includes tissue that the CSF-based crop (headmodel.csf_expansion) turned into water, such as the face and neck. Combined with bone_source: hu, the whole head model then follows CT thresholds, as in planning tools that segment the CT by density.

pct:
  enabled: 1
  bone_source: 'hu'
  bone_hu_threshold: 240     # 1150 kg/m3 with the k-Plan calibration
  soft_hu_threshold: -99     # 900 kg/m3 with the k-Plan calibration
  bone_open_mm: 1           # example; k-Plan does not publish its opening and closing sizes
  bone_close_mm: 1

items.title: From UTE to Pseudo-HU
items.text:
The pseudo-CT is only as good as the line that turns UTE intensity into pseudo-Hounsfield units (pHU), and that line returns HU on the scale of the CT it was fitted to. This page describes the available UTE-to-HU mappings, how PRESTUS generates the pseudo-CT, and how to pair each mapping with the HU-to-density calibration of the same CT.

On this page:

  • Choosing the UTE-to-HU Mapping: the pct.skull_mapping options and the generation steps.
  • Matching the CT Calibration: pairing pct.skull_mapping with pct.density_calibration.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you change pct.skull_mapping from the default, use your own UTE-to-HU line, or set pct.density_calibration.
  • Before you start: A pseudo-CT run set up as in Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run.

items.title: Choosing the UTE-to-HU Mapping
items.text:
pct.skull_mapping sets the linear UTE→pHU mapping of the skull. Soft tissue is set to 42 HU and air to -1000 HU for every mapping.

skull_mapping pHU kosciessa (default) individualised: a line fitted per subject through three UTE histogram points set to 1900, 700, and 300 HU (see below) miscouridou pHU = −2085 UTE + 2329 carpino (deprecated) pHU = -2194 UTE + 2236. Warns prestus:pct:deprecatedSkullMapping; the same line is custom with custom_slope: -2194, custom_intercept: 2236 wiesinger pHU = -2000 (UTE-1) + 42 treeby pHU = -2929.6 UTE + 3274.9 (ucl-bug/petra-to-ct; fitted to 80 kVp CT: use with density_calibration: ucl_lowdose_80kvp, see below) custom pHU = pct.custom_slope UTE + pct.custom_intercept (any other linear map) The generation steps
  • UTE: threshold at 0, bias field correction, then normalisation by the soft tissue peak (normalised UTE intensity = 1). pct_soft_tissue_peak finds the peak.
  • pHU soft tissue (normalised UTE intensity = 1): 42 HU (Wiesinger et al., 2018).
  • pHU air: -1000 HU (Wiesinger et al., 2018; Miscouridou et al., 2022).
  • pHU skull: the linear mapping set by pct.skull_mapping (table above).
  • kosciessa (pct_skullmapping_fit) fits a least-squares line through three points from the UTE histograms of charm cortical and trabecular bone: the lower quarter-max crossing of the cortical histogram → 1900 HU, the crossover of the two histograms → 700 HU, and the upper quarter-max crossing of the trabecular histogram around its x-weighted peak → 300 HU. Bins 0.9–1.1 are replaced by a spline against soft-tissue partial volume. The anchors, width level, and interpolation window are options of pct_skullmapping_fit.
  • 3D Gaussian smoothing (σ=0.8 voxels via ANTs' SmoothImage) prevents abrupt tissue transitions in the simulation grid. Within an eroded skull mask, unsmoothed values are kept to limit partial volume effects.

items.title: Matching the CT Calibration
items.text:
A UTE→HU line returns HU on the scale of the CT it was fitted to. That scale depends on scanner, tube voltage (kVp), and reconstruction kernel: at 80 kVp, bone has about 1.35 times the HU it has at about 120 kVp. The simulation needs density, and turning HU into density needs the calibration of that same CT. Set pct.skull_mapping, pct.mapping_density: k-plan and pct.density_calibration together:

skull_mapping CT the line was fitted to mapping_density density_calibration kosciessa, miscouridou, carpino (deprecated), wiesinger clinical CT, about 120 kVp (assumed; for kosciessa the anchors 1900/700/300 HU are assumed on this scale) any '' (k-Plan default) treeby low-dose CT, 80 kVp, BONEPLUS kernel (UCL) k-plan ucl_lowdose_80kvp custom with petra2density's line (−2080.02, 2133.23) the cph2025 phantom calibration k-plan cph2025 custom with your own line your CT (any scanner and kVp) k-plan path to that CT's phantom table 
pct:
  skull_mapping: 'treeby'
  mapping_density: 'k-plan'
  density_calibration: 'ucl_lowdose_80kvp'   # the 80 kVp CT treeby was fitted to
  mapping_soundspeed: 'k-plan'               # follows from density
  mapping_attenuation: 'k-plan'

pct.density_calibration values:

Value Table '' (default) k-Plan default (config/ct_calibration/kplan_default.csv) 'ucl_lowdose_80kvp' UCL low-dose CT (GE Revolution, 80 kVp, BONEPLUS; CIRS 062M phantom): the CT behind skull_mapping: treeby. Bone has about 1.35× the default's HU for the same density 'cph2025' petra2density's phantom calibration, the CT behind its line −2080.02·UTE + 2133.23 (use skull_mapping: custom). Bone has about 0.85× the default's HU a path any CSV with two columns, HU and density [kg/m³] (lines starting with # are comments), e.g. a phantom scan of your own scanner or a table that goes with a study-specific custom line

Tables are applied piecewise linearly and extrapolated linearly beyond their end points. For a line fitted at another kVp, scan a density phantom with the same protocol and pass its table; no HU conversion between kVp is needed. medium_setup prints the resolved table and records it in the medium statistics.

Only k-plan reads the calibration; with another density mapping it is ignored, with a warning. The other mappings assume a fixed, clinical HU scale. Use them with lines on the clinical scale only; otherwise use k-plan with the matching calibration. PRESTUS warns when skull_mapping: treeby is used without mapping_density: k-plan and density_calibration: ucl_lowdose_80kvp.

HU scale assumed by the other mappings
  • k-wave: Schneider et al.; marsac: 300–2000 HU; air-tissue (needed by pichardo and mcdannold): about −1000 to 1000 HU.
  • webb sound speed and attenuation: GE 120 kVp, B kernel by default; scanner-specific values via pct.webb_*.
  • aubry and mueller rescale by the skull's own minimum and maximum HU. They are insensitive to the HU scale but remove between-subject differences in density level.

items.title: Skull Property Mappings
items.text:
The pseudo-CT holds pseudo-Hounsfield units, while the simulation needs density, sound speed, and attenuation in each skull voxel. Several published mappings make this conversion, and they assume different HU scales and give different skull properties. This page lists the mappings PRESTUS offers for each property, their equations and prerequisites, and how to check the resulting skull properties before simulating.

On this page:

  • From Pseudo-HU to Acoustic Properties: how the mappings are applied.
  • Limits and Interpolation: resampling the CT and regularising the HU and the mapped properties.
  • The HU Reference: the densest-bone HU for mappings that normalise by it.
  • Mapping Skull Density: the pct.mapping_density options.
  • Mapping Skull Sound Speed: the pct.mapping_soundspeed options.
  • Mapping Skull Attenuation: the pct.mapping_attenuation options.
  • Predicting the Modelled Skull Properties: the skull property distributions a run will model, and the references.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you change pct.mapping_density, pct.mapping_soundspeed, or pct.mapping_attenuation from the k-plan default, or want the equations behind a mapping.
  • Before you start: A pseudo-CT (Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run) and a density calibration that matches its UTE-to-HU mapping (Matching the CT Calibration).

items.title: From Pseudo-HU to Acoustic Properties
items.text:
With pct.enabled: 1, choose a mapping for each of density, sound speed, and attenuation. The pseudo-CT is read from the pseudo-CT folder (see Setting Up a Pseudo-CT Run). This is a subtype of a layered medium. Mappings apply only within the uniform skull mask. A property set to "none", or with its field missing, keeps the uniform skull value. Defaults below are those in config_default.yaml.

pct:
  enabled: 1                    # map skull properties from a (pseudo-)CT
  mapping_density: k-plan       # see Mapping Skull Density
  mapping_soundspeed: k-plan    # see Mapping Skull Sound Speed
  mapping_attenuation: k-plan   # see Mapping Skull Attenuation

items.title: Limits and Interpolation
items.text:
The CT is resampled onto the simulation grid with pct.interpolation: linear (default), cubic, or spline. spline is the interpolating cubic spline BabelBrain uses. Cubic and spline interpolation overshoot at sharp edges such as the outer surface of the skull.

pct.limits regularises the CT and the properties mapped from it in one scheme. Each limit is a number, water (the configured water value of that property), or [] for none:

pct:
  limits:
    hu_min: []
    hu_max: []                # BabelBrain CT: 2100
    density_min: 'water'
    density_max: []
    sound_speed_min: 'water'
    sound_speed_max: []
    alpha_coeff_min: []
    alpha_coeff_max: []

HU limits act on the CT before and after resampling, so they also clip the interpolation overshoot, and before the skull is defined from HU (Skull from the CT). Property limits act on the mapped skull values. Ranges that belong to a published mapping, such as the HU range of marsac, stay part of that mapping. The medium statistics (<io.dir_cache>/sub-XXX_<medium>_medium_stats<affix>.json) record the skull HU distribution before and after the HU limits and how many skull voxels each limit changed.

items.title: The HU Reference
items.text:
Some mappings scale by the HU of the densest bone: density marsac-babelbrain and aubry, sound speed aubry, and attenuation mueller and aubry. PRESTUS takes this reference over the whole head: a percentile (pct.hu_reference_percentile, default 99.9) of the CT within the layers pct.hu_reference_layers (default the skull layers) of the segmentation, on the segmentation grid and after the HU limits. The reference therefore does not depend on the simulation grid, its crop, or the interpolation. A percentile below 100 keeps a few bright voxels, such as metal or artefacts, from setting the scale of the whole skull. Voxels above the reference get the properties of the densest bone, in PRESTUS and in the BabelBrain bridge.

pct:
  hu_reference_layers: ['skull']
  hu_reference_percentile: 99.9   # 100 = the largest HU

Skull HU above the reference extrapolate the density and sound speed mappings, keep the lowest attenuation, and raise a warning. With the BabelBrain backend on its CT path, the same reference sets BabelBrain's density scale.

pct.hu_reference_resolution_mm takes the reference after resampling the whole-head CT onto an isotropic grid of that spacing with pct.interpolation, as BabelBrain does on its simulation grid. Use it only to reproduce such a tool. Cubic and spline interpolation overshoot at the skull surface, so the reference then rises with an interpolation artefact and depends on the grid: lower density for all bone below the overshoot.

items.title: Mapping Skull Density
items.text:
Set by pct.mapping_density.

Value Mapping k-plan (default) 4-part piecewise linear fit based on k-Plan defaults; pct.density_calibration replaces the table (see Matching the CT Calibration) k-wave 4-part piecewise linear fit based on Schneider et al. (1996) marsac linear between HU_min = 300 and HU_max = 2000, Marsac et al. (2017) marsac-babelbrain BabelBrain's form of marsac: scaled by the largest skull HU; to emulate BabelBrain's CT path aubry porosity-based mixture of bone and water, Aubry et al. (2003) air-tissue linear air-to-bone calibration (BabelBrain-compatible); use with pichardo or mcdannold sound speed or attenuation Density equations

Several mappings use the porosity of Aubry et al. (2003), with the max. skull HU denominator from Guo et al. (2019):

\[ \phi_\text{skull} = 1 - \frac{\text{HU}}{\text{HU}_\text{max}} \]

k-plan. Piece-wise linear mapping between HU and mass density in kg/m^3 (k-Plan documentation):

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = \text{fit_pairwiselinear}(\text{HU}, \text{density}) \] 
HU = [-990, 60, 1000, 1950]
density = [1.2, 1060, 1530, 2150]

The minimum is regularised to the configured water density. Sound speed and attenuation of the k-plan pipeline follow from density. k-Plan's bone segmentation starts at density values of 1150 kg/m3, which internally regularizes data ranges; PRESTUS does not enforce this. Thermal simulations use a fixed bone density in the heat capacity and heat conduction, as k-Plan:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = 1850 \, \text{kg/m}^3 \]

The heat source keeps the mapped density and sound speed of the acoustic simulation.

k-wave. Pseudo-CT values are shifted by +1000 and thresholded at 300 to align with hounsfield2density:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = \text{hounsfield2density}(\text{HU} + 1000) \]

Density is regularised at the minimum to the configured water density and at a max. skull density rho_bone = 2100 kg/m3.

marsac. Skull pHU are clipped to HU_min = 300 and HU_max = 2000. Unlike Marsac et al., 2017, PRESTUS clips pHU < HU_min instead of excluding them from the skull mask, which would create skull holes.

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = \rho_\text{water} + (\rho_\text{bone} - \rho_\text{water}) \cdot \frac{\text{HU} - \text{HU}_\text{min}}{\text{HU}_\text{max} - \text{HU}_\text{min}} \]

with max. skull density rho_bone = 2100 kg/m3.

marsac-babelbrain. As BabelBrain's CT path (HUtoDensityMarsac). Skull pHU below BabelBrain's bone threshold of 300 HU are raised to it:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = 1000 + 1700 \cdot \frac{\text{HU}}{\max_\text{skull} \text{HU}} \]

aubry. Mixture of bone and water density, both from the configuration:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = \rho_\text{water} \cdot \phi_\text{skull} + \rho_\text{bone} \cdot (1 - \phi_\text{skull}) \]

air-tissue. Linear HU→density between air (HU ≈ −1000) and cortical bone (HU ≈ 1000), as HUtoDensityAirTissue in BabelBrain's Pichardo and McDannold workflows:

\[ \rho_\text{skull} = 1.01237293 \cdot \text{HU} + 1013.67 \]

The minimum is regularised to water density. pichardo and mcdannold need density from this calibration.

items.title: Mapping Skull Sound Speed
items.text:
Set by pct.mapping_soundspeed.

Value Mapping k-plan (default) density-based, k-Plan marsac density-based, Marsac et al. (2017) aubry porosity-based, Aubry et al. (2003) webb linear in HU, Webb et al. (2018); scanner-specific slope and intercept via pct.webb_sos_slope and pct.webb_sos_intercept pichardo frequency-dependent ρ→c, Pichardo et al. 2D interpolation map; needs pct.mapping_density: air-tissue mcdannold polynomial ρ→c, McDannold et al.; needs density first (air-tissue or marsac)

For k-plan, webb, pichardo, and mcdannold, the minimum sound speed is regularised to water sound speed.

Sound speed equations

k-plan.

\[ c_\text{skull} = 1.33 \cdot \rho_\text{skull} + 167 \]

marsac.

\[ c_\text{skull} = c_\text{water} + (c_\text{bone} - c_\text{water}) \cdot \frac{\rho_\text{skull} - \rho_\text{water}}{\rho_\text{bone} - \rho_\text{water}} \]

with max. speed of sound in skull c_skull = 3360 m/s and max. skull density rho_bone = 2100 kg/m3. Water properties come from the configuration.

aubry.

\[ c_\text{skull} = c_\text{water} \cdot \phi_\text{skull} + c_\text{bone} \cdot (1 - \phi_\text{skull}) \]

Tissue sound speeds come from the configuration.

webb.

\[ c_\text{skull} = \text{slope} \cdot \text{HU} + \text{intercept} \times 1000 \]

Defaults (GE 120 kVp, B kernel, 0.5 × 0.6 mm resolution): slope = 0.75, intercept = 1.32 (c = 0.75 · HU + 1320 m/s). Set scanner-specific values from Webb et al. Tables I and II with pct.webb_sos_slope and pct.webb_sos_intercept.

pichardo. Reads MapPichardo.h5 from the BabelBrain submodule: longitudinal speed of sound [m/s] as a function of density [kg/m³] and frequency [MHz]. Interpolation is bilinear with nearest-neighbour extrapolation. MATLAB cannot read the Blosc-compressed H5 without the filter plugin, so PRESTUS uses the same table in functions/medium/MapPichardo.mat. Requires pct.mapping_density: air-tissue (or another density algorithm run first), the BabelBrain submodule initialised at external/BabelBrain, and the simulation frequency in parameters.transducer(1).freq_hz.

mcdannold.

\[ c_\text{skull} = \frac{1}{p(\rho_\text{skull})} \]

where \(p(\rho) = -2.79 \times 10^{-18}\,\rho^4 + 5.31 \times 10^{-16}\,\rho^3 + 1.69 \times 10^{-10}\,\rho^2 - 7.63 \times 10^{-7}\,\rho + 1.24 \times 10^{-3}\). Requires density first (pct.mapping_density: air-tissue or marsac).

items.title: Mapping Skull Attenuation
items.text:
Set by pct.mapping_attenuation.

Value Mapping k-plan (default) uniform: the skull alpha_coeff and alpha_power of medium_properties; to replicate k-Plan set alpha_coeff = 13.3 and alpha_power = 1 mueller HU-based, Mueller et al. (2017), bounds from Yaakub et al. (2023) aubry porosity-based, Aubry et al. (2003) webb exponential HU-based model, Webb et al. (2021); scanner-specific values via pct.webb_att_alpha0, pct.webb_att_beta, and pct.webb_att_c pichardo frequency-dependent ρ→Att from Pichardo et al. 2D interpolation map; prerequisites as for pichardo sound speed mcdannold polynomial ρ→Att from McDannold et al. with linear frequency scaling; needs density first Attenuation equations

k-plan.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull} = \alpha_\text{coeff} \]

Reads alpha_coeff and alpha_power of medium_properties.skull from the config, and warns when they differ from k-Plan's fixed 13.3 and 1.

mueller.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull} = \alpha_\text{min} + (\alpha_\text{max} - \alpha_\text{min}) \left(1 - \frac{\text{HU} - \text{HU}_\text{min}}{\text{HU}_\text{max} - \text{HU}_\text{min}}\right)^{0.5} \]

with α_min = 4 and α_max = 8.7 (see Yaakub et al., 2023). These are 𝛼(f) at 500 kHz (see Aubry, J.-F., 2022 for benchmark simulations). PRESTUS converts them to alpha_0 in 𝛼(f) = alpha_0 x f[MHz] ^ y as alpha_0 = 𝛼(f)/0.5^y, with y the skull alpha_power.

aubry.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull} = \alpha_\text{min} + (\alpha_\text{max} - \alpha_\text{min}) \cdot \phi_\text{skull}^{0.5} \]

with α_min = 0.2 and α_max = 8 (Aubry et al., 2003).

webb.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull}(f) = \alpha_0 \cdot \left(\frac{f}{1\,\text{MHz}}\right)^{\beta} \cdot \exp(c \cdot \text{HU}) \]

Output is k-Wave alpha_coeff [dB/cm/MHz\(^\beta\)] with alpha_power = β. Defaults (GE 120 kVp, B kernel, 0.5 × 0.6 mm): α₀ = 26, β = 1.3, c = −0.0016. Set scanner-specific values from Webb et al. Table IV with pct.webb_att_alpha0, pct.webb_att_beta, and pct.webb_att_c.

pichardo. Reads longitudinal attenuation [Np/m] from MapPichardo.h5 as a function of density [kg/m³] and frequency [MHz]. The value at the simulation frequency is converted to k-Wave alpha_coeff [dB/cm/MHz] with alpha_power = 1 (linear frequency scaling assumed). Prerequisites as for pichardo sound speed; density must be filled first.

mcdannold.

\[ \alpha_\text{skull}(f) = p(\rho_\text{skull}) \cdot \frac{f}{660\,\text{kHz}} \]

where \(p(\rho) = 1.36 \times 10^{-10}\,\rho^4 - 1.41 \times 10^{-6}\,\rho^3 + 5.40 \times 10^{-3}\,\rho^2 - 9.02\,\rho + 5.71 \times 10^{3}\) [Np/m]. Converted to k-Wave alpha_coeff [dB/cm/MHz] with alpha_power = 1. Requires density first.

items.title: Predicting the Modelled Skull Properties
items.text:
To see the skull properties a run will model before simulating, call pct_predict_skull_properties(parameters) or use Predict skull properties on the Nexus Pseudo-CT sub-tab. It applies the configured mappings to the pseudo-CT skull voxels and writes their distributions to cache/sub-NNN_<medium>_pct_prediction<affix>.json, alongside the skull values of the uncertainty bound variants. See Pseudo-CT runs.

References
  • Aubry, J.-F., et al. Experimental demonstration of noninvasive transskull adaptive focusing based on prior computed tomography scans. J Acoust Soc Am 113, 84–93 (2003).
  • Aubry, J.-F. et al. Benchmark problems for transcranial ultrasound simulation: Intercomparison of compressional wave models. J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 152, 1003–1019 (2022).
  • Carpino et al. (2024). Transcranial ultrasonic stimulation of the human amygdala to modulate threat learning. MSc thesis.
  • Guo, S., et al. Feasibility of ultrashort echo time images using full-wave acoustic and thermal modeling for transcranial MRI-guided focused ultrasound (tcMRgFUS) planning. Phys. Med. Biol. 64, 095008 (2019).
  • Lim Fat, D. et al. The Hounsfield value for cortical bone geometry in the proximal humerus: an in vitro study. Skelet. Radiol. 41, 557–568 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1007/s00256-011-1255-7
  • Marsac, L. et al. Ex Vivo Optimisation of a Heterogeneous Speed of Sound Model of the Human Skull for Non-Invasive Transcranial Focused Ultrasound at 1 MHz. International Journal of Hyperthermia. 33. 635–645 (2017).
  • McDannold, N., et al. Transcranial magnetic resonance imaging-guided focused ultrasound surgery of brain tumors: initial findings in 3 patients. Neurosurgery 66(2):323–332 (2010).
  • Miscouridou, M., Pineda-Pardo, J. A., Stagg, C. J., Treeby, B. E. & Stanziola, A. Classical and Learned MR to Pseudo-CT Mappings for Accurate Transcranial Ultrasound Simulation. IEEE Trans. Ultrason., Ferroelectr., Freq. Control 69, 2896–2905 (2022).
  • Mueller, J. K., Ai, L., Bansal, P. & Legon, W. Numerical Evaluation of the Skull for Human Neuromodulation with Transcranial Focused Ultrasound. Journal of Neural Engineering. 14. 066012 (2017).
  • Pichardo, S., et al. Multi-frequency characterization of the speed of sound and attenuation coefficient for longitudinal transmission of freshly excised human skulls. Phys. Med. Biol. 56(1):219–250 (2011). DOI: 10.1088/0031-9155/56/1/014
  • Schneider, U., Pedroni, E., and Lomax A., "The calibration of CT Hounsfield units for radiotherapy treatment planning," Phys. Med. Biol., 41, pp. 111-124 (1996).
  • Webb, T. D., et al. Measurements of the Relationship Between CT Hounsfield Units and Acoustic Velocity and How It Changes With Photon Energy and Reconstruction Method. IEEE Trans Ultrason Ferroelectr Freq Control 65(7):1111–1124 (2018). DOI: 10.1109/TUFFC.2018.2827899
  • Webb, T. D., et al. Acoustic Attenuation: Multifrequency Measurement and Relationship to CT and MR Imaging. IEEE Trans Ultrason Ferroelectr Freq Control 68(5):1532–1545 (2021). DOI: 10.1109/TUFFC.2020.3039743
  • Wiesinger, F. et al. Zero TE-based pseudo-CT image conversion in the head and its application in PET/MR attenuation correction and MR-guided radiation therapy planning. Magn. Reson. Med. 80, 1440–1451 (2018).
  • Yaakub, S. N. et al. Pseudo-CTs from T1-Weighted MRI for Planning of Low-Intensity Transcranial Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: An Open-Source Tool. Brain Stimulation. 16. 75–78 (2023).

items.title: Reading Your Results
items.text:
A finished run leaves a folder of files. Before you use its numbers, check that the run simulated the placement and intensity you intended, and compare its exposure with the safety reference levels. This page lists the files to open first, the checks in order, and how to read the safety summary; every file and column is described in Outputs & Reports, and terms in the Glossary.

On this page:

  • Files to Open First: the report, placement report, metrics table, and maps to open first.
  • Checks Before Using Results: placement, intensity, safety reference levels, and unusual results.
  • Uncertainty of the Estimate: how to see how much results depend on tissue properties.
  • Methods Text: the methods paragraph the report writes for you.

At a glance

  • When you need it: After every run, before you use or report its numbers.
  • Before you start: A finished run and its output folder (<path.sim>/sub-XXX/).

items.title: Files to Open First
items.text:
Results are in <path.sim>/sub-XXX/. Open these first:

File What it is sub-XXX_<medium>_report<affix>.html The simulation report: safety summary, key numbers, figures, and the run log. Start here. sub-XXX_placement_<mode><affix>.html The placement report: where the transducer and the target ended up, drawn on the T1 (head simulations). sub-XXX_<medium><affix>.csv All metrics in one table, for your own analysis. nii/ 3D maps (intensity, pressure, MI, temperature) in the participant's T1 space and in MNI space, to view in any NIfTI viewer.

<medium> is water or layered, and <affix> is your io.output_affix (empty by default).

items.title: 1. Placement and Focus
items.text:
Open the placement report and the report's figures:

  • The transducer sits on the scalp, not inside the head or far from it, and points at the target.
  • The focus lies at the target. The report's intensity overlay should show the hot spot in the target region. In the table, compare real_focal_distance_mm (where the peak actually is) with your focal depth setting, and Ipa_target (intensity at the target) with Isppa_brain (the peak in the brain). A peak far from the target means the placement or the focal depth setting needs a second look.
  • The configuration summary in the report lists the transducer, focal depth, target intensity, and medium that were used. Check that they are the ones you intended.

For many runs, the targeting analysis (sub-XXX_<medium><affix>_targeting.csv) measures the distance between the simulated and the planned focus (Targeting accuracy).

items.title: 2. Intensity in the Brain
items.text:
• transducer.target_isppa_wcm2 is the free-water intensity (30 W/cm² by default). The intensity in the brain (Isppa_brain, Ipa_target) is lower, mostly because the skull reflects and absorbs ultrasound. How much lower depends on the person, the skull thickness, and the angle of incidence.
  • If the run log shows prestus:isppa:largeScale, the field was scaled by more than 4× (or less than 0.25×) from the simulated drive. The result is then an extrapolation; check that it is still realistic for your device.

items.title: 3. Safety Reference Levels
items.text:
The top of the report shows a safety verdict and one card per metric. Each card is coloured by how close the value is to its ITRUSST non-significant-risk (NSR) reference level (Aubry et al., 2025):

Colour Meaning Green below 50 % of the reference level Amber 50–100 % of the reference level Red above the reference level Grey not computed for this run (e.g. no thermal simulation, or a metric that does not apply to this medium) Metric Reference level Mechanical index, transcranial (MI_tc) or in free water (MI) 1.9 Temperature rise (riseT_*) 2 °C Temperature rise above a fixed 37 °C start (riseT37_*) 2 °C Maximum temperature (maxT_*) 39 °C Thermal dose (CEM43_*) brain 2, skull 16, skin 21 min

A red card does not by itself mean the protocol is unsafe, and the verdict then says inspect rather than fail. The ITRUSST thermal criteria are alternatives: an exposure qualifies as non-significant risk through the temperature rise, the maximum temperature or the thermal dose. Check the flagged values against the criteria that apply to your protocol, and read the original consensus for details. PRESTUS reports the comparison; it makes no safety recommendation of its own.

Thermal metrics only appear when a thermal simulation ran (modules.run_heating_sims: 1, with a sonication protocol in timing.*). The report shows the CEM43 form selected by thermal.cem43_iso (Thermal).

items.title: 4. Unusual Results
items.text:
What you see What it may mean The highest intensity is in the skin or skull rather than the brain Expected to some degree near the transducer; a hot spot at the scalp can also mean poor contact or a transducer placed into the head. Check the placement report. The focus is much shallower or deeper than the setting Strong skull refraction, or a target depth outside the transducer's range (min_foc–max_foc of the device). Warnings about points per wavelength (PPW) in the log The grid is too coarse for the frequency; results near the focus may be inaccurate (Spatial and temporal sampling). load_transducer_from_library:uncalibratedAmplitude in the log The transducer's drive at this depth was not checked in k-Wave; absolute intensities carry that uncertainty (Free-water k-Wave drive calibration).

More known messages and their fixes are in Troubleshooting.

items.title: Uncertainty of the Estimate
items.text: Simulated intensities and temperatures depend on assumed tissue properties, which are uncertain, especially for the skull. To see how much your results could change, run the uncertainty mode (default tissue properties and the ITRUSST bounds that maximise and minimise heating and intensity), or use subject-specific skull properties from a pseudo-CT.

items.title: Methods Text
items.text: The report contains an automatically written methods paragraph (with references) describing the software, transducer, grid, tissue properties, protocol, and resulting exposure. Copy it with Copy methods text, and check it against your study before using it in a manuscript.

items.title: Run Time and Resources
items.text:
A simulation run can take a few minutes on a GPU or many hours on a CPU, and its memory decides which GPUs can run it. Knowing this before a run helps to choose the resolution, solver, and device, to request job resources, and to plan a study. PRESTUS predicts the time and memory of a run from its config, and records what each run used.

The calculator below shows the expected time of each stage of a typical run, from the same table the Nexus uses. A head uses the reference head, or with a limited field of view a cylinder around the beam; a free-water grid is sized to the transducer aperture and focal distance. A partial FOV shortens the acoustic simulation from minutes to seconds, but the head is still preprocessed in full, so the CPU stages then take most of the time. The Nexus computes the same prediction from a full config and the subject's own grid. To compare setups, pin each one: the pinned setups appear side by side as stacked bars, numbered, with their settings listed and the settings that differ from setup 1 in bold. The arrows next to each setup reorder them.

The load calculator needs JavaScript.

On this page:

  • Predicted Load: how the time of each stage and the GPU memory are predicted, before any run.
  • From Earlier Runs: time and memory of this project's finished runs.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Before a study or a change of resolution, solver, or device; when setting job resources on a cluster.
  • Where: In the Nexus at the bottom of the Transducer, Medium, Sonication, Solver, and Run tabs; without the Nexus with python -m prestus_nexus.workload and python -m prestus_nexus.estimate.

items.title: Predicted Load
items.text:
Before any run, the Nexus predicts the time of each stage the current config runs, the total, and the GPU memory. The prediction appears at the bottom of the Transducer, Medium, Sonication, Solver, and Run tabs and in the Run tab's Plan. Without the Nexus: python -m prestus_nexus.workload path/to/study.yaml.

  • Grid: sized to the transducer for free water (grid.default_dims: 'auto'), grid.default_dims, the acoustic FOV, or for a head the grid of this project's earlier runs. Without earlier runs, a reference head (the SimNIBS example head, 9–14 L depending on orientation) stands in; the subject's own grid replaces it after its first run.
  • Time steps: as the source setup derives them from the resolution, frequency, sound speeds of the modelled layers, grid.source_cfl, and grid.steady_state_transits.
  • Acoustic simulation and free-water baseline: a fixed start-up time (about 5 s on a GPU) plus grid points with PML × time steps × a rate for the device and solver. The baseline runs on a box around the beam with the same time steps. The GPU is set by hpc.gpu. For a run on this computer (platform: matlab) without hpc.gpu, the Nexus reads the local NVIDIA GPU with nvidia-smi and marks it as detected. Otherwise the prediction spans all GPU types with a rate. A GPU without its own rate is scaled from GPUs of the same generation by memory bandwidth. A solver without its own rate on that GPU is scaled from cpp_gpu (or cpp_cpu): matlab_gpu takes about 3.5 times as long, and double precision about 1.8 times.
  • Thermal simulation: thermal grid points × thermal steps × a rate for the device.
  • Other stages (placement, head model, medium, source, analysis, NIfTI maps): CPU work that takes the same time on any GPU. Each takes a time that depends on the medium and the resolution; head preprocessing is the largest.
  • Segmentation, pseudo-CT, and the HTML report: timed like the other stages once runs have recorded them. Segmentation (SimNIBS charm) runs once per subject and pseudo-CT generation only for UTE-based skulls, so the calculator lists them apart from the total.
  • Not predicted: queue wait on a cluster.

Rates and stage times come from this project's runs when they recorded them, else from nexus/prestus_nexus/throughput.yaml. Each estimate shows a range from the 10th to the 90th percentile of earlier runs. Across studies, measured acoustic times fall within 0.7–1.4 times the prediction for 80% of runs.

The table was measured on the Donders cluster. On other computers, the prediction is less certain:

  • GPUs without measurements (for example desktop RTX cards) are scaled by memory bandwidth from measured GPUs of the same generation, which held to about ±25% for the cluster GPUs. A GPU of a generation without any measured GPU has no rate.
  • CPU runs use the cluster CPU rate; how the time changes with the number of cores is not measured yet.
  • Stages that do not simulate run on the CPU and take the times measured on cluster nodes; a faster or slower CPU changes them.

Runs on any computer record their times in run_stats.jsonl and, with consent, in telemetry, from which the table is refitted.

Refitting throughput.yaml

python -m prestus_nexus.workload fit [--update] <records> ... fits the table from run_stats.jsonl files or telemetry exports (run_end events as JSON lines or a JSON array; sim_stats holds the sizes and stage times). A fitted entry replaces the entry with the same device and solver (or stage and medium), and other entries stay. The bandwidth list (GPU memory bandwidth from NVIDIA specifications, and the generation) is entered by hand and kept. Acoustic entries hold t0_s and ns, fitted on relative error; a fixed start-up time is fitted only from 6 or more runs spanning a 3-fold range of work, else 5 s. Runs more than 2.5 times off the fit are dropped. Stage entries hold s_1mm and exponent: seconds = s_1mm × (1 mm / resolution)^(3 × exponent). workload.validate checks the acoustic model leave-one-study-out. After a refit, python tests/docs/gen_load_data.py updates the calculator data; CI checks that it matches the table.

items.title: From Earlier Runs
items.text:
Each run that simulates appends one line to <path.sim>/run_stats.jsonl. The Nexus shows an estimate from these lines on the Run tab (Show deployment, save & resource details). Without the Nexus:

cd <PRESTUS>/nexus
python -m prestus_nexus.estimate path/to/study.yaml [--stats path/to/run_stats.jsonl]

The estimate uses earlier runs with the same simulation.code_type, acoustic_backend, simulation.medium, and grid.resolution_mm, on the same hpc.partition if there are any, else on any partition. It reports the median and maximum of:

  • Acoustic simulation time, as recorded.
  • Thermal simulation time: seconds per thermal step × the steps of the current timing.* protocol.
  • Peak RAM of the job.

Segmentation, pseudo-CT, BabelBrain preprocessing and queue wait are not estimated. Estimates appear once runs of the project have finished, and get better as more runs are recorded.

What run_stats.jsonl records

Each line holds the acoustic grid the solver ran on (voxels, dimensions, PML, and whether it was axisymmetric) and its time steps, thermal voxels and steps, the acoustic and thermal simulation durations, the duration of each timed stage (stage_<name>_s, as in the run log's ⏱ lines), the modelled skull properties (sound speed, density, and attenuation at the source frequency: 10th, 50th, and 90th percentile over all skull voxels, and the median and path length through skull along each transducer's beam to the focus), the run total, solver (simulation.code_type, acoustic_backend), medium, resolution, hpc.partition, node, CPU allocation, GPU model, and peak RAM. Runs that reuse a cached acoustic result, dry runs, and runs with the stage off record nothing for that stage. Peak RAM is the MATLAB process high-water mark, or under SLURM the job cgroup peak, which includes the k-Wave C++ binary and BabelBrain. It is recorded on Linux only. Nothing is sent anywhere; this is separate from telemetry.

What a finished cluster job used, including its cost and CO₂e, is in the post-job resource report.

items.title: Segmentation
items.text:
The skull reflects, attenuates, and refracts ultrasound, so the simulation needs to know where skull, brain, and soft tissue lie. SimNIBS charm labels these tissues in the MRI; PRESTUS then builds the head model from the labels.

On this page:

  • Running the Segmentation: running SimNIBS charm and reusing its result.
  • SimNIBS Version and charm Settings: choosing the install and changing charm's settings.
  • Defaced Copy for Sharing: a copy of the segmentation without the face.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Every layered simulation. Free-water simulations skip it.
  • Before you start: A T1w image (optionally a T2w) and a SimNIBS install (Installation).

items.title: Running the Segmentation
items.text:
For a layered medium, the first run segments the T1 (and the T2, when path.t2_pattern is set) with SimNIBS charm into <path.seg>/m2m_sub-XXX/. This takes an hour or more. Later runs reuse final_tissues.nii.gz from that folder unless io.overwrite_simnibs: 1. The air-cavity check also reads charm's detailed labelling, segmentation/labeling.nii.gz, because final_tissues.nii.gz has no air label: charm merges the sinuses and other internal air into the background (0). Keep the segmentation/ folder when you tidy up m2m folders.

  • modules.segmentation_only: 1 segments and stops, e.g. to segment all subjects before simulating them.
  • segmentation.use_qform: 1 when charm reports a qform/sform mismatch; segmentation.debug: 1 passes --debug to charm.
  • segmentation.noneck: 1 passes --noneck for a scan without a neck.
startup:
  simnibs_bin_path: /path/to/SimNIBS-4.x/bin   # the SimNIBS install to use
modules:
  segmentation_only: 1                         # segment, then stop
segmentation:
  noneck: 0                                    # 1 for a scan without a neck

items.title: SimNIBS Version and charm Settings
items.text:
startup.simnibs_bin_path selects the SimNIBS install, and with it the version; PRESTUS needs SimNIBS 4 or later. While they are empty, hpc.ld_library_path (the install's libraries for SimNIBS tools) and placement.plantus.env_path (the Python PlanTUS runs in) follow it; a value set there overrides it. To change charm's settings, copy the install's charm.ini (in its simnibs package folder), edit the copy, and set segmentation.settings_file to it; keep it outside the m2m folder. Report the settings you changed.

An existing segmentation is reused even when another version or other settings are selected. PRESTUS then warns, comparing the version in charm_log.html and the settings in settings.ini of the m2m folder with the selection. Set io.overwrite_simnibs: 1 to segment again, which deletes the m2m folder first, or point path.seg to a separate folder per version to keep both. What was built from the old segmentation is detected on reuse: grid, medium, acoustic, and head-model caches, placement runs, and pseudo-CTs record the segmentation's checksum (Cache reuse checks), and a defaced copy is made again.

In the Nexus, the Segmentation card (Medium tab) lists the SimNIBS installs on this computer, shows the version and the existing segmentation, opens charm_report.html, and has the re-run switch. When runs are submitted to a cluster over SSH (Run tab), Scan cluster lists the installs there: conda environments, ~/SimNIBS*, /opt/simnibs*, and the bin folders of the simnibs environment modules. The Nexus keeps the result per host, so it can check a cluster path that does not exist on this computer.

items.title: Defaced Copy for Sharing
items.text:
segmentation.deface: 1 writes a copy of the m2m folder, m2m_sub-XXX_defaced/, with the face removed from the anatomical images by pydeface (install it in the SimNIBS environment). Tissue labels, surfaces, warps, and meshes are copied unchanged, and the original folder is not modified. The copy is made once and again after the segmentation changes. Figures are defaced separately, with io.deface_plots (on by default).

Installing SimNIBS: Installation. Errors: Troubleshooting.

items.title: Sequential Simulations
items.text:
A sonication that follows another can start in tissue that is still warm from the first and adds to the thermal dose already accumulated. Run independently, each simulation starts from the baseline temperature and zero CEM43, so this carryover is missing. Sequential mode chains the runs so that each heating simulation starts from the end-of-run temperature and CEM43 maps of the previous one.

On this page:

  • Planning a Sequence in the Nexus: stances fired one after another, set up in one config.
  • Basic Usage: passing follow-up configs to the pipeline.
  • Cache Reuse: which stages a follow-up run reuses and which it recomputes.
  • Sequential Simulation Parameters: the settings that carry the thermal state forward.
  • Combining with Uncertainty Mode: chaining each uncertainty variant.
  • Output Affix Handling: how files of each run and variant are named.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When you stimulate from different coordinates in sequence and want the cumulative thermal state (for stimulation in parallel, see Multi-Transducer Modelling). A sequence planned in advance is easiest to set up in the Nexus.
  • Before you start: One config per sonication, loaded as structs.

items.title: Planning a Sequence in the Nexus
items.text:
The Sonication sequence card (Sonication tab, under the timing diagram) sets up several stances that sonicate one after another. Add a later sonication adds a stance as a new step, which you place in the Viewer. Each step has its own duration and pulse timing (Pulse timing…), and each pause is modelled as off time. Transducers that should fire at the same time go into one step (Fire with previous step). The strip above the table shows the whole protocol to scale.

The sequence is stored in the config with the async custom schedule. Each step's start goes in transducer(i).timing_offset_s, and each step's timing goes in transducer(i).timing wherever it differs from the timing block, which holds the step with transducer 1. Simulate as chooses how the sequence runs:

Choice How it runs Possible when One joint run The config as it is: one acoustic simulation per transducer and one thermal simulation for the whole sequence. The transducers of a step fire together as a firing group: their fields are summed coherently, and steps whose pulses partly overlap interfere while both are on. Always. Chain of runs One config per step (<config>_step-<k>.yaml, written when you run), chained as sequential follow-ups. Each pause becomes the previous step's timing.post_ptri_dur, and each step gets its own grid. A step with several transducers is one coherent run. Steps do not overlap; each pause is a whole number of timing.post_pt_timestep; no uncertainty mode and no list of target ISPPAs. Automatic (default) One joint run.

With one joint run and grid.async_layout: per_transducer, heat outside transducer 1's grid is lost; use the shared grid or a chain for stances far apart. The card lists what stops a choice, and so does the Issues panel for the automatic choice. Example Protocols shows sequences, transducers firing together, interleaved pulses, and a mixed protocol with uncertainty as the card draws them.

items.title: Basic Usage
items.text:
Each config is a struct. Given config_1, config_2, and config_3 to run in sequence:

Without heat carryover, run each independently:

prestus_pipeline_start(config_1)
prestus_pipeline_start(config_2)
prestus_pipeline_start(config_3)

With heat carryover, pass the follow-up configs via options. The thermal end state is handed over as T1w-space NIfTIs (*_heating_end, *_CEM43_end, *_CEM43_iso_end). Each follow-up resamples them into its own grid with its own transform, so the start state is correct for a follow-up with a different beam axis. The NIfTI stage is enabled for every run in a chain, and dispatch stops with sequential_pipeline:missingThermalEnd if a map is missing. It never starts from the water baseline silently.

sequential_configs.config_2 = config_2;
sequential_configs.config_3 = config_3;
options.sequential_configs = sequential_configs;
prestus_pipeline_start(config_1, options);

Field names in sequential_configs must follow the pattern config_<N> where <N> is a non-negative integer (e.g. config_2, config_3, config_11). The dispatcher picks the field with the lowest numeric value first; only relative order matters. A field that does not match the pattern (e.g. config_abc) stops the run with the error sequential_pipeline:badFieldName.

In the Nexus, Results ▸ Follow-up… with Sequential creates a follow-up config and adds it to the chain under Run ▸ Where to run ▸ Pipeline options, which the run script passes as options.sequential_configs (Run tab).

items.title: Cache Reuse
items.text:
When a follow-up simulation is dispatched, PRESTUS decides which results are reused and which are recomputed:

Stage Default behaviour How to override Grid & medium setup Reused from base run Set io.preproc_affix in the sequential config Acoustic simulation Re-run with the follow-up config Set io.acoustic_cache_affix to an existing affix to reuse prior acoustics Thermal simulation Re-run (cache file gets a unique name automatically) Set io.thermal_cache_affix explicitly to control the cache filename

The head geometry does not change between sequential targets, so preproc can always be shared. Acoustics default to a fresh run because the follow-up may target a different location or use different transducer settings.

To reuse the base run's acoustic results in the follow-up (e.g. same target, different timing protocol):

options.sequential_configs.config_2.io.acoustic_cache_affix = config_1.io.output_affix;

items.title: Sequential Simulation Parameters
items.text: Parameter Description io.adopted_heatmap Path to a temperature heatmap NIfTI (heating_end.nii.gz) used as the thermal starting point. Set automatically from the previous run's output; override to supply a custom starting temperature. io.adopted_cem43 Path to a CEM43 NIfTI (CEM43_end.nii.gz) carried forward for cumulative thermal dose. Set automatically; can be overridden. io.adopted_cem43_iso Path to the ISO-variant CEM43 NIfTI (CEM43_iso_end.nii.gz). Set automatically alongside adopted_cem43. io.preproc_affix Affix for grid/medium cache lookup (defaults to the base run's output_affix). io.acoustic_cache_affix Affix for acoustic cache lookup. Not set by default; acoustics are re-run unless you set this explicitly. io.thermal_cache_affix Affix for the thermal cache file (defaults to the run's own io.output_affix). options.sequential_configs Struct of follow-up configs to dispatch in order (see example above). options.sequential_cleanup_intermediate If true, per-run NIfTI and image files are deleted after the final summary report is successfully generated. Default: false.

items.title: Combining with Uncertainty Mode
items.text:
options.sequential_configs can be combined with parameters.simulation.uncertainty = true when every run keeps the first run's transducer positions: the variants of a follow-up reuse the first run's grid. For stances that change position, use one async run instead, which uncertainty mode wraps. Each follow-up run is executed once per uncertainty variant (default, Temp-H, Temp-L, Trans-H, Trans-L). The default and Temp variants inherit the thermal end-state from the matched variant of the prior run; the Trans variants re-run the acoustic simulation only:

parameters.simulation.uncertainty = true;

options.sequential_configs.config_2 = config_2;
options.sequential_configs.config_3 = config_3;

prestus_pipeline(parameters, options);

After all sequential runs complete, a sequential report is written for all variants. The base run appears as run 1; each follow-up adds a further run entry. The report shows temperature and CEM43 timeseries with the Temp-L to Temp-H band shaded around the default trajectory.

On HPC, job names are prefixed with r1- when sequential configs are present (e.g. PRESTUS-r1-u2-sim-default_sub-001) to keep scheduler job names unambiguous across chained submissions. See Uncertainty Quantification for the uncertainty pipeline.

items.title: Output Affix Handling
items.text:
Every PRESTUS output file embeds an affix, a short string appended to the subject/medium prefix, that distinguishes files produced by different simulation variants or pipeline modes. PRESTUS assigns affixes from the active modes; you rarely set one yourself.

  • A plain sequential follow-up appends _seq<N> to the affix of the run before it, with N the number of its config_<N> field (e.g. _seq2, then _seq2_seq3).
  • An uncertainty variant gets _desc-temphigh, _desc-templow, _desc-transhigh, or _desc-translow.
  • Both combined: _desc-temphigh_seq2.
  • A custom io.output_affix on any sequential config is used as-is; no _seq<N> suffix is added.

Example filenames for subject 1, layered medium, two sequential runs with uncertainty:

sub-001_layered.csv                              ← base run, default
sub-001_layered_desc-temphigh.csv                ← base run, Temp-H
sub-001_layered_desc-templow.csv                 ← base run, Temp-L
sub-001_layered_desc-transhigh.csv               ← base run, Trans-H
sub-001_layered_desc-translow.csv                ← base run, Trans-L
sub-001_layered_seq2.csv                         ← sequential run 2, default
sub-001_layered_desc-temphigh_seq2.csv           ← sequential run 2, Temp-H
…                                                ← and so on for the other variants

If you see a warning that a variant output was not found but the file exists on disk, confirm that io.dir_output was set before calling the pipeline (i.e. path_log_setup has run), and that no custom options.affixes struct was passed with different values than those used during simulation.

Affix construction and report file lookup

Affix sanitisation. load_parameters sanitises the raw affix string before use: characters other than letters, digits, hyphens, and underscores are replaced with underscores; leading underscores and a leading desc- are stripped, and _desc- is prepended. So "pilot" becomes "_desc-pilot".

Full affix table.

Pipeline mode io.output_affix value Single run, no user affix '' (empty) Single run, user sets io.output_affix = 'myreg' '_desc-myreg' Uncertainty, default variant base_affix Uncertainty, Temp-H / Temp-L variant base_affix + '_desc-temphigh' / '_desc-templow' Uncertainty, Trans-H / Trans-L variant base_affix + '_desc-transhigh' / '_desc-translow' Sequential run N, no uncertainty affix of the run before it + '_seq<N>' (N from its config_<N> field) Sequential run N, default variant base_affix + '_seq<N>' Sequential run N, other variants base_affix + '_desc-<variant>_seq<N>' (e.g. '_desc-temphigh_seq<N>') Sequential run N, custom affix supplied the supplied affix, unchanged

base_affix is whatever io.output_affix was on the parameters struct passed to uncertainty_pipeline or prestus_pipeline_start. For most studies it is empty.

How report functions locate files. generate_uncertainty_report reconstructs CSV paths as <io.dir_output>/sub-NNN_<medium><variant_affix>.csv rather than trusting io.filename_table, which may carry a stale value from an earlier pipeline stage. generate_sequential_report uses the explicit affix registry built by sequential_pipeline (one struct per run with output_affix and thermal_cache_affix) for all lookups; io.filename_table is a fallback only.

Thermal cache affix. io.thermal_cache_affix controls the filename of the heating .mat cache (sub-NNN_<medium>_heating_res<affix>.mat). It defaults to the run's own output_affix. Set it explicitly only if you need to point a follow-up run at a specific pre-existing cache file.

See also: Uncertainty Quantification, Multi-Transducer Modelling, Running on a Cluster (HPC)

items.title: Acoustic Simulations
items.text:
The acoustic simulation computes the pressure field the transducer produces in the head. Every reported intensity, focus position, and mechanical index comes from this field, so its settings decide how far the results can be trusted: how finely the grid samples the wave, how long the simulation runs, and which intensity the field is scaled to.

On this page:

  • Main Settings: the few settings most studies change.
  • Spatial and Temporal Sampling: grid resolution, time step, and simulation duration.
  • Amplitude Ramping: how the source is switched on.
  • ISPPA Targeting: scaling the field to a free-water intensity.
  • Memory Use: fitting large runs into memory.
  • Axisymmetric Simulations: fast 2D runs for symmetric setups.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Read ISPPA targeting for every study. The rest matters when you change grid settings or run out of memory.
  • Before you start: Nothing; the defaults are a sound starting point.

items.title: Main Settings
items.text:
The defaults run a 3D simulation with k-Wave's kspaceFirstOrder3D (see the available simulation backends). The settings most studies touch:

grid:
  resolution_mm: 0.5        # spatial step; keep PPW >= 6 in the slowest medium
  source_cfl: 0.15          # dt = CFL × dx / c_max
transducer:
  target_isppa_wcm2: 30     # free-water ISPPA the results are reported at
modules:
  run_water_baseline: auto  # free-water baseline for the ISPPA scaling

The simulation models compressional waves (P-waves) in isotropic media and computes pressure and velocity fields. Shear waves are not modelled explicitly; their scattering contributes to the bulk attenuation coefficient. This makes the run faster and less memory-intensive than an elastic simulation. An elastic skull model is available as a separate backend (kwave_elastic, draft).

Turning off acoustic simulations

With modules.run_acoustic_sims: 0, PRESTUS loads the existing acoustic results from the cache (subject to io.overwrite_files; see Overwrite behaviour). This lets a follow-up thermal simulation reuse an earlier acoustic run. Other modules behave differently: turning them off may skip the step without loading existing data.

items.title: Spatial and Temporal Sampling
items.text:
Accuracy depends on resolving the shortest wavelength in the domain. Two parameters govern this.

Grid resolution (grid.resolution_mm) sets the spatial step dx. With the medium sound speed c and the fundamental frequency f, the number of spatial samples per wavelength is

PPW = c / (f × dx)

The worst case is the slowest medium (water or brain, ~1500 m/s). Keep PPW ≥ 6; PRESTUS warns below grid.min_ppw (jwave stops), and the Nexus flags it before a run.

For head (layered) and phantom media, a grid coarser than 0.75 mm staircases the tissue transitions (skull, scalp), which may affect the results; PRESTUS and the Nexus warn above it.

CFL number (grid.source_cfl) sets the time step dt relative to dx and the fastest medium (skull, ~2800 m/s), which sets the stability limit:

dt  = CFL × dx / c_max
PPP = PPW / CFL

PPP is the number of time steps per wave period. resolution_mm and source_cfl are independent, so you can refine or coarsen the time step without changing the grid. Both must stay within the stability limit.

Rule of thumb: the coarsest grid that satisfies a minimum PPW at frequency f in the slowest medium is dx_max = c_min / (f × PPW_min). At 500 kHz in water (1500 m/s) with PPW = 6: resolution_mm = 0.50 mm.

PPW across tissues, the stability recheck, and the CFL default

PPW varies across tissues. The check against grid.min_ppw uses the slowest medium. At 500 kHz with 0.5 mm resolution, water/brain (1500 m/s) gives PPW = 6 and skull (2800 m/s) PPW ≈ 11. The binding spatial constraint is always in the slow tissues.

The stability recheck can reduce dt below the CFL target. After source setup, prestus_pipeline calls checkStability. If the CFL-derived dt exceeds the estimated stability limit for the heterogeneous medium, source setup is rerun with a smaller time step scaled by grid.source_limit_fraction (default 0.9). The final dt can therefore be smaller than CFL × dx / c_max. The PPW check runs only on the first source setup call; the adjusted call receives dt explicitly and bypasses it.

Overriding source_ppw decouples temporal from spatial resolution. A manual grid.source_ppw only affects the time step (PPP = source_ppw / CFL). The spatial check against grid.min_ppw still uses the actual PPW from c_min / (f × dx). A coarser source_ppw increases dt and reduces runtime without suppressing the spatial warning.

The default CFL of 0.15 is conservative. k-Wave's own default is 0.3. PRESTUS uses 0.15 for extra stability margin in heterogeneous skull simulations, where the theoretical stability limit is an approximation (checkStability). This roughly doubles the number of time steps and the acoustic runtime. If simulations are stable, source_cfl can be raised towards 0.3; validate this against the checkStability output for your medium.

items.title: Simulation Duration
items.text:
