With the default grid.steady_state_transits: 1, the simulation lasts long enough for the wave to cross the domain diagonal once, so the steady-state field is established everywhere:

t_end   = steady_state_transits × grid_diagonal / c_min
N_steps = round(t_end / dt)

where grid_diagonal = sqrt(x_size² + y_size² + z_size²) and c_min is the minimum sound speed across all media (water or brain, ~1500 m/s). Request more transits for compact, reflective domains, or set a fixed duration with grid.sim_time_us. The sensor records p_max_all and p_final over the last grid.steady_state_num_periods (default 3) wave periods.

items.title: Amplitude Ramping
items.text:
A ramped pulse delivers less pulse-average intensity (ISPPA) than the temporal-peak intensity (ISPTP), because intensity scales with amplitude². When timing.pulse_ramp_dur > 0, acoustic_analysis scales the acoustic_Ipa map and every derived ISPPA value (per tissue, at target) by

f = ISPPA / ISPTP

before further analysis. With pulse_ramp_dur absent or zero, f = 1. The factor can also be computed directly with compute_ramp_factor(pd, ramp_dur, shape):

Parameter Description pd Pulse duration [s] ramp_dur Ramp duration per edge [s]; applied at onset and offset, so the ramped interval per pulse is 2 × ramp_dur shape 'linear': linear amplitude taper (intensity integral factor k = 1/3); 'tukey': raised-cosine taper (k = 3/8)

Example: 20 ms pulse, 2 ms ramp per edge (10 % of pd per edge, 20 % total):

Shape k f (ISPPA/ISPTP) linear 1/3 ≈ 0.867 tukey 3/8 ≈ 0.875 Ramp factor formula 
t_flat = pd - 2 × ramp_dur
f      = (k × ramp_dur + t_flat + k × ramp_dur) / pd

Ramping reduces spectral splatter by smoothing the transducer drive at pulse onset and offset instead of switching abruptly.

items.title: I<sub>SPPA</sub> Targeting
items.text:
The acoustic simulation runs at the drive elem_p_amp (from the study config or the transducer library). transducer.target_isppa_wcm2 (default 30 W/cm²) sets the free-water ISPPA the results are reported at. Pressure is linear in drive, so PRESTUS scales the simulated field by

scale_p = sqrt(target_isppa / baseline_isppa)

where baseline_isppa is the free-water peak ISPPA of the same drive. All pressure fields used downstream (p_max_all, p_min_all, p_final) are scaled, so intensities, MI, and heating are consistent. A scalar target scales one run; a vector runs one thermal job per value; an empty target ([]) reports the field at an inline elem_p_amp. A transducer resolved from the library (transducer.serial) needs a target, because its drive is resolved at that ISPPA.

The baseline comes from one of two sources (isppa_baseline):

  1. a free-water simulation with the same grid, source, and backend (acoustic_water_baseline; BabelBrain runs its own), recorded as acoustic_provenance.freefield_isppa_wcm2 with its origin in freefield_source; or
  2. the transducer's calibration ISPPA (tx_calibration.isppa_wcm2, from the library or a calibration file), used only when it matches the target to within 1 %. No scaling is then needed.

modules.run_water_baseline decides when the free-water simulation runs (needs_water_baseline):

Value Runs the baseline when auto (default) a target is set and the transducer has no calibration ISPPA, or the target differs from it by more than 1 % 1 always 0 only when the target differs from a calibration ISPPA

A target is never reported unscaled. When a rescale is needed but no simulated baseline exists (for example run_water_baseline: 0 with an uncalibrated transducer, or a cached result from a run without baseline and run_source_setup: 0), the run stops with prestus:isppa:noBaseline or prestus:isppa:unsimulatedBaseline (isppa_scale_factor). Scale factors above 4 or below 0.25 warn (prestus:isppa:largeScale): check that the target is in the linear regime of the simulated drive.

Check what a run models. The parameter summary at the start of the log and the HTML report (row Modelled intensity) state the free-water ISPPA the results report and how it relates to the calibration ISPPA of the drive. A target that differs from the calibration ISPPA, or the default target on a drive without calibration ISPPA, is marked ⚠️ and warns prestus:isppa:targetVsCalibration. A calibration file (<equipment>-F<focus>mm-I<isppa>wpercm2.yaml, calibration) sets both target_isppa_wcm2 and tx_calibration.isppa_wcm2 to its calibrated intensity. If you copy only its annular drive into a config, also set target_isppa_wcm2 to that intensity; otherwise the results are rescaled to the default 30 W/cm².

Several transducers. target_isppa_wcm2 is set per transducer and refers to that transducer alone. Coherent runs set each transducer's drive to its own target before the simulation; async runs scale each field before combining (Multi-transducer: ISPPA targets). The older calibration.target_isppa_wcm2 is read and moved to transducer(1).target_isppa_wcm2 with a deprecation warning.

Axial profile plot

The baseline run also stores the free-water intensity along each transducer's beam axis (bowl apex to grid edge) as acoustic_provenance.freefield_axial. The axial profile plot (sub-XXX_<medium>_axial_profile<affix>.png / .csv, 3D grids) compares the simulated intensity with the free-water intensity of the simulated transducer settings: the k-Wave baseline profile when the baseline ran, and the analytical O'Neil profile for a single annular transducer (always), both at the drive level of the plotted field after scaling. The plot is omitted for combined async / FOV fields (scaled per source) and for the BabelBrain backend.

items.title: Memory Use
items.text:
Two components dominate acoustic memory:

  • Grid fields: pressure, velocity, and medium maps, proportional to the number of voxels. A 0.5 mm head grid takes roughly 7–8 GB; this scales with resolution, not transducer size.
  • Source signal matrix: one waveform per active source voxel over all time steps. Negligible for a focused single-element transducer; for a large multi-element phased array it can exceed the grid fields.

PRESTUS compresses the source matrix automatically per backend (details below). A coarser grid or a partial acoustic FOV reduces the grid fields; the cpp_* backends stream the source matrix from disk.

How PRESTUS reduces source memory by backend

The source signal matrix has size num_source_voxels × Nt. For a kHz-range aperture at 0.5 mm resolution with the standard CFL of 0.15, Nt is on the order of several thousand, so the dense matrix reaches several gigabytes for large transducers.

matlab_cpu / matlab_gpu: lazy rank-2 factorisation for CW sources. For continuous-wave (CW) stimulation every source voxel's time signal has the form

p(voxel, t) = A_voxel · cos(ω t + φ_voxel)

which two real numbers per voxel describe (amplitude and phase, or the real and imaginary part of a complex amplitude). PRESTUS stores only those two numbers per voxel (CWSourceMatrix.m) and evaluates each time column on demand during the simulation. Memory scales with num_source_voxels only, a reduction by a factor of ~2 000–5 000 for typical parameters. This path is used when code_type is matlab_cpu or matlab_gpu and all transducer elements share a single frequency; otherwise the dense matrix is used. k-Wave's own source scaling (kspaceFirstOrder_scaleSourceTerms), including the per-voxel loop for heterogeneous media, is applied to the stored amplitudes, so no dense matrix is built at any point.

cpp_cpu / cpp_gpu: HDF5 streaming from disk. The source matrix is written to an HDF5 file before the simulation and the C++ binary reads it in blocks during execution. Peak memory is bounded by the block size rather than the full matrix, at the cost of I/O throughput.

Backend Simulation device Source signal representation Peak additional RAM / VRAM matlab_gpu GPU Lazy rank-2 (CW) or dense single 2 × (num_src + Nt) × 4 B (CW) matlab_cpu CPU Lazy rank-2 (CW) or dense single 2 × (num_src + Nt) × 4 B (CW) cpp_cpu / cpp_gpu CPU / GPU HDF5 file, streamed Bounded by I/O block size

For a 10 000-voxel source at Nt = 9 000 time steps: dense = 360 MB; CW lazy = 0.08 MB.

items.title: Axisymmetric Simulations
items.text:
For symmetric media (a 2D phantom or water medium), a 3D axisymmetric problem can be modelled on a 2D grid with kspaceFirstOrderAS (grid.axisymmetric: 1; see k-Wave's focused bowl example). This reduces the computational cost markedly compared with a full 3D simulation. kspaceFirstOrder2D is not a substitute: it models an infinite cylinder, not a focusing shell.

What applies in axisymmetric mode:

  • Specify the grid as [radial x 2, axial]. The (2x) radial axis is assumed to be shorter than the axial axis.
  • Only a single transducer is supported; several transducers with axisymmetric == 1 raise an error.
  • Only annular transducers explicitly support axisymmetric kWaveArray mode. Other transducer types are untested in this configuration.
  • A 3D phantom is cut along its second dimension at the transducer's trans_pos when that is given in 3D, else at the centre slice. Output NIfTIs of phantom runs are written in the phantom file's voxel order and world space.
  • The source keeps every grid point with a non-zero band-limited-interpolation weight, as the 3D path and k-Wave do.

Axisymmetric 2D vs. 3D output

Axisymmetric simulations are 3D simulations performed on 2D input grids. grid.axisymmetric_output sets the form of the results: 'auto' (default) expands them to 3D for phantom media and when heating follows, and keeps the 2D plane otherwise; '2d' keeps the mirrored plane (no heating); '3d' always expands.

items.title: Backend Compatibility
items.text:
Backend (simulation.code_type) Axisymmetry support Notes matlab_cpu ✓ Uses kspaceFirstOrderAS matlab_gpu ✓ Uses kspaceFirstOrderAS with RadialSymmetry option cpp_cpu ✓ Uses the C++ OMP binary kspaceFirstOrderASC cpp_gpu (CUDA) ✗ No CUDA binary supports axisymmetric geometry. PRESTUS falls back to the matlab_gpu path (kspaceFirstOrderAS with gpuArray data cast) with a warning. GPU acceleration is preserved; only the CUDA binary is bypassed. Axis mapping and PML in axisymmetric mode

kspaceFirstOrder2D uses a 2D Cartesian grid with X and Y axes, mapped onto the second and first dimensions of input matrices and coordinates ([y, x]). This mirrors 3D image voxel coordinates [i, j, k], which map onto [Y, X, Z]. kspaceFirstOrderAS uses axial and radial axes, mapped onto the first and second dimensions. Internally, [radial x 2, axial] is remapped onto [axial, radial] and only the columns from the beam axis (the transducer's lateral position) onward are retained. With the axis off centre, the expanded output repeats the outermost simulated value beyond the simulated radius. Medium, source, and sensor are set up in [axial, radial] dimensions. After the simulation, values are either mirrored into a Cartesian 2D grid ([radial x 2, axial] again, as for kspaceFirstOrder2D) or radially expanded into a Cartesian 3D grid.

PML. With PMLInside=false (the PRESTUS default) the PML is applied asymmetrically: the axial dimension receives pml_size voxels on both sides, the radial outer edge pml_size voxels on one side only. The inner radial boundary at r = 0 is a symmetry axis and needs no PML. k-Wave handles this; no configuration change is needed.

items.title: Thermal Simulations
items.text:
Tissue absorbs part of the ultrasound and heats up, and temperature rise and thermal dose (CEM43) are the measures safety guidelines use for this effect. PRESTUS computes both from the acoustic field and the sonication protocol, so the predicted heating depends on the timing, step sizes, and absorption settings described here. The report compares the results with published reference levels; PRESTUS does not make an independent safety recommendation.

On this page:

  • Protocol Timing: describing pulses, pulse trains, repetitions, and the post-stimulation period.
  • Step, Temperature, and Sensor Settings: step sizes and starting temperature.
  • Pulse Model: pulses resolved, or each pulse train averaged (faster).
  • Heat Deposition: how tissue absorption turns the acoustic field into heat.
  • Thermal Dose (CEM43) Calculation: the two CEM43 formulations and their outputs.

At a glance

  • When you need it: Whenever you simulate heating (modules.run_heating_sims: 1).
  • Before you start: A working acoustic simulation, and the timing of your protocol.

Thermal simulations use the output of the acoustic simulation; they cannot run without one. They run in k-Wave by default. With acoustic_backend: babelbrain, BabelBrain's own Pennes solver can be used instead (thermal_backend: babelbrain). See Simulation backends for valid combinations and how the results compare, and BabelBrain thermal for the timing mapping and tissue-property differences. Known limitation: BabelBrain thermal uses its own built-in tissue thermal properties, so the thermal fields in medium_properties apply only to the k-Wave thermal backend.

items.title: Protocol Timing
items.text:
Protocol timing follows the nomenclature of the TUS Calculator, which you can use to specify the protocol. All three levels of nesting (pulse, pulse train, pulse train repetition) must be set. For a single pulse train without repetitions, set ptri and ptrd equal to ptd.

Example: a 20 s, 5 Hz, 10 % duty-cycle protocol as a single pulse train repetition:

timing:
  pd: 0.02               # pulse duration (PD) [s]
  pri: 0.2               # pulse repetition interval (PRI) [s]
  ptd: 20                # pulse train duration (PTD) [s]
  pt_timestep: 0.02      # modelling time step inside a PT, with equal_step_duration: 1 [s]
  ptri: 20               # pulse train repetition interval (PTRI) [s]
  ptrd: 20               # pulse train repetition duration (PTRD) [s]
  post_ptri_dur: 20      # steady-state duration following the PTRD [s]
  post_pt_timestep: 1    # modelling time step between PTs and after the PTRD [s]
  equal_step_duration: 0 # 0: one step per on and off period; 1: fixed step duration pt_timestep

Continuous pulse train protocols can be modelled either as a single pulse train repetition with multiple pulse trains (as above) or as multiple pulse train repetitions of a single pulse train.

A coarser protocol neglects the heating dynamics between pulses and models one longer pulse per train. Collapsing the off period lets the simulation use a coarser step size there:

timing:
  pd: 2
  pri: 2
  ptd: 2
  pt_timestep: 0.02
  ptri: 20
  ptrd: 20
  post_ptri_dur: 0
  post_pt_timestep: 1

Pulse ramps. With timing.pulse_ramp_dur (and pulse_ramp_shape), each pulse rises and falls over that time instead of switching on and off. Heat scales with the squared amplitude, so the thermal simulation scales the heat of every pulse by the same factor as the pulse-average intensity (compute_ramp_factor; for example 0.93 for a 1 ms linear ramp on a 20 ms pulse). With an async custom schedule, each transducer's factor uses its own timing.pd. The temperature course within a pulse is not resolved; thermal time constants are much longer than a ramp. The protocol figure draws the ramped pulse.

Post-stimulation period. Heat dissipation continues after the final pulse. Run the simulation until a steady state is reached by setting timing.post_ptri_dur; its time step is timing.post_pt_timestep, separate from pt_timestep. For a continuous pulse train, a steady-state phase can also be part of an extended PTR interval; post_ptri_dur also gives protocols with repetitions a steady-state phase. For long intervals between pulse trains, a coarser post_pt_timestep may be sufficient.

items.title: Step, Temperature, and Sensor Settings
items.text: Parameter Role timing.pt_timestep Step size for the on and off periods of each pulse within a pulse train. Used only with equal_step_duration: 1; PD and PRI − PD must be integer multiples of it. Only with thermal.pulse_model: 'pulse_resolved'; with the default 'train_averaged' the in-train step follows from the grid (see Pulse Model). timing.equal_step_duration 1: every on and off period is split into steps of pt_timestep. In the first example above (PD 20 ms, PRI 200 ms, PTD 20 s, pt_timestep 20 ms), each of the 100 pulses takes 1 step with stimulation and 9 without (10 × 100 = 1,000 steps). 0 (default): every on and off period is one simulation step (2 × 100 = 200 steps), which reduces the computational load. Only with thermal.pulse_model: 'pulse_resolved'; with the default 'train_averaged' the in-train step follows from the grid (see Pulse Model). timing.post_ptri_dur Duration of the post-stimulation period after the PTRD. thermal.temp_0 Starting temperature in degrees, per tissue.

items.title: Pulse Model
items.text:
thermal.pulse_model sets how the pulses enter the simulation. 'train_averaged' (default) heats through each pulse train with the heat source weighted by the duty cycle within the train (PD/PRI), as k-Plan does, and steps it at 0.1 · dx² / the largest thermal diffusivity. 'pulse_resolved' heats during each pulse and cools during each gap, one segment each. Temperatures are recorded every timing.post_pt_timestep.

A pulse cycle (PRI) of 0.1–1 s is short against tissue thermal time constants, so both give nearly the same temperatures: on a 150 s protocol in a head (sub-009, 0.5 mm grid), peak rises differed by at most 0.8 % and thermal dose by about 1 %, while heating took 116 s instead of 400 s. 'train_averaged' does not show the temperature ripple within a train, and lowers the peak where a pulse is long against the time a hot spot takes to cool (a small, sharp hot spot, or pulses of hundreds of ms): there, use 'pulse_resolved'. Async schedules that fire transducers in turn within a train always resolve the pulses.

The figure shows both for one point with a single thermal time constant τ, a schematic stand-in for diffusion and perfusion: change the timing to see when averaging departs from resolving the pulses (long pulses against τ).

The pulse-model figure needs JavaScript.

items.title: Heat Deposition
items.text:
The acoustic field deposits heat at the rate Q = 2·α_abs·I = α_abs·p²/(ρc), with the absorption coefficient α_abs [Np/m] at the source frequency. Each tissue in medium_properties specifies α_abs in one of two ways (see Medium properties):

  • absorption_fraction: a fraction of the attenuation coefficient. The defaults use this for every tissue, so a change of alpha_coeff also changes absorption.
  • absorption_coeff [dB/(cm·MHz^y)]: a fixed coefficient, with the tissue's attenuation power law y (alpha_power). It does not follow changes of alpha_coeff.

A tissue sets one of the two; the other stays empty. When a config layer (a study YAML file, a struct passed to load_parameters, or an override) sets one of them for a tissue, load_parameters empties the other one inherited from earlier layers, such as the default absorption_fraction. One run can combine both. For example, brain absorption as a fraction and skull absorption as a coefficient:

medium_properties:
  brain:
    absorption_fraction: 0.77
  skull:
    absorption_coeff: 3.78   # clears the default skull absorption_fraction

A layer that sets both for one tissue stops with the error medium_absorption_layer:bothSet. If you change the struct in MATLAB after loading, empty the other field yourself (parameters.medium_properties.skull.absorption_fraction = [];); otherwise the medium setup stops with thermal_absorption_model:bothSet. Empty and NaN values count as not set; a tissue with neither uses a fraction of 1.

With headmodel.smooth_properties: true, α_abs is formed per tissue and then smoothed as one map, so at a tissue boundary it stays between the two tissues' values.

A pseudo-CT skull with mapped attenuation has no matching absorption map. A skull absorption_coeff is then applied as the fraction absorption_coeff / alpha_coeff of the mapped attenuation, with a warning (medium_setup:absorptionModelForced).

The log, the run summary, and the HTML methods text give each tissue's model with its effective coefficient and fraction (α_abs/α) at the configured attenuation. The medium log gives the mapped range for a pseudo-CT skull. With io.save_property_maps, both are written as absorption_np [Np/m at the source frequency] and absorption_fraction maps.

items.title: Thermal Dose (CEM43) Calculation
items.text:
PRESTUS computes both CEM43 formulations in every k-Wave thermal simulation. Both are written to the CSV output, exported as NIfTI volumes and shown as separate figures. The HTML report (dashboard, safety verdict, methods text) uses the formulation selected by thermal.cem43_iso. With the BabelBrain thermal backend only BabelBrain's own dose is available (R = 0.25 below 43 °C, 0.5 at or above 43 °C): the ISO maps are NaN, and load_parameters sets cem43_iso to 0 with a warning, so the report uses BabelBrain's dose.

Both forms are based on the thermal isoeffective dose of Sapareto & Dewey (1984), CEM43 = Σ Δt · R^(43 − T).

items.title: k-Wave Form (Default)
items.text:
CEM43 as implemented in k-Wave's kWaveDiffusion: R = 0.25 for 37 ≤ T < 43 °C, R = 0.5 for T ≥ 43 °C, and no dose below 37 °C.

cem43 = cem43 + ...
        dt ./ 60 .* ...
        (0.25 .* (T >= 37 & T < 43) + ...
         0.5  .* (T >= 43)).^(43 - T);

items.title: ISO Form
items.text:
Set thermal.cem43_iso: 1 to use this form in the HTML report. It is computed by cem43_iso_increment and combines:

  • ISO 14708-3:2017, Clause 17.1, Formula (1): R = 0.25 for T < 43 °C and R = 0.5 for T ≥ 43 °C, "valid for temperatures between 39 °C and 57 °C". Table 101 gives the tissue thresholds brain 2, bone 16, and skin 21 CEM43, which ITRUSST adopts (Aubry et al., 2025) and PRESTUS uses as reference levels (get_risk_limits).
  • ITRUSST biophysical safety consensus (Aubry et al., 2025): dose is accumulated over the whole time the tissue is above 39 °C, including cooling; and because thermotolerance "is not maintained beyond 43 °C, nor does it return upon cooling", R = 0.5 is used for all time steps after 43 °C has been reached (citing Sapareto & Dewey, 1984). PRESTUS tracks this with T_max.
  • PRESTUS choice: voxels that reach 57 °C (current T or T_max) are set to CEM43 = ∞. ISO 14708-3 only states that the formula is not valid above 57 °C; ∞ is a conservative flag for that range, not taken from either source.
cem43_iso = cem43_iso + ...
        dt ./ 60 .* ...
        (0    .* (T < 39  & T_max < 43) + ...
         0.25 .* (T >= 39 & T < 43 & T_max < 43) + ...
         0.5  .* (T >= 43 | T_max >= 43)).^(43 - T);
cem43_iso(T >= 57 | T_max >= 57) = Inf;

items.title: Output Naming
items.text:
Suffix Description CEM43 / CEM43_end k-Wave form (max over protocol / at the end of the simulated protocol) CEM43_iso / CEM43_iso_end ISO form (max over protocol / at the end of the simulated protocol)

Both suffixes apply to NIfTI filenames (sub-XXX_<medium>_T1w<affix>_CEM43_iso.nii.gz, etc.) and to CSV columns (CEM43_brain, CEM43iso_brain, etc.).

The maximum and end maps and the per-tissue time courses use every simulation step. The focal-plane time courses and the heating video (the plane through the transducer in 3D, the whole grid in 2D) keep every k-th step when all steps would exceed thermal.max_focal_plane_gb (default 2 GB; 0 keeps every step).

References
  • Sapareto SA, Dewey WC (1984). Thermal dose determination in cancer therapy. Int J Radiat Oncol Biol Phys 10:787–800. https://doi.org/10.1016/0360-3016(84)90379-1
  • ISO 14708-3:2017. Implants for surgery. Active implantable medical devices. Part 3: Implantable neurostimulators. Clause 17.1, Formula (1), Table 101. https://www.iso.org/standard/60539.html
  • Aubry J-F, Attali D, et al. (2025). ITRUSST consensus on biophysical safety for transcranial ultrasound stimulation. Brain Stimul 18:1896–1905. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brs.2025.10.007
  • Martin E, et al. (2024). ITRUSST consensus on standardised reporting for transcranial ultrasound stimulation. Brain Stimul 17:607–615 (Eq. 5: Sapareto & Dewey form only). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brs.2024.04.013

items.title: PRESTUS Telemetry
items.text:
PRESTUS can send anonymous usage statistics, one record per pipeline event, so the developers can see which features and platforms are in use, improve run-time estimates, and publish simulation statistics across sites. Participation is voluntary, you choose what to share in three levels, and nothing is sent without your choice. This page shows how to make or change that choice, how batch and cluster runs handle it, and every field a record may contain.

On this page:

  • Choosing What to Share: the prompt, the three levels, how to record or change your choice, the PRESTUS_TELEMETRY override, and batch or cluster runs.
  • Collected Data: every field of a record, grouped by level.

At a glance

  • When you need it: To decide what to share, to change your choice, or to silence the prompt on a cluster.
  • Before you start: Nothing; your choice lives in ~/.prestus/telemetry.json.

items.title: Choosing What to Share
items.text:
Usage statistics come in three levels. You can share any combination:

Level Name in settings What it adds Usage and errors basic Which features, platforms, and versions are used, and whether runs succeed (error identifier and failing stage, never the message text). Performance performance Hardware, requested resources, grid size, stage times, and peak memory. These calibrate the predicted load. Summary outcomes (anonymous) outcomes Eight rounded summary statistics: brain intensity and its ratio to free water, mechanical index, targeting error, brain and skull temperature rise, and the duty cycle and duration they depend on; plus the median modelled skull properties. Never maps, coordinates, or target names.

Every record also carries a small envelope whichever levels you share: a random installation ID, a random run ID, the PRESTUS version, the run type, the run status, and the levels themselves.

The prompt shows Share all (recommended) with the three levels below it, all ticked. Untick the levels you do not want to share; unticking all of them shares nothing. How the prompt appears depends on the session:

  • Interactive console session: the levels are listed; press Enter to share all, type the numbers of the levels to share (e.g. 1 2), or 0 to share none.
  • MATLAB GUIs and the PRESTUS Nexus: a dialog with the same boxes, and Save or Ask me later. In the Nexus, Tools ▸ Usage statistics… opens it at any time, and the status bar shows what you share.
  • Non-interactive session (matlab -batch, deployed app, SLURM/PBS job, or a session with neither desktop nor display; see below): no prompt is shown and the run never waits for an answer.

The prompt repeats every run until you make a choice. A choice made before the levels existed keeps sharing what it covered (usage, performance, and the skull medians); an interactive session offers the levels once. To change your choice:

  • Share levels: run telemetry_set_consent(true) in MATLAB for all levels, or name them, e.g. telemetry_set_consent({'basic', 'performance'}).
  • Share nothing: run telemetry_set_consent(false).
  • Undecided again: telemetry_setup_reset() deletes the file, so the next run asks again.

items.title: Per-Process Override (PRESTUS_TELEMETRY)
items.text:
The PRESTUS_TELEMETRY environment variable sets the choice for one MATLAB process, without a prompt and without writing ~/.prestus/telemetry.json:

Values and precedence Value (case-insensitive) Effect for this process off, 0, false Nothing sent, no prompt. on, 1, true All levels shared if no choice is recorded, no prompt. A recorded choice still applies. The random ID in ~/.prestus/uuid.txt is created on the first send. levels, comma-separated (e.g. basic,performance) Those levels shared if no choice is recorded, no prompt. unset or empty No override: the recorded choice applies, or the prompt/notice described above. anything else Warning prestus:telemetry:invalidEnv (once per value per MATLAB session), then treated as unset.

PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=off takes precedence over a recorded choice: it sends nothing even after you chose to share. Sharing through the variable never overrides a recorded choice; it only applies when no choice is recorded. The variable never changes the recorded choice; use telemetry_set_consent for a lasting one. Set the variable before MATLAB starts (PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=off matlab -batch "...", or export PRESTUS_TELEMETRY=off in a job script) or with setenv('PRESTUS_TELEMETRY', 'off') in the session.

items.title: Batch and Cluster Runs
items.text:
PRESTUS never prompts, and never waits for an answer, in these sessions:

How these sessions are detected
  • matlab -batch runs (detected with batchStartupOptionUsed, R2019a and later), whether or not a display is attached: cron jobs, CI runners, and scripts started from a terminal;
  • deployed applications and jobs under SLURM (SLURM_JOB_ID) or PBS/Torque (PBS_JOBID);
  • sessions with neither the MATLAB desktop nor a display (e.g. matlab -nodisplay -r ... from cron). An interactive matlab -nodisplay terminal session is also treated this way; record a choice there with telemetry_set_consent.

The full notice is printed to stdout (visible in job logs) on every run, but no choice is recorded and no data is sent unless a choice was already recorded or PRESTUS_TELEMETRY is set. The notice reappears on every run until you record a choice or set PRESTUS_TELEMETRY.

To choose from an HPC environment, either:

  1. Run PRESTUS once interactively (e.g. on a login node) and answer the prompt,
  2. Run telemetry_set_consent(true), a list of levels, or false in MATLAB,
  3. Set PRESTUS_TELEMETRY in the job script, for that job only, or

  4. Create ~/.prestus/telemetry.json by hand:

    {"opt_in": true, "levels": ["basic", "performance", "outcomes"], "decided_on": "YYYY-MM-DD", "prestus_ver": "", "notice": 3}

items.title: Technical, Development, and Deployment Runs
items.text: Test and CI runs that exercise prestus_pipeline are tagged run_type: technical automatically, so their pass/fail rate can be tracked separately from real deployment usage on the usage statistics page. Set PRESTUS_RUN_TYPE=technical yourself when running PRESTUS purely to validate an install or a pipeline change, and PRESTUS_RUN_TYPE=development (in your shell or startup.m) on a machine where you develop PRESTUS; leave it unset for real runs (default: deployment). Jobs that PRESTUS submits to a cluster report the run type of the session that submitted them, including one set with setenv in MATLAB. Independently of the run type, prestus_branch and prestus_dirty mark runs from a checkout off main or with local changes.

items.title: Collected Data
items.text:
Each pipeline run emits a run_start record and then run_end (on clean exit) or run_error (if the pipeline throws an unhandled exception), with the same run_id. A run with a start but no end record was stopped from outside, e.g. by a scheduler's time or memory limit. The tables below list every field that may be sent, by level. A field listed under several levels is sent when any of them is shared.

Never stored in the usage statistics: subject IDs, file paths, directory names, coordinates, target names, free text, IP addresses, host names, or any map or image of the simulation. Free-text settings are sent as classes only (transducer_model, hpc_partition). Like any web service, the hosting provider (Supabase) keeps a request log with the sender's IP address and approximate location for 1 day; it is not linked to the statistics.

items.title: Every Record
items.text: Fields Field Description event Event type: run_start, run_end, or run_error telemetry_schema Version of the record format (currently 3) consent_levels, consent_notice The shared levels, and the version of the notice the choice was made under run_type technical (test/CI run), development, or deployment (default). See Technical, Development, and Deployment Runs. uuid Random UUID generated locally on first send; stored in ~/.prestus/uuid.txt. Not linked to your identity or machine. run_id Random UUID generated per pipeline run, so the records of one run can be told apart prestus_ver, prestus_hash Version string (from git describe or the VERSION file, e.g. v0.5.1) and short git commit hash of the running PRESTUS status "success" or "error" (on run_end and run_error)

items.title: Usage and Errors (basic)
items.text: Fields Field Description prestus_branch Branch class of the PRESTUS checkout: main, development, other, or unknown (never the branch name) prestus_dirty yes when tracked PRESTUS files differ from the commit, else no or unknown matlab_ver, platform, kwave_ver MATLAB release (e.g. R2024a), CPU architecture from computer('arch'), and the k-Wave version from getComputerInfo sim_platform Execution platform: matlab, slurm, qsub, etc. code_type, acoustic_backend, thermal_backend k-Wave code variant (matlab_cpu, matlab_gpu, cpp_cpu, cpp_gpu), acoustic solver (kwave, kwave_elastic, jwave, or babelbrain), and thermal solver medium, pct_enabled Medium type (water, layered, or phantom) and whether pseudo-CT is enabled pct_density, pct_speed, pct_atten Names of the pseudo-CT mappings (names, not values) modules_enabled, pipeline_mode Names of the modules.* flags set to 1, and the pipeline mode: single, async, multi_isppa, or sequential acoustic_fov, headmodel_reuse Booleans: a limited acoustic field of view is set; headmodel.reuse_across_placements transducer_type, freq_hz, n_transducer_elements Geometry type (e.g. focused_bowl), nominal frequency [Hz], and element count of the first transducer transducer_model Equipment model of the first transducer when its serial or name matches a shipped entry (e.g. CTX_500); custom otherwise. Never the name or serial. n_transducers, transducer_coupling Number of transducers and how they are combined (simulation.transducer_coupling) duration_s Total pipeline wall-clock time in seconds error_id, failed_stage MATLAB error identifier (e.g. MATLAB:badsubscript; no message text) and the stage the run was in when it failed (e.g. acoustic)

items.title: Performance (performance)
items.text:
Fields Field Description cpu_model, ram_gb, gpu_model CPU model name, total RAM [GB], and GPU device name (no_pct without the Parallel Computing Toolbox, none without a GPU) precision Floating-point precision: single or double hpc_timelimit_h, hpc_memory_gb Requested wall time [h] and memory [GB] of the job (hpc.timelimit, hpc.memorylimit) hpc_partition Class of hpc.partition: gpu (the name contains "gpu"), other, or empty when unset; never the partition name n_cpu_alloc CPU cores of the SLURM allocation (SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK); null outside SLURM resolution_mm, fit_alpha_power Grid resolution [mm], and whether attenuation is refitted to one power law source_cfl, source_ppw, steady_state_transits, sim_time_us Time-step and duration settings of the acoustic simulation (grid.*; null when unset) sim_stats.acoustic_voxels, sim_stats.acoustic_dims, sim_stats.acoustic_pml Grid points and dimensions of the acoustic grid the solver ran on, and its PML thickness in grid points sim_stats.axisymmetric 1 for an axisymmetric (2D) acoustic grid sim_stats.acoustic_nt, sim_stats.acoustic_s Acoustic time steps and simulation time in seconds sim_stats.thermal_voxels, sim_stats.thermal_steps, sim_stats.thermal_s Thermal grid points, time steps, and simulation time in seconds sim_stats.stage_<name>_s Duration in seconds of each timed pipeline stage (e.g. stage_preproc_s) sim_stats.peak_ram_gb, sim_stats.n_cpu, sim_stats.gpu_mem_gb Peak RAM of the job [GB] (Linux only), CPU cores of the allocation or machine, and GPU memory [GB] (a MIG slice reports its own) sim_stats.queue_wait_s Seconds the SLURM job waited in the queue

A stage that did not simulate (reused cache, stage off) leaves its fields out. A failed run sends the stages it finished.

items.title: Summary Outcomes (outcomes)
items.text:
Rounded to two significant figures (temperatures to 0.1 °C, skull medians to three significant figures), for the first transducer and the first field a run analyses. Values a run does not compute, such as brain values in a water run, are left out. These records also carry medium, pct_enabled, the solvers, the transducer model, type and frequency, and resolution_mm, so the numbers can be read without the other levels.

Fields Field Description outcomes.isppa_brain_wcm2 Peak pulse-average intensity in the brain [W/cm²] outcomes.brain_transmission Brain ISPPA divided by the free-water ISPPA of the same drive: the share of intensity that reaches the brain outcomes.mi_brain Peak mechanical index in the brain outcomes.focal_error_mm Distance from the intended focus to the centre of the −3 dB focal region [mm] outcomes.riset_brain_c, outcomes.riset_skull_c Peak temperature rise above baseline in brain and skull [°C] outcomes.duty_cycle, outcomes.sonication_s Overall duty cycle (pulse duty × train duty, 0–1) and total sonication time [s] from timing.* sim_stats.skull_c_median, sim_stats.skull_rho_median, sim_stats.skull_atten_median Median sound speed [m/s], density [kg/m³], and attenuation at the source frequency [dB/cm] of the modelled skull, over all skull voxels sim_stats.skull_path_c_median, sim_stats.skull_path_rho_median, sim_stats.skull_path_atten_median The same medians over the skull on the beam path

items.title: Usage Statistics
items.text: See the Usage Statistics page for live charts populated from the anonymised telemetry database.

items.title: Testing
items.text:
PRESTUS is tested at five levels, from checks that take seconds and run on every change to benchmarks that need a GPU or a real subject and run before a release. This page tells you which level a change needs, what data, hardware, and time each level takes, and how to add a test.

On this page:

  • Level 0: Static Checks: the doc, parameter, link, and Nexus checks that run on every push.
  • Level 1: Unit Tests: data-free tests of each function's logic, grouped by area.
  • Level 2: Physics Benchmarks: free-water fields against the O'Neil solution and the ITRUSST benchmarks, with their tolerances.
  • Level 3: Pipeline Tests: the whole pipeline on synthetic water, a segmented subject, and the demo subject, with golden metrics.
  • Level 4: Backends and the Nexus Round Trip: jwave and BabelBrain against k-Wave, and Nexus configs loaded in MATLAB.
  • Release Checklist: the tests to run before tagging a release.
  • Rules for New Tests: where a new test goes and the rules it follows.

The MATLAB tests use matlab.unittest and live in tests/; the Nexus tests use pytest and live in nexus/tests/. run_all_tests(level) runs a MATLAB level and fails (non-zero exit under matlab -batch) when any test fails. It also records the wall time, CPU time and peak memory of every test and test class in prestus_test_resources_<level>_<run>.csv (folder PRESTUS_TEST_RESOURCES_DIR, default the system temp folder) and prints the slowest tests; memory is measured on Linux only.

Level What it guarantees Command Needs Time Runs 0 Static Docs match the code, the site builds, the Nexus works see Level 0 Python ~2 min CI, every push 1 Unit Every function's logic, incl. config, placement, scaling, caches, HPC parsing, reports run_all_tests('unit') MATLAB ~15 min (macOS, checkout on a network drive; less on a local disk) CI, every push 2 Physics The solver path reproduces analytic and published reference fields run_all_tests('physics'), ('itrusst') MATLAB (+ ITRUSST data) ~5 min CPU (2D), plus the unit tests, which run_all_tests('physics') also runs CI weekly; 3D on a GPU node before a release 3 Pipeline Whole pipeline on synthetic and real data, numbers stable against a reference run_all_tests('water') … ('demo_golden') k-Wave CPU; SimNIBS outputs; demo data 10 min – hours before a release 4 Backends jwave / BabelBrain agree with k-Wave; Nexus ↔ MATLAB round trip runtests('tests/test_jwave.m') etc. conda envs, GPU, MATLAB 10–60 min after backend or environment changes

items.title: Level 0: Static Checks
items.text:
python tests/docs/gen_function_index.py --check   # doc_functions.md lists every function
python tests/docs/gen_doc_icons.py --check        # doc/assets/icons match the Nexus drawings
python tests/docs/gen_load_data.py --check        # load calculator data matches throughput.yaml
python tests/docs/check_param_docs.py             # every config key documented; defaults match
python tests/docs/check_links.py                  # relative links and anchors resolve
python tests/docs/check_images.py                 # images and PRESTUS_bin files exist (--bin DIR: local clone)
zensical build --strict -f mkdocs.yaml            # site builds without warnings, as deployed (pip install -r requirements-docs.txt)
mkdocs build --strict -d /tmp/prestus-site        # optional: MkDocs + Material (CI, non-blocking)
(cd nexus && python -m pytest -q -m "not matlab")

gen_function_index.py without --check regenerates doc/doc_functions.md (it keeps written descriptions and takes new ones from each file's help line). gen_doc_icons.py without --check rewrites the option-table icons in doc/assets/icons/ from nexus/prestus_nexus/ui/choice_icons.py, the drawings of the Nexus drop-downs. gen_load_data.py without --check rewrites doc/javascripts/load_model_data.js, the data of the load calculator on Run time and resources, from nexus/prestus_nexus/throughput.yaml. check_param_docs.py compares the Default column of doc_parameters.md with config_default.yaml. The Nexus tests include the schema drift test (test_schema.py: overlay vs. config_default.yaml and functions/), which also guards the list of extra config keys MATLAB uses for its unknown-key check.

items.title: Level 1: Unit Tests
items.text:
cd tests
run_all_tests          % same as run_all_tests('unit')

No data, SimNIBS, k-Wave simulation, or GPU is needed. A failed test prints its full diagnostic; a skipped test prints why it was skipped.

Area Files Configuration test_load_parameters, test_config_layering (toolbox → project → study layering, stale project defaults, unknown keys, non-interactive warnings, prestus_config_upgrade), test_config_upgrade (keys from v0.5.0 on converted to current names), test_study Intensity scaling test_isppa_policy (needs_water_baseline, isppa_baseline, isppa_scale_factor, apply_isppa_scaling), test_focal_reference, test_focal_fwhm Caches test_cache_signature Transducers & calibration test_transducer_library, test_transducer_model (tag model), test_library_conditions, test_matrix_transducer, test_cw_source_matrix, test_calibration_session (the GUI/Nexus calibration steps, meta.fit) Placement & neuronavigation test_transducer_placement (tag manual), test_plantus_placement (tags validation, dispatch), test_neuronav_io, test_neuronav_batch, test_placement_report, test_placement_positions Coordinates test_transform Head model test_head_preprocessing, test_integration_headpreproc, test_deface_m2m Thermal test_thermal_parameters, test_thermal_dose (ISO CEM43 against Sapareto & Dewey values) Backends (logic only) test_babelbrain_insitu_isppa, test_babelbrain_thermal_timing, test_babelbrain_air_regions (needs Python with numpy/scipy/nibabel; skipped otherwise) HPC test_hpc_job_report, test_parse_memory_tags, test_hpc_submit Security test_shell_quote_arg, test_r_quote_string, test_run_command, test_command_injection Nexus MATLAB session test_nexus_bridge (nexus_bridge protocol and allow-list, nexus_neuronav and nexus_calibration on synthetic data) Helpers, reports, suite wiring test_helper, test_reports, test_suite_wiring

items.title: Level 2: Physics Benchmarks
items.text:
These check numbers, not just that code runs. Both use a focused bowl in lossless water (the ITRUSST BM1 source: ROC 64 mm, aperture 64 mm, 500 kHz, 60 kPa) run through prestus_pipeline.

test_physics_water: against the analytic O'Neil solution (k-Wave focusedBowlONeil), no data needed:

Check Tolerance (2D axisymmetric) Focal position on axis 0.5 mm Focal peak pressure 2 % −3 dB (intensity) axial focal length 5 % Four-ring annular array in phase (CTX-500 ring diameters on the same bowl) against O'Neil summed over the rings: focal position / peak pressure / −3 dB length 1 mm / 2 % / 5 % (2026-10-08: 0.50 mm, +0.10 %, +0.04 %; the summed peak is flat, ±0.5 mm costs 0.08 % pressure) Doubling the drive doubles the pressure 1 % A target ISPPA on an uncalibrated transducer is met in water 2 % With run_water_baseline: 0, an unmet target stops the run error prestus:isppa:noBaseline

test_itrusst_benchmark: benchmarks PH1-BM1-SC1 (focused bowl) and PH1-BM1-SC2 (20 mm plane piston, a flat annular element) of Aubry et al. (2022): the pressure amplitude in the central plane against the published k-Wave reference (60 points per wavelength). Download INTERCOMPARISON-PH1-DATA-V1.0 from Zenodo and set PRESTUS_ITRUSST_DATA to it; the test skips otherwise.

Metric Bowl: tolerance (2D) Bowl: result 2026-10-02 Piston: tolerance (2D) Piston: result 2026-10-02 Focal pressure 2 % +0.2 % 2 % 0.0 % Focal position shift 0.5 mm 0.0 mm 0.5 mm 0.0 mm L∞ (max abs. difference / reference max) 4 % 2.1 % 3 % 1.6 % L2 (relative norm) 3 % 1.5 % 1 % 0.4 %

For the piston, every on-axis near-field maximum has the same amplitude (2 p₀), so the focal pressure and position are taken beyond half the near-field distance (a²/2λ), which leaves only the last axial maximum.

run_all_tests('physics')       % unit + test_physics_water and test_water_baseline_box (2D, ~7 min CPU)
setenv('PRESTUS_ITRUSST_DATA', '/path/to/INTERCOMPARISON-PH1-DATA-V1.0')
run_all_tests('itrusst')       % 2D BM1 bowl + piston, 3D BM1 bowl
run_all_tests('physics_3d')    % 3D O'Neil check

The 3D variants (tags physics_3d, itrusst_3d; ~6 M voxels at 0.5 mm) belong on a GPU node: set PRESTUS_PHYSICS_CODE_TYPE (e.g. cpp_gpu) and submit the MATLAB call as a job. Their tolerances are provisional (focal pressure 5 %, position 1 mm; ITRUSST L∞ 10 % and L2 6 %; O'Neil focal length 10 %) until their first run on the reference node.

Tolerance policy. A benchmark's tolerances are set from its first passing run on the reference machine plus a margin, recorded with that run's values in the test file, and then kept fixed. Loosen a tolerance only together with an explanation in the changelog; a benchmark that starts failing after a change is a finding, not a test to adjust.

items.title: Synthetic Water Pipeline
items.text:
run_all_tests('water')     % unit + slower unit checks + 3D water pipeline + multi-ISPPA

test_integration_water runs the full pipeline with simulation.medium: water on a small 3D grid (CPU k-Wave), test_isppa_rescaling the multi-ISPPA pipeline. test_telemetry_pipeline checks that a run sends run_start and run_end, and a failing one run_error with its stage (nothing leaves the machine). The level also runs the slower data-free checks: test_transducer_model tag fit (optimiser) and test_plantus_placement tag integration (mocked PlanTUS subprocess; needs Python 3). Fixture: fixtures/make_minimal_parameters.m (single-element bowl, drive level, no target ISPPA), fixtures/make_synthetic_segmentation.m.

items.title: Subject Smoke Tests
items.text:
test_integration_pipeline reaches checkpoints on a SimNIBS-segmented subject; each level includes the ones above it:

Level Coverage Duration run_all_tests('head') smoke_config, smoke_head (head preprocessing to medium masks) 1–5 min run_all_tests('acoustic') + smoke_acoustic 10–60 min run_all_tests('all') + smoke_thermal 10–60 min 
export PRESTUS_TEST_DATA=/path/to/demo/data      # folder containing m2m_sub-001/
export PRESTUS_DEMO_CONFIG=/path/to/config.yaml   # optional; default config/config_tutorial.yaml

items.title: Demo Subject (All Placement Modes)
items.text:
test_integration_demo uses demo subject sub-009 (SimNIBS segmentation, UTE-derived pseudo-CT, Localite data) in a folder outside the repository, PRESTUS_DEMO_DATA (check its layout with setup_demo_data('/path/to/prestus_testdata')):

prestus_testdata/
├── bids/sub-009/anat/           sub-009_T1w.nii.gz, sub-009_UTE.nii.gz
├── simnibs/m2m_sub-009/          SimNIBS output (incl. pseudoCT, MNI transforms)
├── localite/sub-009/ses-02/localite/Session_*/TMSTrigger/TriggerMarkers_Coil0*.xml
├── coords/sub-009_heuristic_target.json   {"target_name": "MD_thalamus", "mni_target_mm": [-6,-16,4]}
├── configs/config_demo_{manual,localite,heuristic}.yaml
├── golden/sub-009_manual_metrics.json     reference metrics (see below)
└── sim_outputs/                  written by the tests
Level Checks Duration demo_inputs input files exist ~1 s demo_config the three placement configs load ~1 s demo_localite Localite XML → finite voxel positions ~1 s demo_pct pseudo-CT readable ~1 s demo_head head preprocessing (manual, pseudo-CT) 1–5 min demo_acoustic full acoustic pipeline (3D) 10–60 min (GPU) demo_thermal thermal on the cached acoustics 10–60 min demo_golden key metrics vs. the stored reference seconds

Golden metrics. test_demo_golden reads the result table of the manual-placement demo run and compares Isppa_brain (5 %), Psptp_brain and MI_brain (3 %), the focus position I{x,y,z}_brain_vox (1 voxel), maxT_brain (0.2 °C) and CEM43iso_brain (20 %) with golden/sub-009_manual_metrics.json. Without a reference it writes …metrics.candidate.json and reports the test as incomplete: review the candidate (e.g. against the last release), then rename it. Update the reference only for intended changes and say so in the changelog. Run it after demo_acoustic and demo_thermal.

items.title: Level 4: Backends and the Nexus Round Trip
items.text:
File Checks Needs smoke_test_backends.m BabelBrain and jwave importable, bridge scripts present (<30 s) conda envs test_babelbrain.m staged: paths, input writing, transducer mapping, dry run, full FDTD (tags quick, nogpu, full) BABELBRAIN_PYTHON, GPU for full test_jwave.m jwave (Helmholtz) vs k-Wave on the same water simulation: peak, FWHM, field correlation (tag quick without the timing sweep) JWAVE_PYTHON nexus/tests/test_matlab_roundtrip.py configs written by the Nexus load in load_parameters with identical values MATLAB (PRESTUS_MATLAB) nexus/tests/test_real_configs.py every study config in $PRESTUS_REAL_CONFIG_DIR round-trips real configs run_all_tests('slurm_live') (test_hpc_job_report) submits a 5 s SLURM job (1 core, 1 GB) and checks the resource report built from its real sacct record; skipped without sbatch a SLURM cluster run_all_tests('telemetry_live') (test_telemetry_live) the telemetry server accepts the run_start, run_end and run_error events PRESTUS builds, with run types technical and development; adds 4 rows that usage statistics leave out; weekly in CI network nexus/tests/test_bridge.py (matlab-marked part), test_bridge_pages_matlab.py the real nexus_bridge; the Localite and Calibration pages end to end (synthetic Localite study; CTX_250_001 profiles from local/profiles) MATLAB 
runtests('tests/test_babelbrain.m', 'Tag', 'nogpu')
runtests('tests/test_jwave.m', 'Tag', 'quick')

cd nexus && python -m pytest -q      # includes the MATLAB round trip when MATLAB is found

items.title: Release Checklist
items.text:
1. CI green (levels 0–1, and the latest weekly physics run).
  2. run_all_tests('itrusst') and run_all_tests('physics_3d') on the GPU node.
  3. run_all_tests('demo_acoustic'), run_all_tests('demo_thermal'), run_all_tests('demo_golden').
  4. test_babelbrain (full) and test_jwave if a backend or its environment changed.
  5. Nexus round trip (cd nexus && python -m pytest -q).

items.title: Rules for New Tests
items.text:
• New function or fix → a methods (Test) block in the test_*.m of the function's area; a new file only for a new area. run_all_tests finds every test class in tests/ and runs a test at the levels its level tag belongs to (prestus_test_levels.m). Give each class the shared path fixture and one level tag, and add no addpath of its own:

    classdef (SharedTestFixtures = {prestus_paths}, TestTags = {'unit'}) test_x < matlab.unittest.TestCase

    A file that spans levels tags each methods (Test, TestTags = {...}) block instead; standalone marks tests no level runs. test_suite_wiring fails for a test without exactly one level tag. - Anything that changes numbers → extend a physics benchmark, or the golden metrics, so the change is visible. - New pipeline stage → a tagged method in test_integration_pipeline.m and, if it warrants it, a level in prestus_test_levels.m. - New demo subject or placement mode → extend test_integration_demo.m with a private loader like load_demo_config. - Tests write only to tempdir (or PRESTUS_DEMO_DATA/sim_outputs) and skip, not fail, when optional data or tools are missing (assume*).

items.title: Time Reversal: Refocusing, Aberration Report, and Pose Search
items.text:
The skull delays and attenuates the parts of the beam differently, so the waves from different parts of the transducer no longer arrive at the target in phase: the focus weakens and shifts. With time_reversal.enabled: true, PRESTUS measures this with one extra simulation per target, using acoustic reciprocity, and uses it to report the aberration, give refocusing phases for arrays, and score alternative transducer poses.

On this page:

  • Main Settings: the switches and the files they write.
  • Phases by Transducer Type: the phases each transducer type can use, and the summary metrics.
  • Applying the Phases: running the acoustic simulation with the refocusing phases.
  • Pose Search: scoring poses around the planned one from the same reverse run.
  • Pose Workflow: search, forward verification, and final run in one call.
  • Run Time and Memory: run time and memory of the reverse run.
  • Assumptions and Limits: where the method does not apply.

Experimental

This feature is new and not yet validated against forward simulations. Treat its predictions as a ranking signal and check any pose or phase set you intend to use with a regular acoustic simulation.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When the focus through the skull is weaker or shifted and you want to correct phases (arrays) or choose a better pose (single element or annular array).
  • Before you start: A working acoustic simulation of the planned pose on a 3D Cartesian grid.

items.title: Main Settings
items.text:
time_reversal:
  enabled: true          # reverse run: aberration report and refocusing phases
  apply_phases: false    # true: use the time-reversal phases in the acoustic run
  placement_search:
    enabled: false       # true: score poses around the planned one (curved annular transducers, 3D grid)
  pose_workflow:
    enabled: false       # true: search, forward verification and final run in one call

Outputs per transducer: <prefix>_timereversal_summary.csv (metrics), <prefix>_timereversal_elements.csv (relative transfer, current and time-reversal phase, and the phase error with which each element arrives at the target), and, with a pose search, <prefix>_timereversal_poses_T<i>.csv.

items.title: Phases by Transducer Type
items.text:
Transducer Phases it can use Report Matrix array One per element: full refocusing All metrics; apply_phases uses the per-element phases Annular array (elem_n > 1) One per ring: the axially symmetric part of the correction All metrics; apply_phases uses the ring phases Single element None Coherence and predicted focal shift; nothing to apply

The animation below follows these steps on a cross-section: the planned drive through the skull, the reverse run from the target, and the refocused drive for each transducer type. The readouts use the same coherence and gain as the summary file. It is a schematic (2-D, straight rays with a delay and loss in the skull, slowed down); PRESTUS solves the full wave equation on the head model.

The metrics in <prefix>_timereversal_summary.csv:

  • coherence_elements: |Σ contributions| / Σ |contributions| over the elements with the current phases. 1 means the elements arrive in phase; refocus_gain_pressure = 1 / coherence_elements is what refocusing gains at the target.
  • coherence_aperture: the same over the whole surface, including the phase spread within each element, which no element phase can correct.
  • **shift__mm*: predicted focal shift with the current drive (axial > 0: deeper than the target), and with the time-reversal drive (shift_refocused_*).
How the reverse run works

A point source is placed at the target and run as a continuous wave on the grid, medium, and time axis of the acoustic simulation (reverse_point_source_field). By reciprocity, the pressure this source produces at a point x equals the pressure that a source at x would produce at the target (up to one constant common to all points). Recorded on the transducer surface, the reverse field therefore gives, for every element, the amplitude and phase with which it reaches the target through the skull (time_reversal_refocus):

G_e = sum over the element's grid points of (weight × reverse field)
pressure at the target = sum_e  A_e · exp(i·phi_e) · G_e

Driving each element with the phase −angle(G_e) (phase conjugation, i.e. time reversal) makes all elements arrive in phase: the largest target pressure the element amplitudes allow.

Predicted focal shift. Near the target the forward field is approximated by F(y) = Σ_j q_j · exp(−i·k·(|x_j − y| − |x_j − t|)): the skull aberration seen from the target is taken to be the same for points within a few millimetres of it (isoplanatic patch), and only the path through the tissue around the target changes. The peak of |F| gives the shift (predict_focal_shift). The approximation degrades with the size of the shift and the strength of the aberration: large predicted shifts mean "this pose focuses badly", not an exact focus position.

items.title: Applying the Phases
items.text: With apply_phases: true, the time-reversal phases replace the element phases before the acoustic simulation, and the source is rebuilt. The free-water baseline has already run with the geometric phases, so ISPPA targeting (target_isppa_wcm2) keeps the element drive amplitudes of the geometric drive: the refocused run shows what the same transducer output delivers when refocused. Whether your hardware can apply arbitrary phases (and with which precision) is not checked.

items.title: Pose Search
items.text:
For transducers that cannot refocus, the pose is the main lever: where the transducer sits on the scalp and where it points. With placement_search.enabled: true (curved annular transducers, 3D grid), the same reverse run also scores poses around the planned one. Each pose costs an interpolation of the recorded field, not a simulation.

The result is <prefix>_timereversal_poses_T<i>.csv, sorted by p_corrected_rel (target pressure relative to the planned pose with geometric aim), with the apex, corrected aim point, and target in grid voxels, T1 voxels, and RAS mm. A pose is set up as a manual placement with trans_pos = apex and focus_pos = aim point (placement.manual.coordinate_space: ras), and transducer.focal_distance_ep = the apex-to-aim distance minus the bowl depth (curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm). The acoustic run keeps the planned pose. To verify the best poses with forward simulations and run the chosen one, use the pose workflow, or set up a pose by hand with time_reversal_pose_parameters(parameters, pose_row). In the Nexus, Results ▸ Poses ▸ Use this pose… creates a follow-up config at the selected pose (Follow-up runs).

time_reversal.only: true stops the run after this stage (no water baseline, acoustic, or thermal simulation), for a report or pose table on its own.

Candidate poses and scoring

Candidates (reciprocity_pose_candidates): beam directions tilted from the planned one up to max_angle_deg, in steps of angle_step_deg, all aimed at the target. For each direction the exit plane sits placement.skin_gap_mm off the scalp (heuristic, MNI, PlanTUS, and TUS_entry placements) or at the planned pose's gap (manual and Localite), so the required focal depth changes with the direction. Where the scalp curves, the bowl is moved outward until its surface overlaps the scalp no more than the planned bowl does (push_mm in the pose table), so all poses are seated alike. A single element cannot steer: its apex is placed at the curvature radius from the target instead, and its aim correction is lateral only. With jitter_mm (one or more distances, e.g. 0.5 or [0.5 1 2 5]), the planned pose with its apex moved by each distance is scored too (rows of kind jitter), the local search often run with forward simulations. jitter_mode: grid moves the apex ± along each grid axis, as when editing voxel coordinates; jitter_mode: scalp slides the transducer over the scalp perpendicular to the beam in 8 directions and seats it against the scalp, which suits shifts beyond about 1 mm. Poses whose surface overlaps the head by more than the planned surface does plus 2 % of its points are dropped (inside_fraction); the planned pose is always kept. The reverse run records the field over the region these poses cover.

Scoring (reciprocity_score_poses): for each pose, the surface is sampled (annular_aperture_points) and the target pressure is a sum over the reverse field there. Per pose:

  • target pressure and coherence with geometric aim and steering;
  • predicted focal shift;
  • aberration-corrected aim: aim and steer at target − predicted shift (tilting the bowl about its apex), repeated aim_iterations times, so that the predicted focus lands on the target; the target pressure after this correction ranks the poses;
  • the gain ring refocusing would add.

Grid. The simulation grid ends close to the planned transducer, so tilted poses can lie outside it. The reverse run of a pose search therefore uses its own grid: the full grid (also with a partial acoustic FOV, whose crop the forward run keeps), padded with water on the sides the candidate poses need (the log reports the padding). The padding makes the reverse run larger, and so longer, than the forward run.

items.title: Pose Workflow
items.text:
time_reversal.pose_workflow.enabled: true turns a run into the whole placement workflow, in one call of prestus_pipeline_start (pose_workflow_pipeline). It needs one curved annular transducer (ring array or single element) and a head model (simulation.medium: layered). The placement_search settings apply; placement_search.enabled is set by the workflow.

  1. Search (<affix>_posesearch): the reverse run on the full grid scores the candidate poses; no forward simulation.
  2. Verify (<affix>_pose<id>_<geo|aim>): forward runs, acoustics only, of the planned pose (the reference, aimed at the target) and the n_top best poses by predicted target pressure after aim correction, plus the pose ids in poses. aim sets the aim of each run: corrected (at the aberration-corrected aim point; the planned pose is then run with it too), geometric (at the target), or both. verify_fov: partial (default) runs them on an acoustic FOV around each beam. The poses run are listed in <prefix><affix>_poseverify_selection.csv.
  3. Results and final run: per verification run, the mean intensity in a sphere of target_radius_mm around the target and the distance of the −3 dB focal centroid and peak from the target (axial and lateral), next to the predicted values, in <prefix><affix>_poseverify_results.csv. The runs are ranked by rank_by (target_intensity or focus_error), among those within max_focus_error_mm of the target if set; the log reports the rank agreement between predicted and simulated intensity. With final_run: true, the best pose then runs on the full grid with the configured modules (thermal, report): <affix>_posebest.

On MATLAB the stages run one after the other. On SLURM or qsub, each stage is submitted: a small CPU job after the search job submits the verification runs, and another after those (whether they succeeded or not) collects the results and submits the final run. This needs a cluster that lets jobs submit jobs. A stage whose outputs exist is skipped unless io.overwrite_files: always, so calling the workflow again after a failure continues where it stopped.

The verification and final runs place the transducer as a manual placement in RAS mm (apex = trans_pos, aim point = focus_pos), with the focal depth of the pose:

  • a drive from the calibration library (transducer.serial) is resolved again for the pose's focal depth (calibrated phases and amplitudes);
  • inline ring phases are replaced by geometric steering to the aim point in water, the drive the pose scores assume;
  • a single element has no phases; its poses already place the geometric focus on the target or the corrected aim point.

The runs keep the config's intensity setting. With target_isppa_wcm2, each run is scaled to the same free-water ISPPA, so the simulated intensities compare poses at the same device setting; the predictions compare them at the same element drive. The two differ where the poses' focal depths differ much (the free-water focal intensity changes with steering depth).

Cost: one reverse run (as long as a full-grid acoustic run, more memory: search_memorylimit), n_top + 1 (or twice that with aim: both) partial-FOV forward runs, and one full run.

items.title: Run Time and Memory
items.text:
One k-Wave run per distinct target, about as long as the acoustic simulation (longer by the padding of a pose search), recording the pressure time series (grid.steady_state_num_periods periods) at the sensor points: the transducer surface (refocusing), plus the candidate region (pose search). Scoring takes seconds per pose.

Memory stays below that of the acoustic simulation: the forward source is released during the stage and rebuilt afterwards, the padded grid reuses the forward source's element weights (no second source is built), and the recording is reduced to one complex amplitude per point in blocks, without a double-precision copy (0.5 mm head runs of the forward simulation peak at 25–31 GB).

items.title: Assumptions and Limits
items.text:
• Linear, fluid acoustics. With acoustic_backend: kwave_elastic the reverse run uses the fluid medium (warning). jwave forward runs use the same medium, so the k-Wave reverse run applies.
  • The transducer surface lies in one medium (coupling water); k-Wave scales a pressure source by the local sound speed.
  • Cartesian grids only (no axisymmetric runs).
  • Not with acoustic_backend: babelbrain, which has its own refocusing (babelbrain.do_refocusing, phased-array presets only).
  • The pose search ignores calibrated phase offsets of the library entry (it steers geometrically in water) and treats each pose as a rigid bowl. The verification runs use the library drive, so they include the offsets.
  • The pose scores interpolate the recorded field (cubic) at the transducer surface; at ~7 points per wavelength the interpolation error is about 1 % of the target pressure, the size of the differences between ±0.5 mm poses.
References: related work and benchmarks
  • Pinton (2026), Whole-skull acoustic transparency from a single time-reversal solve for reciprocity-based transducer placement and aperture optimization in transcranial focused ultrasound, arXiv:2609.27852: the same principle (one time-reversal solve, then placement, aperture, and orientation searched on the recorded map), with Fullwave 2 on a CT skull.
  • BabelBrain refocusing: phase correction for phased arrays from a back-propagated field (babelbrain.do_refocusing).
  • SCOUT (2024, PMC11592240): position of a single-element transducer optimised with repeated forward k-Wave simulations.
  • Park et al. (2019), Comput Methods Programs Biomed 179: placement by the lowest average reflection coefficient along straight beam lines (no wave simulation).
  • PlanTUS: geometric placement criteria (skull angle, thickness, distance).

items.title: Transducer Definition
items.text:
The transducer definition sets the source of the simulated pressure field: its frequency, element geometry, drive amplitude and phases, and its position relative to the target. The simulated focus position, focal size, and intensity follow from these fields. For a device in the transducer library, transducer.serial fills them in; this page explains each field and how to define a device the library does not hold.

On this page:

  • Transducer Fields: the fields of a transducer and a full inline definition.
  • Amplitude and Phases: the drive, set by the focal depth setting and target ISPPA, and the calibrated phases and amplitudes behind it.
  • Transducer and Focus Positions: the transducer and focus positions.
  • Transducer-Target Distance: exit-plane and bowl distances to the focus.
  • Annular Array: ring geometry, including flat elements.
  • Matrix Array: element layouts, steering, and its beam-axis constraint.

At a glance

  • When you need it: When your device is not in the transducer library, or to understand the fields the library fills in. With transducer.serial you rarely set these yourself.
  • Before you start: The geometry of your device (from the manufacturer).

items.title: Transducer Fields
items.text:
A transducer comes from the shipped transducer library (transducer.serial: geometry, phases, and drive are filled in) or is defined in full in the study config. Every field is listed in the parameter documentation.

A full definition of an annular array, bypassing the library:

transducer:
  serial: IS_PCD15473_01001
  type: annular
  freq_hz: 300000.0
  focal_distance_ep: 60.0
  annular:
    elem_n: 10
    elem_id_mm: [10.0, 22.1, ...]
    elem_od_mm: [21.1, 28.8, ...]
    curv_radius_mm: 100.0
    dist_geom_ep_mm: 92.7

The fields fall into three groups:

Group Fields Where described Type and geometry type (annular or matrix), freq_hz, and the sub-struct of that type (annular or matrix) Annular definition, matrix definition Drive and steering focal_distance_ep and target_isppa_wcm2; calibrated annular.elem_phase_deg and annular.elem_p_amp (advanced); matrix arrays steer automatically Amplitude and phases Position and target trans_pos, focus_pos, focal_distance_ep, or focal_distance_bowl Transducer and focus positions, Transducer-target distance

items.title: Amplitude and Phases
items.text:
An annular array is driven by two settings: the focal depth setting (transducer.focal_distance_ep) steers it, and the target free-water ISPPA (transducer.target_isppa_wcm2) sets the drive level. PRESTUS derives the element phases and amplitudes from them:

  • With a library serial, from the device's calibration entry at that depth (the transducer library).
  • Without one (custom geometry), geometric steering phases to that depth (compute_phases, as a library device's geometric baseline) and a nominal uniform drive, which ISPPA targeting then scales. Flat rings (curv_radius_mm: .inf) need element phases.

The element values are advanced settings, for a drive found by calibration against free-water hydrophone measurements:

  • transducer.annular.elem_p_amp: amplitude of the acoustic source per element (Pa). Without a target ISPPA (target_isppa_wcm2: []) it sets the drive level and is required.
  • transducer.annular.elem_phase_deg: phase of the acoustic source per element (degrees). Replaces the steering to the focal depth setting.

Note

Per-element calibration of phases, gains, and drive against axial hydrophone profiles (the transducer library) is implemented only for annular arrays. Matrix arrays can instead get a steering correction, which scales the element amplitudes by the measured focal-peak factor at each steering target. For matrix arrays, PRESTUS computes the phase of each element from transducer.trans_pos and transducer.focus_pos. Calibrated phases (one per element) can replace the geometric phases via transducer.matrix.elem_phase_override_deg.

items.title: Transducer and Focus Positions
items.text:
See transducer placement for how a position is chosen.

  • transducer.trans_pos: position of the transducer bowl (XYZ; T1 voxels by default, or RAS/MNI mm via placement.manual.coordinate_space). Used for placement and for the phase calculation of matrix arrays.
  • transducer.focus_pos: position of the stimulation target (XYZ; same coordinate space as trans_pos). Defines the focal point and the automatic steering of matrix arrays.

In water simulations with annular arrays, the placement is determined from the edge of the PML layer.

Positions in mm for phantom and water simulations

For phantom and water simulations the transducer and focus positions can be given in millimetres rather than voxel indices, with two optional config fields:

Field Description trans_pos_mm Transducer position in mm from the centre of grid voxel [1, 1, 1] ([x, y, z]; 0 mm = voxel 1). Converted to voxel indices at runtime as round(mm / grid.resolution_mm) + 1. focus_pos_mm Focus position in mm from the centre of grid voxel [1, 1, 1] ([x, y, z]). Same conversion applies.

These fields are resolution-independent: the same config works unchanged when grid.resolution_mm changes. When both voxel-index and mm fields are present, the mm fields take precedence. Phantom NIfTI outputs reuse the input header, so world-space orientation and voxel dimensions stay consistent across all pipeline stages.

items.title: Transducer-Target Distance
items.text:
The figure shows the PRESTUS definitions for annular transducer distances. Specify one of the two fields. Without either, PRESTUS computes a geometric distance from trans_pos and focus_pos, if both are set.

  • focal_distance_ep: expected distance from the transducer exit plane to the stimulation focus (mm). This often corresponds to the focal depth setting of the driving system or the transducer calibration (BabelBrain's TPO distance). The exit plane lies curv_radius_mm − dist_geom_ep_mm in front of the bowl apex; dist_geom_ep_mm is BabelBrain's NaturalOutPlaneDistance.
  • focal_distance_bowl: expected distance from the transducer bowl to the stimulation focus (mm). Computed internally from focal_distance_ep, dist_geom_ep_mm, and curv_radius_mm.

items.title: Annular Array
items.text:
An annular array consists of concentric ring-shaped elements on a spherically curved surface. All elements share one acoustic axis, so focusing is axial only. Lateral steering is not possible; the transducer must be repositioned to change the target.

Use an annular array when your hardware is a single-focus or multi-ring bowl transducer with calibrated per-element amplitudes and phases. This is the simpler and better-validated configuration.

Element geometry is defined by inner and outer diameters (elem_id_mm, elem_od_mm) and bowl curvature (curv_radius_mm). Each element has an independent pressure amplitude (elem_p_amp) and phase (elem_phase_deg), calibrated empirically. PRESTUS includes a calibration pipeline for annular arrays that matches the simulated pressure to free-water measurements.

items.title: Flat Elements
items.text:
curv_radius_mm: .inf makes the elements flat, e.g. a plane piston (the ITRUSST benchmark's 20 mm source). The face lies at trans_pos, normal to the trans_pos → focus_pos direction, and is also the exit plane (bowl depth 0); focus_pos only sets the beam direction. Supported with the kWaveArray source (grid.use_kWaveArray: 1):

Grid Element Rings (elem_id_mm > 0) 2D axisymmetric line across the axis (addLineElement) yes 2D line normal to the beam no 3D disc (addDiscElement) no (single disc)

Not supported: the makeBowl source (use_kWaveArray: 0), BabelBrain, transducer calibration, and the placement planners, which assume a bowl.

items.title: Matrix Array
items.text:
A matrix array consists of many small elements on a curved or flat surface. Each element is driven with an independent phase delay, so the focus can be steered electronically in three dimensions without moving the transducer.

Use a matrix array when your hardware supports electronic steering (e.g. a phased array system) or to simulate volumetric targeting without repositioning the transducer. The focal pressure a steered array delivers can be calibrated against hydrophone measurements over the steering range: see Steering correction of matrix arrays.

Phase delays are computed from the geometry of each element, trans_pos, and focus_pos; no manual phase input is required. elem_phase_override_deg replaces them with calibrated phases.

Matrix element layout and shape
  • Element positions are defined analytically (Fibonacci, Fermat spiral, or rectangular grid) or loaded from a coordinate file.
  • Element shape is rectangular (rect), circular (disc), or curved (bowl). The aperture of disc/bowl elements is equal-area to elem_width_mm × elem_height_mm unless elem_diameter_mm is set.
  • For curved arrays, curv_radius_mm and dist_geom_ep_mm define the bowl geometry used for visualisation and offset calculations.
  • Flat arrays (is_curved: false) have every element facing +z and need rect or disc elements; their coordinate file is in the transducer frame (origin at the array centre).
  • Rectangular elements laid out in more than one orientation take a per-element rotation from the coordinate file (extract_from_file.rot_col).
  • An optional Clover configuration replicates the array into a multi-aperture arrangement of n_leaves leaves on a parent bowl (ROC_parent), az_sep_deg apart (default 360 / n_leaves) and tilted by elevation_deg (default: the smallest non-overlapping tilt).

items.title: Beam Axis Constraint
items.text:
Element orientation and phase delay computation (create_matrix_karray) assume that the transducer's natural beam axis is aligned with the grid +Z direction. This holds for the standard single-transducer placement (transducer at one face of the grid, firing toward the target). In multi-transducer configurations where a matrix transducer fires along a different axis (e.g. a second transducer opposing the first along −Z), element normals and phase delays are computed incorrectly. Annular transducers are not affected. A matrix bilateral setup would need the beam direction derived from (focus_pos − trans_pos) rather than hardcoded to [0, 0, 1] in create_matrix_karray.

KWaveArray vs. simple elements

source_create builds the acoustic source for k-Wave simulations in one of two ways:

  1. Realistic kWaveArray elements (use_kWaveArray = 1, recommended). Uses the k-Wave kWaveArray class to define elements via physical parameters (position, radius, apodisation) rather than discrete grid voxels. Elements render smoothly at any grid resolution. Independent per-element delays and weights enable dynamic focusing. Element overlap is handled through weighted contributions. Supports annular rings, axisymmetric 2D simulations, matrix arrays, and GPU acceleration.
  2. Simple custom elements (use_kWaveArray = 0). Creates bowl-shaped (3D) or arc-shaped (2D) pressure source regions per element with the k-Wave makeBowl function. Each element receives an identical continuous wave (CW) signal. Suited to uniform single-element setups. Grid discretisation can introduce staircasing artefacts in the source mask.

items.title: Transducer Library
items.text:
A simulation reproduces a real device only if it uses that device's ring geometry, phases, and drive. PRESTUS ships a static library that holds these settings for each supported transducer and driving-system combination, fitted to free-water hydrophone axial profiles where profiles exist, so that a study names the device and a focal depth instead of entering element settings. You can refine an entry against your own hydrophone measurements (Calibration).

On this page:

  • Using a Library Entry: selecting an entry, the lookup order, how phases and drive are computed, and the entry schema.
